#### PHOTO-BOX-PATTERN — Lid motif and pattern hollowing (LuBan: Inner pattern)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Box, inner pattern (§3.2.4, PDF p.49–52). An "intrude" option was announced on 2 Aug 2025 (blog: box-intrude-inner-pattern; video l1EzpLK9jjg "LuBan Box intrude inner pattern", title only). The manual, dated 19 Aug 2025, does not list it, so its Box text predates the option (our reading).
- **What it makes:** Uses the features inside the box outline (§3.2, Fig. 67) on the lid or the whole box (§3.2.4, Figs. 72 and 74, PDF p.49–52). The options:
  - ignore them;
  - extrude them up from the lid;
  - indent them into the lid, plus a separate piece that fits the indent;
  - cut them through the lid (hollow lid);
  - hollow the whole box in their shape (hollow box).
- **Fabrication:** 3D print.
  - Print an indent lid flipped, with the indent facing the bed, and set the pattern depth to one layer height (§3.2.4, PDF p.50).
  - Two-colour lid, in the slicer, with the flipped lid and inner pattern aligned (§3.2.4, PDF p.51):
    1. Delete the lid and generate G-code for the pattern.
    2. Restore the lid, delete the pattern, set Z hop to the pattern depth and generate G-code for the lid.
    3. Print the pattern and leave it on the bed.
    4. Print the lid on top of it. Z hop lifts the nozzle on travel so it doesn't drag across the printed pattern.
  - The two prints can use different filament colours (Fig. 73, PDF p.51).
  - Pushing a separately printed pattern into the lid is hard: "a 3D printed object is usually a bit larger than its digital model due to a shell printed around it", and no tolerance is applied to the pattern (§3.2.4, PDF p.50).
- **Inputs:** The inner-pattern polygons from PHOTO-BOX: holes in the template's shape, or disjoint features inside an auto-generated boundary (§3.2, Fig. 67, PDF p.47–48).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inner pattern | `motif_mode` | What to do with the inner features | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `ignore`) | `ignore`, `extrude`, `indent`, `hollow_lid`, `hollow_box` (§3.2.4); `intrude` (blog only; meaning UNCONFIRMED) | §3.2.4 (PDF p.49–51); blog: box-intrude-inner-pattern |
| pattern depth ("the depth of the pattern") | `motif_depth_mm` | Height of an extruded pattern, or depth of an indent | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED. Advised: one layer height for the overprint method (§3.2.4); a bit less than the thickness for a box light, e.g. 4 mm at 5 mm (§3.2.8) | §3.2.4 (PDF p.50); §3.2.8 (PDF p.55) |
| — (LuBan applies no tolerance here) | `motif_fit_tolerance_mm` (AD3D-only) | Clearance on the separate pattern piece so it presses into the indent | (suggest: same as `fit_tolerance_mm`) | ≤ 0 | §3.2.4 (PDF p.50) says the tolerance is not used; AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D-only) | `motif_islands` | What to do with pieces that would float in a hollow lid | (suggest: `bridge`) | `keep` (warn), `bridge`, `drop`, `separate_part` | AD3D proposal; LuBan warns only in prose (§3.2.4) |
| — (AD3D-only) | `motif_bridge_mm` | Width of the bridges that tie islands to the lid | (suggest: 1.2 mm) | > 0 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D-only) | `motif_min_feature_mm` | Features thinner than this after offsetting are reported, and optionally kept at this width | (suggest: 0.8 mm) | ≥ 0 | AD3D proposal; addresses the feature loss described in §3.2.4 (hollow box "low-resolution") and §3.2.8 (LuBan may "remove the inner pattern completely") |

- **Outputs:**
  - ignore, extrude, hollow lid, hollow box: base + lid. Implied, not stated: only indent's part count is given. Fig. 74 shows a grey base and a blue lid for both hollow options (PDF p.52).
  - indent: three models, the base, the lid and the inner pattern (§3.2.4, PDF p.50; §3.2.8, PDF p.55).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - extrude and indent take a pattern depth (§3.2.4, PDF p.50). Fig. 72 (PDF p.50) shows extrude (raised) and indent (recessed, with the separate pattern piece in red).
  - indent gives three models, and the tolerance is not applied to the inner pattern (§3.2.4, PDF p.50).
  - hollow lid: the lid gets a hollow pattern, and "some parts of the pattern may not be connected to the boundary of the lid" (§3.2.4, PDF p.51); the triangle in Fig. 74 left looks like such a floating piece (PDF p.52; our reading). In that figure the template's white features (Fig. 67 second column) are cut through and the dark gaps between them stay as lid strips (our reading).
  - hollow box: the box is hollowed in the pattern's shape. The result depends on the box's X/Y size and its thickness: at a fixed X/Y, a large thickness gives a low-resolution pattern and a small thickness a high-resolution one (§3.2.4, PDF p.51; Fig. 74 centre and right, PDF p.52).
  - Nested boxes change the pattern's shape as they shrink (§3.2.5, Fig. 75, PDF p.51–52).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - Export lid and pattern as one multi-part 3MF, aligned and flipped. A multi-material printer, or one filament change at the layer above the pattern, then prints the two-colour lid as a single job instead of LuBan's four-step delete/slice/Z-hop routine (§3.2.4).
  - Optional insert clearance on the pattern piece. LuBan applies no tolerance, so the manual warns that pushing a printed pattern into the lid is "difficult" (§3.2.4).
  - Island handling for hollow lids: highlight floating pieces and offer bridge, drop or separate part. LuBan only warns in prose (§3.2.4).
  - A feature-loss report highlights pattern features that vanish at the current thickness or nesting level, so the user sees why the "resolution" drops (§3.2.4 hollow box; §3.2.8 outline image).
  - `motif_depth_mm` defaults to one layer height from the printer profile, as the overprint method needs (§3.2.4; PLAN §4 profiles).
  - Live preview while dragging depth and thickness (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - extrude: union the pattern prisms onto the lid's top face. indent: subtract the same prisms (depth d) from the lid; the insert is those prisms offset by `motif_fit_tolerance_mm`.
  - hollow lid: subtract through-prisms, then label connected components to find islands.
  - hollow box: one cavity per pattern region, offset inward by a thickness-driven amount, with walls between them. The negative offset (Clipper2) makes small regions vanish, which matches the manual's thickness/resolution remark.
  - manifold for the booleans; `validate()` on every output (PLAN §1).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-BOX-LID).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Meaning of "intrude", which appears only in the blog and a video title. (suggest: the pattern grows downward from the lid's underside into the box, keeping the top flat; check against video l1EzpLK9jjg.)
  - Hollow box details: the offset per side, and whether the lid and floor open over the pattern regions (Fig. 74 centre and right show pattern-shaped openings through the top).
  - Whether extrude adds the pattern depth to the Table 1 height; whether an indent may cut through the lid.
  - Whether a pattern can go on the base or the lid underside.
  - Pattern depth default and limits.

#### PHOTO-BOX-NESTED — Nesting box set (LuBan: Nested box)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Box, nested box = yes (§3.2.5, PDF p.51–52). Added in blog: box-3rd-release.
- **What it makes:** A set of boxes that fit inside one another, generated "until the size of the innermost box cannot be reduced further" (§3.2.5, Fig. 75, PDF p.51–52).
- **Fabrication:** 3D print, each box as its own base and lid; Fig. 75 shows three boxes, each with its own lid and pattern (PDF p.52). No further print notes.
- **Inputs:** Same as PHOTO-BOX.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| nested box | `nested` | Generate a nested set | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: off) | yes, no | §3.2.5 (PDF p.51); blog: box-3rd-release |
| nested box clearance | `nested_clearance_mm` | Extra shrink per level, on top of the thickness | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: ≥ 0.3 mm) | §3.2.5 (PDF p.51) |
| — (AD3D-only) | `nested_max_levels` | Cap on the number of boxes | (suggest: none, i.e. until the size runs out) | ≥ 1 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D-only) | `nested_motif_fit` | How the pattern follows the shrinking boxes | (suggest: `offset`, as LuBan) | `offset` (LuBan behaviour; features erode), `scale` (pattern scaled to each lid, keeps its look) | AD3D proposal; §3.2.5 notes the pattern changes shape |

- **Outputs:** One base + lid (+ pattern) per level; file naming UNCONFIRMED. LuBan users inspect the parts with Object → Select and the toolbar slider (§3.2.5, PDF p.51).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - At each level the box size and the lid indent (basic and twist) are shortened by the thickness and the nested box clearance. Generation stops when any of these values reaches zero or below. The inner pattern's shape changes as the boxes shrink (§3.2.5, PDF p.51).
  - Fig. 75 shows three levels; each smaller lid keeps fewer pattern features, and the smallest keeps only a few (PDF p.52; our reading).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - The number of levels and each box's size update live while dragging clearance or thickness (PLAN §4).
  - A parts list with per-level names (`box1_base`, `box1_lid`, …) and an explode view, instead of the Object → Select slider (§3.2.5).
  - An option to scale the pattern per level instead of eroding it; Fig. 75 shows the pattern fading level by level.
  - Levels are built in parallel with rayon, can be cancelled, and export as one multi-part 3MF (PLAN §4).
  - Guaranteed fit: each inner box's exterior is checked against the next outer box's interior plus the clearance, and any failure is reported. The manual describes no such check (§3.2.5).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** Loop: E(k+1) = offset(C(k), −clearance) (Clipper2); the next box's exterior height ≤ its parent's interior height − clearance; Dl(k+1) = Dl(k) − (T + clearance) (manual rule; per side or total UNCONFIRMED). Stop when the polygon is empty or any height or indent ≤ 0. Run PHOTO-BOX per level, in parallel (rayon).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-BOX-PATTERN).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Whether "shortened by the thickness and the nested box clearance" is per side or total, and how Z shrinks.
  - Whether the tolerance also applies between nested boxes.
  - Default clearance; whether the lid type can differ per level.
  - Output file names.
  - Related videos (titles only): aUYYmJLh1_k "LuBan Box v3" and zNQmO7yB0-A "LuBan Box v3 amendment"; the outer size and nested options arrived with Box 3rd release (blog: box-3rd-release).

#### PHOTO-BOX-LIGHT — Glow box / letter lamp (LuBan: Box light)

- **LuBan path:** A recipe on top of Box, with two variants (§3.2.8, PDF p.53–56):
  1. Simple: import a letter template into Box (Fig. 79, PDF p.54).
  2. Stronger: File → Invoke 2D window → File → Open (the template) → Tool → Geometry → Distance transform (keep the default threshold, OK) → Tool → Threshold → Between, enter "-1000 0" → File → Export → PNG. Then import the outline image into a new Box with the inner size option and the inner pattern set to indent (steps 1–6, Figs. 80–81, PDF p.54–55).
- **What it makes:** A hollow letter- or shape-box that holds LEDs, wires and batteries and glows (Fig. 78, PDF p.53).
  - Simple variant: thin walls (1–3 mm) let light through the whole box (§3.2.8, PDF p.54).
  - Stronger variant: thick walls, with the letters as thin indented windows in the lid inside a border (§3.2.8, Figs. 80–81, PDF p.54–55). The manual says only that "the indent on the lid must be thin enough for light to penetrate"; that light then shows mainly through the letters is our reading.
- **Fabrication:** 3D print the base and lid only; the inner pattern part is not printed (Fig. 81, PDF p.55).
  - Simple variant: walls of 1–3 mm, "otherwise, light cannot penetrate through the box" (§3.2.8, PDF p.54).
  - Any lid type works. Flat and inlay are preferred because they print with little support, and a flat lid with magnet sinks opens and closes easily (§3.2.8, Fig. 81, PDF p.55–56).
  - Translucent filament is implied by Fig. 78 but not stated (UNCONFIRMED).
- **Inputs:** A B/W template. The manual's example writes "S" and "G" in Microsoft Word in Verdana Pro Black, with condensed spacing so the letters overlap, then zooms in, takes a screenshot and crops it (§3.2.8, Fig. 79, PDF p.54).
- **Parameters:** Recipe values; the manual adds no new settings.

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inner / outer size | `size_ref` | inner: the inside follows the letters and the outside grows by T. outer: the outside equals the letters and the inside shrinks by T | recipe: either (simple variant); inner (outline variant) | `inner`, `outer` | §3.2.8, Fig. 79 (PDF p.54–55) |
| box thickness | `wall_mm` | Wall thickness; thin for the simple glow, thick for the outline variant | recipe: 1–3 mm (simple variant); "as great as you want", e.g. 5 mm (outline variant) | — | §3.2.8 (PDF p.54–55) |
| inner pattern = indent | `motif_mode` = `indent` | Turns the letters into thin windows in the lid | recipe | — | §3.2.8 (PDF p.55) |
| pattern depth | `motif_depth_mm` | A bit less than the thickness, leaving a thin skin, e.g. 4 mm for a 5 mm thickness | recipe | — | §3.2.8 (PDF p.55) |
| lid type | `lid_style` | Any; flat or inlay preferred; Fig. 81 shows flat with magnet sinks | recipe | — | §3.2.8, Fig. 81 (PDF p.55–56) |
| Distance transform threshold (2D window dialog) | — (not needed in AD3D) | Threshold that separates object from background before the distance map | "Use the default value" (value UNCONFIRMED) | — | §3.2.8 step 4 (PDF p.54) |
| Threshold → Between "-1000 0" | `outline_mm` (AD3D-only replacement) | Keeps background within 10 px of the letters, since one pixel = 100 distance units, giving a 10-px outline; "-200 0" gives 2 px | LuBan recipe: 10 px. AD3D: (suggest: 2 mm) | LuBan: "You can use different values"; AD3D: > 0 | §3.2.8 step 5 (PDF p.55) |
| — (AD3D-only) | `glow_mode` | `walls` (simple thin-wall box) or `windows` (thick box with letter windows in the lid) | (suggest: `windows`) | `walls`, `windows` | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D-only) | `skin_mm` | Material left under each letter window (= T − pattern depth) | (suggest: 1 mm, the skin left by the manual's example of a 4 mm depth at 5 mm thickness) | > 0 | AD3D proposal; §3.2.8 (PDF p.55) |
| — (AD3D-only) | `text`, `font` | Letters typed directly in any installed font | — | — | AD3D proposal; replaces the Word screenshot step |
| — (AD3D-only) | `cable_hole_d_mm` | Optional hole in the base wall for a power lead | (suggest: 0 = none) | ≥ 0 | AD3D proposal; the recipe keeps wires and batteries inside with no exit |

- **Outputs:** Base, lid and inner-pattern files; print the base and lid only (§3.2.8, Fig. 81, PDF p.55).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Simple variant with outer size: the interior shrinks by the box thickness, which the manual accepts "since it is only for housing some LED lights" (§3.2.8, PDF p.54).
  - Distance map: positive on the object, negative on the background, and more negative further from the object; one pixel length is 100 units (§3.2.8 steps 4–5, PDF p.54–55).
  - The outline image has two polygons close together: the outer one (the expanded letters) and the inner one (the letters). Use inner size. With outer size, shrinking the outer polygon may affect the inner one and "cause LuBan to remove the inner pattern completely" (§3.2.8, PDF p.55).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - A one-step "glow box" preset: text or image in, outline offset set in mm (Clipper2), lid windows and skin thickness set directly. No Word screenshot, distance transform or pixel thresholds (§3.2.8).
  - AD3D builds the border from the letters in mm, so it knows the border width. It picks inner size automatically and warns before any offset would cut into a letter, instead of LuBan removing the inner pattern completely (the outer-size failure in §3.2.8).
  - Backlight preview: an LED inside the box shows the glow through walls or windows at the chosen skin thickness, reusing LITH-BACKLIGHT-PREVIEW (PLAN §4 realistic preview).
  - An optional cable hole and a magnet flat lid (Fig. 81) in the same preset.
  - Live preview and 3MF parts as in PHOTO-BOX (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** Letter polygons L come from font outlines (e.g. the `ttf-parser` crate; our choice) or a traced image. Boundary B = offset(L, +`outline_mm`) (Clipper2). Then run PHOTO-BOX with P = B, inner pattern = L, `motif_mode` = indent and `motif_depth_mm` = T − `skin_mm`, which yields base + lid. The backlight preview comes from M2.
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-BOX-NESTED; a preset on PHOTO-BOX; backlight preview from M2).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - The default threshold of the distance-transform dialog.
  - Recommended filament (white or translucent) and LED type; neither is stated.
  - Related, not covered here: Pandora, "a light box to cast a shadow image" whose cover "can be a customized lithophane" (blog: pandora; video 7IM0AVVqhjw, title only), is a separate Projection generator (PROJ-PANDORA). Video BWqCCePXOIM "Text outline" (title only) may show a newer outline workflow.

#### PHOTO-BOX-LITHO — Lithophane-lid box (LuBan: Box lithophane)

- **LuBan path:** A recipe combining Box and the stencil lithophane (§3.2.9, PDF p.56–58):
  1. Photo magic → Box with an inlay lid and the outer size option, then save the model (Fig. 84 left, PDF p.56).
  2. In a 3D window, open the lid file → Edit → Environment → Orthogonal / Perspective projection (or F1) → View → Viewing angle → Z (click again if the letters face away) → View → Zoom → In → View → Copy → File → Invoke 2D window → View → Paste → Tool → Threshold → Manual → Tool → Data → Invert (if the letters aren't already white) → File → Export → PNG (Figs. 84 right and 85, PDF p.56–57).
  3. File → Create → Lithophane, stencil shape, with the new template and the photo (§2.19); set the lithophane's size X equal to the box's (§3.2.9, PDF p.57).
  4. Click Save model and open the saved lid.stl → Mesh → Statistics, and read bounding cube X and Y (Fig. 86). Open the lithophane → Object → Transform, choose "Size" (not "Scale") and "Flexible" (not "Fixed"), set X and Z to the lid's X and Y → OK → File → Export → STL (Fig. 87, PDF p.57–58).
- **What it makes:** A shaped light box whose lid is a lithophane cut to the lid outline and lit from inside (Figs. 82 and 88, PDF p.56–58).
- **Fabrication:** 3D print the base and the lithophane, then fit lights, wires and batteries (§3.2.9, PDF p.58). Lithophane print tips are in §2.23 (LITH-PRINT-TIPS), which prefers printing a flat lithophane vertically.
- **Inputs:** A template image and a photo (Fig. 83, PDF p.56).
- **Parameters:** Recipe values.

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lid type = inlay | `lid_style` = `inlay` | The lithophane replaces an inlay lid | recipe | — | §3.2.9 (PDF p.56) |
| outer size | `size_ref` = `outer` | Keeps the box from growing beyond the template | recipe | — | §3.2.9 (PDF p.56); conflicts with the Table 1 note (PDF p.48) |
| stencil lithophane: template, photo, Center X and Y, Photo scale | `litho_*` (keys from LITH-STENCIL) | Lithophane cut to the new template; centre and scale place the photo | see LITH-STENCIL | — | §3.2.9 (PDF p.57); §2.19 (PDF p.35) |
| lithophane size X | — (AD3D: derived automatically) | First set equal to the box's size X | recipe | — | §3.2.9 (PDF p.57) |
| Object → Transform: Scale or Size = Size; Fixed / Flexible = Flexible; X, Z | — (AD3D: automatic) | Resizes the lithophane to the lid's bounding X and Y; the lithophane lies in XZ, the lid in XY | Fig. 87 example: X 197 → 194.6, Y 6.32, Z 110 → 107.2 | — | §3.2.9, Fig. 87 (PDF p.58) |
| Mesh → Statistics: Bounding cube X / Y / Z | — (AD3D: live dimensions) | Lid size check | Fig. 86 example: X 194.6 [4.694, 199.3], Y 107.2 [4.898, 112.1], Z 5 [25, 30]; cube volume 1e+05; mesh volume 6.597e+04; 7702 vertices, 15396 triangles | — | Fig. 86 (PDF p.58) |
| — (AD3D-only) | `lid_kind` | Solid lid or lithophane lid | (suggest: `solid`) | `solid`, `lithophane` | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D-only) | `litho_fit_tolerance_mm` | Clearance of the lithophane in the inlay recess | (suggest: = `fit_tolerance_mm`) | ≤ 0 | AD3D proposal |

- **Outputs:** The base from Box plus the resized lithophane STL. The original lid is not printed (§3.2.9, PDF p.58).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The new template's letters are thinner than the original, because the inlay lid shrinks them by half the box thickness (§3.2.9, PDF p.57).
  - The box thickness and the new template's boundary can make the lid and the lithophane mismatch in size, hence the Statistics + Transform step (§3.2.9, PDF p.57–58). In the example the lithophane came out 197 × 110 mm against a 194.6 × 107.2 mm lid, 2.4 mm and 2.8 mm too large (Figs. 86–87; our arithmetic).
  - The lithophane lies in XZ and the lid in XY, so the lid's X and Y map to the lithophane's X and Z (§3.2.9, PDF p.58).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - One generator: `lid_kind` = lithophane builds the lithophane directly on the exact inlay-lid polygon, with fit tolerance, so outline and size match by construction. This replaces the screenshot, threshold, invert, stencil, Statistics and Transform steps (§3.2.9).
  - Photo position, scale and rotation are dragged directly on the lid in the viewport, with the backlight preview (LITH-BACKLIGHT-PREVIEW; PLAN §4).
  - One 3MF holds the base and the lithophane lid, each in the print orientation its source recommends: the lithophane upright as the lithophane section advises (§2.23), the base on its floor.
  - Works with inner or outer size and with any lid style that leaves a flat panel, which removes the Table 1 vs §3.2.9 conflict.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** The inlay recess polygon from PHOTO-BOX-LID feeds the M2 stencil-lithophane generator, which clips the heightfield to that polygon and closes the edge with walls along the traced boundary (Clipper2); `validate()` on the result. LuBan later added dedicated lithophane boxes (blog: lithophane-15th-release; lithophane-17th-release for CMYK; lithophane-18th-release for double-sided; vector-image-template for DXF/SHP templates); LITH-BOX covers those.
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-BOX-LIGHT), after M2's stencil lithophane.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Table 1 forbids outer size with an inlay lid, yet this recipe uses both. Which one reflects current LuBan?
  - Whether LuBan's later "lithophane box" (blog: lithophane-15th-release; video 87n4-Jll8vA "LuBan lithophane v15 Box", title only) replaces this recipe, and what its parameters are (LITH-BOX).
  - Lithophane thickness, resolution and positive/negative for the lid: per LITH-COMMON and LITH-STENCIL. Fig. 87's example lithophane is 6.32 mm thick (its Y size); the default is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Whether the lithophane needs its own clearance in the inlay recess. The recipe sizes it to the lid's bounding box only (Figs. 86–87).
  - Related videos (titles only): jDU-OmR4-fo "LuBan Lithophane v17 CMYK Stencil and Box lithophane", Z0HPp89BDXQ "Vector image template for lithophane box", pOBxn7Mc-xw "LuBan Lithophane v18 Double-sided lithophane box".

### Photo magic: Cell, Cutter, Extrusion (3.3–3.5)

These three Photo magic methods turn one image (or, for Cutter and Extrusion, a line of typed text) into simple 2.5D parts. **Cell** makes a perforated halftone plate whose hole sizes follow the photo's brightness, for 3D printing or laser. **Cutter** makes a cookie cutter, optionally with an imprint pattern that is either built in or printed as a separate stamp. **Extrusion** raises a silhouette or text as a keychain, sign or tilted statue on a base. Loading the image, converting it to black and white, and Save model are shared steps specified in PHOTO-COMMON (part 3). Cutter reuses the Box method's inner-pattern rules (§3.4 intro → §3.2; see PHOTO-BOX and PHOTO-BOX-PATTERN in part 3). The manual shows a parameter panel for only one of these methods, Cutter (Fig. 64, PDF p.46). So the LuBan labels in the Cell and Extrusion tables are the manual's section-heading and body-text terms, not verified panel labels. Most defaults and ranges below are UNCONFIRMED, and numbers taken from figure captions are recorded as examples, not as defaults. Even the Fig. 64 values may not be factory defaults, because LuBan saves "parameters in many functions" in MU Setting.txt and reloads them at start (§1.6, PDF p.14).

#### PHOTO-CELL — Perforated Plate (LuBan: Cell)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Cell (manual §3.3, PDF p.59). The Photo magic panel and its method drop-down are introduced in §3 and Fig. 64 (PDF p.46).
- **What it makes:** A flat plate pierced by a regular grid of holes inside a solid border. Each hole's size follows the photo's local brightness. Seen in front of a contrasting background, or used as a mask that casts a shadow picture onto a wall, the holes read as a halftone image (§3.3, §3.3.1; Fig. 89–91, PDF p.59–60).
- **Fabrication:**
  - Method: "3D printed or laser engraved" (§3.3 intro); "laser cut or engraved" (§3.3.3).
  - Printing: set the thickness to a whole number of slicer layers (§3.3.3).
  - Laser: the sheet sets the thickness, and LuBan uses the value only to render the result (§3.3.3).
  - Resolution: the finest detail the machine can make, e.g. 0.2 mm for a 0.4 mm nozzle (§3.3.6).
  - Display: bright cells in front of a black background, or dark cells in front of a white one (§3.3.1). It can also be projected onto a wall as a negative to form a positive image (§3.3.1; Fig. 91, PDF p.60).
  - User examples (our reading of the photos):
    - Fig. 89 (PDF p.59) is a black print with square holes, held in front of a light striped background. The face reads as a positive, which is the "dark cells on a white background" situation.
    - Fig. 91 (PDF p.60) is a clear, light sheet with a fine cell pattern. It looks engraved rather than cut through, and is held in front of the wall it projects onto.
  - Print orientation is not stated (UNCONFIRMED; suggest: flat on the bed).
- **Inputs:**
  - One photo, loaded with "Select photo" → "Browse" (§3 intro; Fig. 64, PDF p.46). Formats and colour-to-grey conversion follow PHOTO-COMMON.
  - Cell is not among the methods that §3 says need a manual black-and-white conversion first (balloon, box, cutter, extrusion, morphing; §3 intro, PDF p.46). Its figures also turn grey levels into graded hole sizes (Fig. 90, Fig. 94, Fig. 95). So it uses intensity, not a binary mask (our reading).
  - Conflicting hint: §3.9 (PDF p.76) tells Pillar users not to convert to black and white, unlike "the methods presented in the earlier sections", where manual conversion "may help you obtain better results than leaving LuBan to do the auto conversion". Read literally, that includes Cell (§3.3). We trust the graded figures over that general sentence (UNCONFIRMED).
- **Parameters:** No Cell panel screenshot exists. Apart from "Select photo" (§3 intro, Fig. 64), the labels below are the manual's heading terms (§3.3.1–3.3.6).

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: not stated for Cell. Save model is shared behaviour (PHOTO-COMMON). An STL for printing is our guess; any 2D file for laser is UNCONFIRMED.
    - Closest precedents: the next Photo magic method, Layering, saves each layer "as a DXF and an SVG file for laser cutting, and also ... as an STL file for 3D printing" (§3.6, PDF p.68).
    - The 2019 Chinese decks show Mesh → LuBan methods writing DXF and SVG for laser, STL for printing, and LuBan's own SHP format (luban-docs §5).
  - AD3D, print: one closed body, `<name>-cell.stl` or `<name>-cell.3mf` (units in mm).
  - AD3D, laser or CNC: `<name>-cell.svg` and `<name>-cell.dxf`. These have a `cut` layer (outer border, plus every hole when `laser_holes` = `cut`) and an `engrave` layer (the holes when `laser_holes` = `engrave`, and e.g. a label). Cut paths are kerf- or tool-compensated.
  - The parameters are saved in the `.ad3d` project.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - X and Y are locked to the photo's aspect ratio. In LuBan a typed size applies only after pressing Enter (§3.3.2, §1.8).
  - Hole size follows brightness, and Bright/Dark sets the direction (Fig. 90). Fig. 94 uses the Dark mapping: big holes in the bright face, small or no holes in the dark hair (our reading).
  - Cell pitch is 10 × resolution (§3.3.6). Fig. 95 shows about 20×30, 10×15 and 5×7 cells on the same plate at resolution 0.5, 1 and 2. That matches a pitch of 10 × resolution on a plate of about 100 × 150 mm (our inference). How LuBan fills the leftover when the size isn't a whole number of cells is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Hole limits in Fig. 95 (our pixel measurement of a 600 dpi render, UNCONFIRMED):
    - In the resolution-1 and resolution-2 panels, the largest holes leave a web of about 0.11 × pitch, i.e. about one resolution unit.
    - The smallest holes in the resolution-1 panel are about 0.12 × pitch wide.
    - Some dark cells in the resolution-2 panel have no hole at all.
    - So resolution may act as both the minimum web and the minimum hole. Hole widths in the resolution-1 panel look continuous, not stepped by one resolution unit.
  - All three hole shapes sit on a square grid (Fig. 94, our reading).
  - The border is a solid frame (§3.3.4). Fig. 93 (right) has a much wider frame, but the two renders differ in perspective, so whether the plate grows or the hole field shrinks cannot be read from it (UNCONFIRMED).
  - For laser, thickness affects only the rendering (§3.3.3).
  - The structure "can also be used as a negative and projected onto a wall to form a positive image" (§3.3.1, Fig. 91). For cut-through holes, a positive projection needs hole area that grows with brightness, which is the Dark mapping (our reasoning). Which mode the manual means is UNCONFIRMED, and Fig. 91 may show an engraved sheet rather than holes.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview while dragging.** Low-res while the slider moves, full-res on release, within the ≤ 50 ms preview budget (PLAN §4; CLAUDE.md). LuBan needs Enter after every typed size (§3.3.2, §1.8).
  - **Cell size and finest detail are set separately.**
    - LuBan ties the cell to 10 × resolution (§3.3.6). A 0.2 mm resolution therefore means 2 mm cells, and 10 mm cells mean a 1 mm resolution.
    - AD3D takes `cell_size_mm` from the user and `min_web_mm` / `min_hole_mm` from the machine profile, and shows how many tone levels result.
    - On an FDM printer the XY limit is about one extrusion width (≈ 0.4–0.45 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle), not half the nozzle as §3.3.6 suggests. The profile accounts for this (ours).
  - **Tone-true hole sizing.**
    - Hole area, not side length, is made proportional to the target tone, after gamma and contrast (the Squama image controls of PLAN §4, reused). LuBan states no tone-to-size rule (§3.3).
    - Sizes are clamped by the minimum hole and minimum web.
    - Optional error diffusion keeps smooth gradients even when there are only a few tone levels.
  - **Viewing preview.**
    - The plate is rendered in front of a black or a white backdrop, and as a shadow cast by a point light onto a wall at a set distance (the Fig. 91 use).
    - The user picks Bright/Dark by looking at the result, and the modes are named by what they look like ("holes look dark" / "holes look light"). LuBan only names the two situations (§3.3.1).
  - **Honeycomb lattice option.** Fig. 94 shows only square-grid layouts, even for hexagonal holes. Hex packing gives more even webs (ours), and PLAN §4 already plans hexagonal cells for Squama.
  - **Laser- and CNC-ready 2D export** with separate cut and engrave layers (PLAN §4). LuBan only says thickness is used for rendering (§3.3.3) and never says which 2D file it writes.
    - `laser_holes` chooses whether holes are cut through or engraved as dots. §3.3 offers "laser engraved" but never says how it differs from cutting.
    - Cut paths are offset by kerf/2: holes inward, the outer border outward. Engrave paths are not offset (research 08 §2.6).
    - The thickness shown in the preview comes from the measured sheet thickness.
    - CNC: inside corners of square and hex holes are rounded to at least the tool radius, and holes smaller than the tool are dropped. Dogbones aren't needed, because nothing fits into these holes (ours; see research 08 §2.7 on CNC inside corners).
  - **Thickness snaps to a whole number of layers** using the printer profile; §3.3.3 leaves this arithmetic to the user.
  - **Size snaps to whole cells plus the border**, so there are no clipped cells at the edges.
  - **Robust, scriptable output** (PLAN §4; CLAUDE.md):
    - watertight by construction, checked by `validate()` and a test with random parameters;
    - 3MF with units, and streamed STL;
    - a CLI batch mode, e.g. one plate for each photo in a folder.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Tones and hole sizes.**
    1. Convert to greyscale.
    2. Average each cell with a summed-area table to get a tone t ∈ [0,1].
    3. Hole coverage c = t for a `light` backdrop, or 1 − t for a `dark` one.
    4. Size each hole from its area: a square has side s·√c, a circle has r = s·√(c/π), and a hexagon follows its own area formula.
    5. Drop holes smaller than min_hole and cap sizes at s − min_web. With `dither` on, the difference goes into the error diffusion.
  - **Direct per-cell mesher,** like the Squama mesher (PLAN §2).
    - Each cell is a tile whose outer square (a hexagon for the hex lattice) shares vertices with its neighbours, with one hole in it.
    - The top and bottom caps are triangulated between the square and the hole. Hole walls are quads. Outer walls exist only at the border.
    - No booleans are needed and there are no T-junctions, and rows mesh in parallel with rayon.
    - When holes may touch (`min_web_mm` = 0), fall back to a Clipper2 union/difference followed by a 2.5D extrusion.
  - **2D export:** the same hole polygons, offset with Clipper2.
  - The core function is `perforated_plate(params, image) → Mesh | Paths`.
  - References:
    - research 04 §B.10: "Cell: halftone, with holes sized by intensity; resolution = cell/10";
    - research 04 §C: classical image processing, no ML;
    - research 03 §13: Clipper2 and manifold; research 08 §2.2: keep manifold for validation only, with a direct mesher as the default;
    - PLAN §1: the `image` and `clipper2` / `i_overlay` crates;
    - the same screening code can serve TOOL-HALFTONE and PHOTO-HALFTONE-3D (part 7).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after TOOL-TEXT-OUTLINE; PLAN §3 lists Cell in M5; research 04 §D rates Cell/Pillar low difficulty, 1–2). Our suggestion is to build it first within M5, because it reuses M1 Squama's image-to-cell averaging and its direct-mesher pattern.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Every default and range, and the exact panel labels. The manual has no screenshot of the Cell panel.
  - The full list of cell shapes. LuBan's Thermal net offers "Triangle, rectangle, hexagon, and circle" (video F20FZvL0r9g, transcript chunk [00:09]), but that is a different feature.
  - How tone maps to hole size (linear in side, area or radius?). Whether hole sizes are rounded to resolution steps, giving about 10 levels. "Resolution = cell/10" hints at this but doesn't say it, and the hole widths in Fig. 95 (centre) look continuous (our measurement).
  - Whether a minimum hole or web is enforced, and whether touching holes merge. Fig. 95 suggests both minimums are about one resolution unit (our measurement).
  - Whether Cell binarizes its input at all. Its figures are graded, but §3.9 (PDF p.76) implies that every method before Pillar uses LuBan's auto black-and-white conversion.
  - Whether the border sits inside Model size X/Y. How a size that isn't a whole number of cells is handled (Fig. 95 right).
  - Which mode the manual means for positive projection (§3.3.1).
  - What "laser engraved" (§3.3) produces: engraved dots on a sheet, as Fig. 91 may show, or cut-through holes.
  - LuBan's output files for laser (DXF? SVG?) and for print. Compare §3.6 Layering (DXF + SVG + STL) and luban-docs §5.
  - Units: thickness and border appear only as bare numbers in the captions; mm is assumed.
  - Related LuBan features covered in part 7:
    - the later 3D "Halftone" model (blog: halftone-2; entry PHOTO-HALFTONE-3D);
    - the 2D halftone tools for laser engraving (blog: halftone, halftone-line, halftone-1; entries TOOL-HALFTONE, TOOL-HALFTONE-LINE);
    - bitmap-to-vector conversion "for the ease of laser cutting" (blog: bitmap-to-vector-conversion; entry TOOL-VECTORIZE in part 7). Whether LuBan users route Cell output through it is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Sources to check:
    - Video z20h8VsRwHE "LuBan Cell" (2:48) has no transcript in the repo; watch it to confirm the panel and defaults.
    - Videos TIwrBJQrCGM and JwrUiKXbC5M "LuBan Halftone" (11:17, 10:11; titles only), to see how Halftone differs from Cell.
    - Blog: _cell has only a one-line description ("Generate a cell structure to represent a photo").

#### PHOTO-CUTTER — Cookie Cutter (LuBan: Cutter)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Cutter (manual §3.4, PDF p.61). The panel is shown in Fig. 64 (PDF p.46).
- **What it makes:** A 3D-printable cookie cutter whose blade follows the outline of a black-and-white image or of typed text. An optional inner pattern imprints the cookie; it is either built into the cutter's base or printed as a separate stamp (§3.4, §3.4.4; Fig. 96–104, PDF p.62–65; blog: cookie-cutter, cookie-cutter-2nd-release, cookie-cutter-4th-release).
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D print (blog: cookie-cutter, "3D printable cookie cutter").
  - Fig. 96 (PDF p.62) shows a user's printed outline-only cutters in light filament, next to the decorated cookies they cut (our reading).
  - Wall stack (§3.4.5, Fig. 102): a thin blade at the top starts the cut, the cutter wall is then pushed into the dough, and a thicker base wall stops the cut.
  - The renders show the base on the bed and the blade up (Fig. 99–103, our reading); print orientation is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Edge chamfer (§3.2.6, PDF p.52; §3.4.7):
    - a 45° chamfer removes the "extra material at an edge between the base and the wall due to upper layers compressing the base", which "may even cut one's finger";
    - it needs no support;
    - a few layer heights is enough.
  - Base holes let air out while cutting (§3.4.6).
  - A separate stamp is a second print. Its chamfer keeps it located against the cutter; "without the edge chamfer, the two parts may slide against each other" (§3.4.7, Fig. 104, PDF p.65).
  - Printed parts come out slightly larger than the model (§3.2.4, PDF p.50), which matters for the stamp fit.
  - Food safety and choice of material are not covered by the sources (UNCONFIRMED; the owner decides).
- **Inputs:**
  - A black-and-white image (§3 intro; blog: cookie-cutter), loaded with "Select photo" → "Browse" (Fig. 64). An image that was not converted by hand is converted by LuBan's "auto conversion" (§3.9 intro, PDF p.76; see PHOTO-COMMON).
  - Or typed text in a chosen font; "text symbols or even icons" are possible this way (§3.4.2, Fig. 98).
  - Multi-line text, special effects or overlapping letters have to be laid out elsewhere (e.g. MS Word), screenshotted, and loaded as an image (§3.4.2).
  - The inner pattern is any feature inside the outer boundary. If no boundary encloses everything, LuBan generates one and treats every disjoint feature as inner pattern (§3.4 → §3.2; Fig. 67, PDF p.48).

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan, outline-only and integrated: one body. Since the 3rd release, "all components ... are generated as one body" (blog: cookie-cutter-3rd-release).
  - LuBan, separate: two objects, the outline cutter and the inner pattern (blog: cookie-cutter-4th-release; Fig. 100 right, Fig. 104).
  - LuBan file names and formats are UNCONFIRMED. Save model is in PHOTO-COMMON. For comparison, the Box method's Save model writes "several files", among them a `lid.stl` (§3.2.9, PDF p.57).
  - AD3D: `<name>-cutter.stl`, plus `<name>-stamp.stl` in separate mode. Alternatively one `<name>-cookie-cutter.3mf` with one or two named objects, in mm. Optionally, a rendered cookie-preview image.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - **Inner pattern and automatic boundary** follow the Box method (§3.4 → §3.2, Fig. 67). In Fig. 67 (second column) the automatic boundary is a convex polygon (our reading).
  - **Clearance** (§3.4.4, Fig. 101):
    - Each feature gets an outline offset by the clearance.
    - At clearance 1 the offsets don't meet, and LuBan uses "a bounding convex polygon as the mutual outline".
    - At 3 they meet and form an "oddly shaped" outline.
    - At 7 the outline looks natural.
    - The manual warns that changing the clearance "may produce some unexpected results".
  - In Fig. 64 (sunflower, Integrate) and Fig. 100 left (outline only), the outline is a convex polygon even around a complex shape. Fig. 100 centre (integrated) and Fig. 101 at clearance 3 and 7 instead show non-convex outlines that follow the pattern (our reading).
  - **Walls** (§3.4.5):
    - The blade is thinner than the cutter wall, and the base wall thicker.
    - Blade height is 1.5 × blade thickness (hard-coded). Cutter-wall height is inner size Z. Base height is the base thickness.
    - In Fig. 102 all three thicknesses are measured from one dashed line on the inner face. So the walls grow outward and the inside stays at the set size (our reading).
  - **Base holes** (§3.4.6; blog: cookie-cutter-3rd-release; Fig. 103):
    - only with integrate or separate;
    - placed automatically;
    - none are made if there is no room, even when the option is on;
    - they don't interfere with the pattern;
    - they sit in the base plate when integrated and in the stamp plate when separate (our reading).
  - **Flip** (§3.4.1): a cutter produces a mirrored dough shape, and "Yes" mirrors about Y (Fig. 97). The "Hello" text in Fig. 98–99 is mirrored as seen from the blade side, i.e. flip was on (our reading).
  - **Text:** LuBan sets the cutter text in the chosen font (Fig. 98). Multi-line, special-effect or overlapping text needs MS Word, a screenshot, and "Select photo" (§3.4.2).
  - Text-box values (sizes, depths, the text string) update the display only after Enter. Drop-downs and radio buttons such as Inner pattern and Flip photo update at once (§1.8, PDF p.15–16).
  - **Release history:**
    - inner pattern (blog: cookie-cutter-2nd-release);
    - one body, clearance, and holes kept clear of the pattern (blog: cookie-cutter-3rd-release);
    - separate objects (blog: cookie-cutter-4th-release);
    - stopper (blog: cutter-stopper), released after the Aug 2025 manual.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview while dragging** (PLAN §4). LuBan warns that clearance changes give unexpected outlines (§3.4.4), which is slow to explore when every value needs type-then-Enter (§1.8).
  - **A robust shared outline.**
    - By default it is a morphological closing: offset by +r, then by −r, with round joins. r is raised automatically until the outline is a single loop.
    - Offset-union (LuBan-like) and convex hull remain available as explicit choices.
    - The outline is drawn live over the image.
    - LuBan jumps to a convex polygon or produces notched shapes (§3.4.4, Fig. 101).
  - **Cookie preview.**
    - The imprinted cookie is rendered as it will look.
    - `mirror` defaults to on, and the preview shows why.
    - LuBan renders only the cutter (Fig. 97–104), so the user has to reason out the mirror from §3.4.1, and Fig. 64 shows "No" selected.
  - **Text and vector input.**
    - Multi-line text, letter spacing, merging of overlapping letters and outline stroke are built in.
    - SVG/DXF outlines can be imported directly, with no threshold step.
    - LuBan needs MS Word plus a screenshot for these (§3.4.2).
  - **Unambiguous size.** `size_reference` plus live dimension labels. LuBan's X/Y change meaning depending on whether a pattern exists (§3.4.3, Fig. 99).
  - **Explicit wall stack.**
    - Blade height is editable, defaulting to 1.5 × thickness (hard-coded in LuBan, §3.4.5).
    - The "should" rules (blade < cutter wall < base wall) become live warnings. Further warnings fire when the cutter wall is thinner than 2 extrusion widths or the blade thinner than 1, using the machine profile (ours).
    - Total height (flange + wall + blade) is shown and checked against the printer bed.
  - **Separate-stamp fit.** An explicit `stamp_fit_mm` in the chamfer seat, using one fit tolerance from the printer profile (LuBan's own advice in §3.2.7). Printed parts come out larger (§3.2.4), and no fit tolerance is documented for the cutter (UNCONFIRMED).
  - **Visible vent holes.** Shown live and adjustable (min/max diameter, minimum ligament), with a message when none fit. LuBan simply omits them when there is no room, and the manual mentions no warning (§3.4.6).
  - **Validated output.**
    - Every output is checked as watertight with consistent winding, backed by a test with random parameters (CLAUDE.md). LuBan's cutter parts were disconnected until the 3rd release (blog: cookie-cutter-3rd-release).
    - Export is 3MF with named parts and units (PLAN §4).
  - **Projects and batch** (PLAN §4): presets (e.g. thin dough, fondant), undo/redo and project files, and a CLI batch, e.g. one cutter per letter of a word.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Image path:**
    1. Binarize (PHOTO-COMMON).
    2. Build a contour tree with marching squares and simplify it. vtracer (Rust, MIT; research 03 §5) is an alternative tracer.
    3. Classify the outer boundary and the inner pattern from the tree (§3.2 rule; research 04 §B.10).
  - **Text path:** glyph outlines of the installed system fonts, read by a TTF/OTF parser.
    - The crate is not chosen yet: `ttf-parser` is the choice proposed in PHOTO-BOX-LIGHT (part 3), and opentype.js in the UI is an alternative (research 08 §2.13 lists it).
    - Personal use, so AD3D reads system fonts and bundles none.
  - **Outline:** Clipper2 offset and union, then closing, with the convex hull as fallback (research 03 §13; PLAN §1 `clipper2` / `i_overlay`).
  - **Walls:**
    - outward offsets of the inner outline give the blade, cutter wall and base flange;
    - they are extruded as stacked 2.5D bands that share boundary loops, so the body closes without booleans.
  - **Inner pattern and chamfer:**
    - the pattern, clipped to the interior, is extruded on the base plate (integrated) or on a stamp plate (separate);
    - the chamfer is a two-level offset loft.
  - **Vent holes:** a distance transform of the plate area minus (pattern ⊕ margin) minus a rim margin, then greedy largest-circle placement.
  - **Mirroring** is applied to the polygons before building, with winding kept consistent.
  - **Checks:** a final `validate()`, with manifold for the union check where the bands meet the pattern.
  - The core function is `cookie_cutter(params, image | text) → [Mesh]`.
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-EXTRUSION; PLAN §3; research 04 §D rates Extrusion/Cutter/Box low difficulty, 1–2). Our suggestion: build it together with Box (§3.2), because both use the same contour, inner-pattern and outline module.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Panel labels for clearance, blade/cutter/base wall, base thickness, base hole and edge chamfer. What the row cut off at the bottom of Fig. 64 is (perhaps "Inner clearance", from the glyph tops; our reading).
  - All defaults and ranges. The Fig. 64 values (40, 10, Integrate, 7, Flip = No, Photo, Arial) are what that screenshot shows, not stated defaults. They may even be last-used values restored from MU Setting.txt (§1.6, PDF p.14).
  - Why Fig. 64 says "Width in X" / "Depth in Z" while the text says "Inner size X, Y, Z". Is inner size Y a separate field?
    - Fig. 64 shows Inner pattern = "Integrate", so it was taken on the 2nd cookie-cutter release (2019-11-21) or later (blog: cookie-cutter-2nd-release).
    - Its menu bar already has the Object menu, which the 2018–2019 Chinese decks show appearing only in a later build (luban-docs §2.1).
    - Whether it predates the Aug 2025 manual text's labels is UNCONFIRMED.
  - How the heights stack (base + wall + blade?). What Z measures when there is an inner pattern (Fig. 99 right: to the base plate or to the pattern top).
  - What Inner size X/Y mean when the image has an inner pattern but Inner pattern is set to ignore (§3.4.3 only distinguishes "no inner pattern" from "has an inner pattern").
  - What the stopper does (blog: cutter-stopper; video pn76-ca647s "LuBan Cutter Stopper", 3:55, no transcript in the repo). Get the transcript before implementing it.
  - Stamp fit tolerance in separate mode, and the rule for vent-hole size and placement.
  - The outline rule in outline-only mode (convex in Fig. 100 left).
  - Output file names and formats. Units: assumed mm (the manual gives mm only for the edge chamfer, Fig. 76).
  - Videos to watch (no transcripts in the repo):
    - 08zIxrljivI "LuBan Cookie cutter" (2:12);
    - CUNiL_8_I38 "LuBan Cookie cutter v3" (2:17);
    - kOAMuqSAYbs "LuBan Cookie cutter v4" (1:53);
    - possibly related: BWqCCePXOIM "Text outline" (9:04) and wDikiVpunws "Add background shape to an image" (3:15).

#### PHOTO-EXTRUSION — Silhouette Extrude (LuBan: Extrusion)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Extrusion (manual §3.5, PDF p.65).
- **What it makes:** A 3D model that extrudes a 2D pattern from a black-and-white image or typed text, or extrudes its background instead. The extruded slab can be raised, tilted, tapered and joined to an optional base by a swept support. Typical results are name keychains, desk signs and silhouette statues (§3.5–3.5.8; Fig. 105–111, PDF p.65–68; blog: extrusion).
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D print (the photos in Fig. 105 and Fig. 108).
  - The "support beneath an extrusion" (§3.5.7) is modelled geometry, the blue body in Fig. 107–110, not slicer support (our reading).
  - User prints in Fig. 105 (PDF p.65; our reading):
    - left: a single-colour "KEEP CALM AND FIGHT CROHN'S" sign with a crown icon, its letters raised on supports above a base;
    - centre: a round Medusa medallion;
    - right: eleven two-colour name keychains, orange base and black letters, each with a key ring through a hole at one end. Blog: extrusion-2nd-release adds "keychain hole and color".
  - In the printed examples the base is on the bed (Fig. 108, our reading); orientation is otherwise UNCONFIRMED.
- **Inputs:** A black-and-white image (§3 intro; an unconverted image goes through LuBan's auto conversion, §3.9 intro, PDF p.76), or text typed in directly (§3.5; §3.5.2 points to §3.4.2). The font and text controls are as in PHOTO-CUTTER. Positive mode extrudes "a 2D pattern" and Negative mode extrudes "the background of the pattern" (§3.5.1).
- **Parameters:** Manual Fig. 8 (§1.8, PDF p.15) is a screenshot of the Extrusion panel (Method = Extrusion, text "LuBan"), so the labels marked "verbatim from Fig. 8" are on-screen spellings and the values in the Default column are the values shown there. Whether those shown values are LuBan's defaults or the author's edits is UNCONFIRMED. Other labels are the manual's heading terms (§3.5.1–3.5.8) and Fig. 107's symbols.

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: UNCONFIRMED (Save model is in PHOTO-COMMON). Whether pattern and base are exported as separate coloured bodies is UNCONFIRMED (blog "color"; Fig. 105).
  - AD3D: `<name>-extrude.3mf`, with `pattern` and `base` as separate, named, coloured parts ready for multi-material printing, in mm.
  - AD3D: `<name>-extrude.stl`, one merged body.
  - AD3D: for two-colour prints on a single extruder, a note gives the Z height at which to change filament.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - X and Y are locked to the pattern's aspect ratio and update after Enter (§3.5.3, §1.8).
  - E_T is the slab thickness, E_L the vertical raise, and A the front-face angle (§3.5.4, Fig. 107).
  - Expansion is front face divided by end face (§3.5.5). Fig. 108 (our reading, PDF p.67):
    - At 0.5 the eagle face is small and the support flares out to a large footprint on a large hexagonal base.
    - At 1 the support keeps the eagle's cross-section.
    - At 3 the eagle face is largest and the support narrows to a small footprint on a visibly smaller base.
    - The overall model stays about the same size, so model size X/Y seems to bound the whole model, not the pattern alone (UNCONFIRMED).
  - Clearance is indicative and keeps the model size; more clearance means a smaller extrusion (§3.5.6, Fig. 109). The base stays the same size in all three renders, and at clearance 0 the tilted wing overhangs the base rim (our reading).
  - "Void" disables the support (§3.5.7). With void and a raised or tilted face, the slab would float; LuBan's handling of this is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Base thickness 0 removes the base, after Enter (§3.5.8).
  - The keychain hole goes at a corner, and none is made if no corner has room (§3.5.8).
  - Negative mode (Fig. 106 right, PDF p.66): the background, including the white gaps between the scrolls inside the heart, is extruded as a plate that fills the whole base rectangle with no visible margin. The pattern itself (the black heart outline and scrolls) becomes openings with walls running down towards the base (our reading).
  - Positive mode (Fig. 106 centre): the heart pattern stands on vertical supports above a larger grey rectangular base (our reading).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview while dragging** (PLAN §4). LuBan needs Enter after typed changes, even to drop the base (§3.5.8, §1.8).
  - **Absolute clearance** in mm, plus an explicit `size_reference`. LuBan's clearance is only "indicative" (§3.5.6).
  - **Keychain hole placement.** Automatic or dragged by hand, with a check on the ring wall. When no corner fits, an external loop tab is added. LuBan simply leaves the hole out, and the manual mentions no warning (§3.5.8).
  - **Multi-colour output.** Base and pattern are separate coloured parts in the 3MF (PLAN §4: 3MF with multiple parts), or a colour-change height is given for single-extruder printers. This matches the two-colour tags in Fig. 105; LuBan's "color" is undocumented (blog: extrusion-2nd-release).
  - **Printability check.** Overhang shading on tilted faces and arc risers, and a warning when "void" leaves a floating slab (§3.5.4, §3.5.7).
  - **Native multi-line text and layout.** Under §3.4.2 (which §3.5.2 points to), multi-line text has to come in as an image, so a sign like the multi-line "KEEP CALM" one with a crown icon in Fig. 105 (left) has to start as an image (our reading).
  - **Batch name tags.** Read names from a list and nest the tags onto the printer bed (PLAN §4 batch/CLI and printer profiles; APP-BATCH and APP-NEST in part 1). Fig. 105 (right) shows 11 tags.
    - Whether LuBan's Batch menu (visible in Fig. 64) covers Photo magic is UNCONFIRMED. Neither the manual nor the Chinese decks describe that menu (luban-docs §2.1).
    - The only batch feature the blog names is batch slicing of models (blog: batch-slicing).
  - **Validated output.** Watertight by construction, with a self-intersection check for large tapers or tight arc risers. `validate()` and a random-parameter test run on every output (CLAUDE.md). 3MF carries units.
  - **Explicit base shapes:** ellipse, regular n-gon and outline offset. Fig. 108–109 show bases like these, but §3.5.8 doesn't list the options.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Pattern:** polygons with holes, from binarized contours (PHOTO-COMMON) or glyph outlines.
    - Negative = base region minus pattern (Clipper2).
    - Fit the pattern to the size and clearance with a Clipper2 offset of its projected footprint.
  - **Slab:** the polygon extruded by E_T, tilted by A, and raised by E_L.
  - **Riser:**
    - copies of the slab's underside loop are sampled along a profile curve (vertical line, straight slant, concave arc or convex arc);
    - they are scaled from 1 at the slab to 1/expansion at the base;
    - neighbouring rings are joined by ruled quads. This is watertight because every ring is the same polygon, with the same vertex count, scaled.
  - **Base:** a rectangle with filleted corners (via offset), an ellipse, an n-gon, or an outline offset (closing), then extruded.
  - **Keyring hole:** the corner with the largest inscribed circle (from a distance field), then subtract the circle.
  - **Join and check:** join slab, riser and base on shared loops or with a manifold union, then `validate()`.
  - The core function is `silhouette_extrude(params, image | text) → [Mesh]`.
  - References:
    - research 04 §B.10: "Extrusion: with elevation, angle, taper 'expansion', base and keychain hole";
    - research 03 §13: Clipper2 and manifold.
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-PILLAR; PLAN §3; research 04 §D rates Extrusion/Cutter/Box low difficulty, 1–2). Our suggestion is to build it before Cutter, which reuses its text-to-outline code.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Whether the values shown in Fig. 8 (§1.8, PDF p.15) are defaults, and all ranges. Labels not visible in Fig. 8 are section-heading terms.
  - Fig. 8 has no "Round corner" row: it may be a later addition (Fig. 111 shows round corners) or sit below the panel's scroll (Fig. 8's panel has a scroll bar and ends at File size).
  - What A is measured from. Whether the pattern is rotated about X (so it looks shorter from above) or sheared.
  - How E_L, the support profile and expansion fit together geometrically. Which face is the "end" face (our reading: the one at the base).
  - What Model size X/Y measures (the pattern, the footprint, or the whole model as Fig. 108 suggests). How the indicative clearance maps to mm, and whether it acts on the support's footprint (Fig. 109 reading).
  - How the base follows the end face when expansion changes. Fig. 108 (right) shows a smaller base at expansion 3 (our reading).
  - The list of base shapes. Whether "round corner" is a number.
  - Keychain hole: which corner is tried first, and whether its size is a diameter.
  - What "color" means (blog: extrusion-2nd-release): a preview colour, as in the lithophane "filament color" (blog: lithophane-3rd-release), or coloured export, as in the OBJ of true-colour puzzles (blog: true-color-puzzle). LuBan's output formats.
  - Whether the background in Negative mode is bounded by the model rectangle or by the base shape. In Fig. 106 (right) the base is a rectangle, so the two coincide.
  - Units: assumed mm throughout; the section prints none.
  - Videos to watch (no transcripts in the repo):
    - K2kceUJeMkc "LuBan Extrusion" (2:30);
    - Qz0eCTxISIs "LuBan Extrusion 2" (4:04);
    - BayXxBGsKOk "LuBan Extrusion v3" (6:43);
    - possibly related: YOzsrsZzbYc "Make a coin from a photo" (2:50, title only). Fig. 105 (centre) is a coin-like medallion made with Extrusion, but the video's approximate date (~2019 in videos_dated.txt) may predate Extrusion (blog: extrusion, 2020-01-12).

### Photo magic: Layering, Morphing (3.6–3.7)

Layering builds a stack of flat layers from one or more photos (§3.6, §3.6.1). The top layer is the image's pattern, and every hole shrinks by a fixed offset in each layer below, which gives a stepped relief (§3.6.4; Fig. 115, PDF p.69). The layers are laser-cut from one DXF/SVG per layer or 3D-printed from STL (§3.6, PDF p.68). Morphing merges two or three photos, or typed text, into one model that shows a different image along each axis, or that shows the images as hollows in a cube (§3.7, §3.7.1, §3.7.2, PDF p.74). The manual states no defaults, ranges or units for either method, so every default here is UNCONFIRMED. Values seen in figures are example settings, not defaults. Shared Photo magic behaviour (method list, Select photo / Browse, black-and-white preparation, Enter to update, Save model) is specified in PHOTO-COMMON.

Figure and page numbers refer to "Hello LuBan.pdf" (Aug 2025). "Our reading" marks an interpretation of a figure, and "ours" marks an AD3D proposal; neither is a LuBan fact.

#### PHOTO-LAYER — Layered Cutout (LuBan: Layering)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Layering (manual §3 intro, PDF p.46; §3.6–3.6.6, PDF p.68–71).
- **What it makes:** A multi-layer model made from one or more photos (§3.6, §3.6.1; blog: layering, "Generate a multi-layer object from a photo"). The top layer is the photo's pattern. Each hole shrinks by the layer offset from one layer to the next, until no holes remain or the requested layer count is reached (§3.6.1, §3.6.4; Fig. 115, PDF p.69). An optional frame can surround the pattern (§3.6.5).
- **Fabrication:**
  - Laser: cut the per-layer DXF/SVG files. 3D print: use the STL files (§3.6, PDF p.68).
  - The user pieces in Fig. 112 (PDF p.68) and Fig. 120 (PDF p.71) look like laser-cut wood (our reading).
    - Fig. 112 (center) is photographed against a red-lit wall (our reading).
    - Fig. 112 (right) stands on a clear display stand. Its top layer is light and the lower layers are dark (our reading).
    - In Fig. 112, hearts on stems stick out past the triangular frame (our reading; see Clipping).
  - Glue, assembly and alignment method are not stated (UNCONFIRMED).
  - Our reading of §3.6.4 and Fig. 115: only holes change between layers, so every layer has the same outer outline. All three layers in Fig. 115 share one circular outline.
  - Printed as one body with the top layer up, the stack needs no supports. Each layer's solid lies entirely on the layer below it (our derivation from §3.6.4).
- **Inputs:** One or several photos (§3.6.1).
  - Black-and-white preparation is implied but not stated for Layering. The §3 intro (PDF p.46) names "a balloon, box, cutter, extrusion, or morphing" and leaves out layering. §3.9 (PDF p.76) refers to manual black-and-white conversion "in the methods presented in the earlier sections", which include §3.6. See PHOTO-COMMON.
  - Input formats for this method are not stated (UNCONFIRMED). AD3D: PNG/JPG, plus SVG/DXF vectors.

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: "Each layer is saved as a DXF and an SVG file for laser cutting, and also saved as an STL file for 3D printing" (§3.6, PDF p.68).
  - AD3D laser output: per-layer SVG/DXF, or nested sheets, with separate cut and engrave layers. Optionally a jig sheet and a one-page stacking guide (PDF assembly guides, PLAN §4).
  - AD3D print output: one watertight STL of the assembled stack, or a 3MF in mm with one object per layer (each with its own colour). Per-layer STLs are optional.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Disconnected inner patterns or features are ignored (§3.6, PDF p.68). In Fig. 113 (PDF p.69), concentric rings that do not touch give only the outer ring. Joining the rings with a cross keeps them all.
    - A second example (our reading): the cat photo in Fig. 125 (left, PDF p.73) has a separate eye dot, and the eye is missing from the generated structure in Fig. 126 (right, PDF p.74). The dot of the "i" in "Cutie" is joined to its stem in Fig. 125, and it survives.
  - The real number of layers can be smaller than requested: "When a layer has no holes, no more layers will be generated" (§3.6.1). Fig. 115 (PDF p.69) shows this; the text cites Fig. 114 by mistake. The top layer is the photo pattern, the middle layer has shrunken holes, and the bottom layer is solid.
  - Layer size X and Y keep the 2D pattern's aspect ratio. Change one, press Enter, and the other follows (§3.6.2). Text boxes need Enter; other controls update at once (§1.8, PDF p.15–16; also luban-docs Get started p.6).
  - Layer offset sets how much each hole shrinks per layer (§3.6.4). Figs. 117–118 also show steps along the inner edge of the frame band, so the frame's opening shrinks like any other hole (our reading).
  - Expansion resizes the frame. If it is too big, the frame "may be disconnected from the features", and then the features are ignored (§3.6.5).
    - So when the frame and the features separate, LuBan keeps the enclosing frame and drops the features, even when the features have more area. Fig. 113, where only the outer ring is kept, fits the same rule (our inference).
  - Round corner rounds the frame's corners. Clipping removes features outside the frame (§3.6.5, Fig. 118).
  - Solid base = Yes forces a solid base (§3.6.6). In Fig. 119 the holes are see-through with No and closed with Yes (our reading).
  - Each photo adds its own number of layers, stacked in the Layer order (§3.6.1). In §3.6.8 the original photo goes "on the top" as one layer above a shaped-frame image (see PHOTO-LAYER-SHAPED).
  - Manual errata: Fig. 113's caption says "Center right" twice. §3.6.1 cites Fig. 114 where Fig. 115 is meant. Fig. 125's caption repeats Fig. 124's (PDF p.73).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview:** dragging layer offset, layer count, expansion or size updates the preview at reduced resolution, then at full resolution on release (PLAN §4).
    - LuBan's text boxes, such as Layer size X and Y, need a typed value plus Enter (§1.8, §3.6.2).
    - Its spin boxes, such as Number of layers (Fig. 114), update at once (§1.8). The control types for Layer offset and Expansion are UNCONFIRMED.
  - **No silent drops:** islands are highlighted and counted before export, and `island_policy` chooses keep, bridge or drop. LuBan simply ignores them (§3.6, Fig. 113; §3.6.5).
    - In print output a kept island is always supported. Holes only shrink downward, so each layer contains the solid of the layer above (our derivation from §3.6.4).
    - In laser output a kept island becomes a separate nested part, and its outline is engraved on the layer below as a placement guide.
  - **Honest layer count:** the panel shows e.g. "requested 6, generated 3: no holes left after layer 3" instead of silently making fewer (Fig. 115).
  - **Laser-ready files:** each cut path is offset by kerf/2, outlines outward and holes inward. Layer thickness comes from the measured sheet thickness in the material profile. All layers are nested onto sheets of the profile size, with cut and engrave paths on separate layers. LuBan writes one DXF and SVG per layer (§3.6), and the manual mentions no kerf or nesting for Layering (research 08 §2.6, §2.9; PLAN §4).
  - **Alignment that works:** every layer shares the same outer outline. AD3D can emit a jig sheet with a pocket of that outline (plus clearance) that squares the stack during gluing, or hidden pin holes through every layer except the top.
  - **Smooth vectors:** the binarized photo is traced once into curves, and all offsets are done in mm with Clipper2, so edges stay smooth at any size. SVG/DXF input is accepted directly.
    - LuBan's blog reports "bumpy artifacts" from bitmap templates. It added DXF/SHP vector templates for stencil and box lithophanes only (blog: vector-image-template).
    - Vector input for Layering is not documented. Whether Layering's DXF/SVG output is smoothed is UNCONFIRMED.
  - **Better print output:** one watertight STL of the whole stack, or a 3MF with each layer as its own coloured object in mm, plus the Z heights at which to swap filament for a two-tone print. LuBan writes one STL per layer (§3.6; PLAN §4).
  - **Realistic preview:** per-layer material colours, an exploded-view slider, and a movable light beside or behind the stack to judge depth and shadow, like the lit display in Fig. 112. This extends PLAN §4's realistic preview, which names Squama and lithophanes.
  - **Fabrication checks:**
    - Bridges thinner than 2× kerf (laser) or the nozzle width (print) are flagged.
    - CNC paths get tool-diameter compensation, and holes narrower than the bit are flagged.
    - No dogbones are needed, because layers have no mating slots (research 08 §2.7; PLAN §4 machine profiles).
  - **Optional non-uniform steps:** `offset_profile` allows a different offset per layer. LuBan has one constant offset (§3.6.4).
  - **Projects, batch and speed:**
    - The photo list, per-photo layer counts, order and frame are saved in the project with undo/redo.
    - The CLI can batch a folder of patterns.
    - Per-layer offsets run in parallel with rayon, and jobs can be cancelled (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Trace:** binarize (PHOTO-COMMON), then trace to polygons with holes using vtracer (MIT; research 03 §5) or findContours-style border following plus Douglas–Peucker (research 04 §C). Scale to `size_x_mm`.
  - **Connectivity:** union with Clipper2, then classify components.
    - LuBan-compatible mode keeps the outermost component: the one that encloses the others, or the frame when there is one. This is our inference from Fig. 113 and §3.6.5; LuBan's exact rule is UNCONFIRMED.
    - Otherwise apply `island_policy`.
  - **Frame:**
    - Fit a circle or regular polygon around the features. Use the smallest enclosing circle, or the smallest enclosing regular n-gon with apex up as in Figs. 117–118 (a small LP over the n edge normals; ours).
    - Offset it by `frame_expansion_mm`. Round corners with a Clipper2 round-join offset.
    - Band = frame − inset(frame, `frame_width_mm`). Clipping = features ∩ frame.
  - **Layers:**
    - Layer j (j = 0 at the top): solid_j = outline − ⋃ inset(hole, j·`layer_offset_mm`), using Clipper2 negative offsets.
    - Stop after the first layer with no holes (§3.6.1).
    - `solid_base` appends a plain outline layer when the last generated layer still has holes. This is ours; whether LuBan adds a layer or fills the last one is UNCONFIRMED.
    - Research 04 §B.10 gives the general Photo Magic pipeline (threshold → contours → offset → extrude).
  - **3D:** each layer is an extruded polygon (manifold CrossSection extrude), so per-layer STLs are watertight by construction. The single-body STL is the manifold union (research 03 §13).
  - **Nesting:** an SVGnest-style no-fit-polygon nester or packingsolver (research 03 §12). sparrow alone only solves strip packing (research 08 §2.9).
  - **Speed and tests:**
    - While dragging, trace a downsampled image to stay within the ≤ 50 ms budget (CLAUDE.md).
    - A proptest over random blob images, offsets and layer counts must pass `validate()`.
    - criterion benchmarks run at preview and full resolution (PLAN §5).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-CELL; PLAN §3 lists Layering under Photo Magic; CLAUDE.md build order step 5).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - No defaults, ranges or units are stated for Layer size, Layer thickness, Layer offset or Expansion.
    - The 2018 Mesh → LuBan panel asks for a unit (m, dm, cm, mm or inch) on entry (luban-docs Get started p.3–p.4).
    - Whether Photo magic has a unit setting is UNCONFIRMED. The luban-docs decks cover no Photo magic.
  - What are the exact panel labels and control types (text box or spin box) for Layer size, Layer thickness, Layer offset, Frame shape, Expansion, Round corner, Clipping and Solid base? Only Fig. 114 shows part of the panel.
  - What is the full Frame shape list (rectangle? hexagon? none/original?), and what does Expansion = 0 mean (frame touching the features)? Fig. 117 right still shows features attached at +3 (our reading), so 0 is probably not "inner edge touching".
  - Is the frame band width fixed, user-set or derived from the pattern? The manual gives no width.
  - Is Round corner on/off or a radius, and what radius?
  - When features are disconnected, which component survives? §3.6.5 and Fig. 113 suggest the enclosing component (the frame or the outer ring), not the largest (our inference).
    - Do features that touch only at a corner pixel count as connected (4- or 8-connectivity)?
  - Which colour counts as material?
    - In Figs. 112–113, dark lines on white become material.
    - In Figs. 121–124, white features on grey become material.
    - The manual's figures appear to draw black as grey. Fig. 63 (PDF p.46) shows its "black and white image" in grey, and Fig. 121's grey template background is the black (value 0) of step 6.
    - Hypothesis (ours): the colour touching the image border is background. See `material_polarity` and PHOTO-COMMON.
  - Is the top row of Layer order the top layer, as §3.6.8's "Set the original photo on the top" suggests? Is the initial order by file name, as in poly-face lithophanes (§2.15.1, PDF p.26)?
  - With several photos: must they have the same pixel size? Which photo sets the aspect ratio? Does the offset restart for each photo's group?
  - Is Solid base an extra layer, or does it replace the last one? Does it count toward Number of layers?
  - Is STL output one file per layer only, or is there also a combined model? How are the files named, and how is the export started (§3.6 names no button)?
    - The 2018 Stack method writes a "<model>_<Method>_<HH-MM-SS>" folder with Cut, Asm and STL subfolders. "Asm" holds an assembly drawing for each layer (luban-docs Get started p.9–p.10).
    - Whether Layering does the same is UNCONFIRMED (see PHOTO-COMMON Save model).
  - Does LuBan's Layering apply kerf, nest layers, or add labels or alignment aids? None are mentioned.
  - Does Layering trace its DXF/SVG with the same converter as the 2D window's "Tool -> Convert -> Bitmap (binary image) -> Vector" (blog: bitmap-to-vector-conversion)?
  - Related videos (titles only; no transcripts in the repo): zbALjR4R3BE "LuBan Layering" (9:20); MZWfjyJSqYE "Photo display stack" (6:25; relation UNCONFIRMED).
