#### PHOTO-LAYER-SHAPED — Layered Cutout with Template Frame (LuBan: Arbitrary-shaped frame)

- **LuBan path:**
  - §3.6.7 (PDF p.71–73) gives ten numbered steps: run LuBan, File → Invoke 2D window, File → Open, then seven Tool-menu operations (steps 4–10).
  - Then File → Invoke 3D window, and apply the Layering method (File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Layering) to the combined image (§3.6.7 last paragraph, PDF p.73).
  - §3.6.8 (PDF p.73–74) reuses the workflow for a photo with an inner pattern.
- **What it makes:**
  - A layered cutout whose outer edge follows any silhouette. A template shape is filled with a feature pattern and edged with an outline band (Figs. 120, 124).
  - In §3.6.8 the original photo becomes a single top layer over the shaped frame, e.g. "Cutie" text on a cat (Fig. 126).
- **Fabrication:** As PHOTO-LAYER. Fig. 120 (PDF p.71) shows a dog and a butterfly by a LuBan user that look laser-cut and stacked (our reading).
- **Inputs:**
  - A black-and-white template image and a feature image (Fig. 121, PDF p.71).
    - The template's shape is white in Fig. 121, and step 6 makes black 0 and white 255.
    - Stencil lithophanes use the same convention: "black pixels indicate background and white pixels indicate regions" (§2.19, PDF p.35).
  - For §3.6.8: the original photo plus a solid template made from it with "any image processing software" (Fig. 125, PDF p.73). The §3.6.7 steps also need a feature image; Fig. 126 (left) uses a triangulated lattice (our reading).
  - AD3D also accepts SVG/DXF templates.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| File → Open (both images) | `template.image`, `features.image` | Load the template and the feature image | none | 2 images | §3.6.7 steps 2–3 (PDF p.72) |
| Tool → Report → Statistics | (automatic) | Check both image sizes | n/a | n/a | §3.6.7 step 4 |
| Tool → Body → Resize | `features.fit` | LuBan: resize one image so both have the same size. AD3D: fit the pattern into the template | manual in LuBan (suggest: fill) | AD3D: stretch / fit / fill | §3.6.7 step 5 |
| Tool → Threshold → Manual | `template.threshold` | Split the template's foreground from its background, so black = 0 and white = 255 | user-selected ("Select a threshold"); default UNCONFIRMED (suggest: automatic Otsu) | UNCONFIRMED (presumably 0–255 for 8-bit images). The output is 0 / 255 (step 6) | §3.6.7 step 6 |
| Tool → Data → Set mask value (input 0) | (automatic: features ∩ template) | Mask the feature image by the template; background pixels become 0. LuBan: click the feature image and OK, then the template and OK, then enter 0 | 0 is the value step 7 says to enter; the dialog's default is UNCONFIRMED | n/a | §3.6.7 step 7; Fig. 122 (PDF p.72) |
| Tool → Geometry → Distance transform | (automatic) | Distance map: each pixel's distance to the object boundary, positive on the object and negative on the background (step 8). One pixel of length = 100 (step 9). The dialog asks for a threshold that separates object from background | "Use the default value" (value UNCONFIRMED) | n/a | §3.6.7 steps 8–9; Fig. 123 (PDF p.73) |
| Tool → Threshold → Between ("0 1000") | `template.band_width_mm` | Pixels with distance values between the two numbers become white and the rest black. "0 1000" keeps the band from the template edge to 10 px inside it: the outline band | No default stated. The manual's worked value is "0 1000" (10 px); "0 200" (2 px) is another example | AD3D: mm, > 0 (suggest 3) | §3.6.7 step 9; Fig. 123 (PDF p.73) |
| Tool → Arithmetic → Max (Img1, Img2) | (automatic: band ∪ masked features) | Combine the outline image with the masked features | n/a | n/a | §3.6.7 step 10; Fig. 124 (PDF p.73) |
| File → Invoke 3D window, then Layering | PHOTO-LAYER parameters | Run Layering on the combined image | n/a | n/a | §3.6.7 last paragraph (PDF p.73) |
| (any image processing software) solid template | `template.source` | Where the template comes from | image | AD3D: image / vector (SVG, DXF) / auto_silhouette | §3.6.8; Fig. 125 (PDF p.73) |
| original photo "on the top", "one layer only" | `sources[0].layer_count` = 1 | Recipe: the original photo is a single top layer above the shaped-frame layers | n/a | n/a | §3.6.8; Fig. 126 (PDF p.74) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `features.offset_x_mm`, `features.offset_y_mm`, `features.scale`, `features.rotation_deg` | Place the pattern inside the template | 0, 0, 1, 0 | any | ours; precedent: stencil lithophane Center X/Y and Photo scale (§2.19, PDF p.35) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `template.invert` | Swap shape and background | off | on/off | ours |
| — (AD3D addition) | `template.close_mm` | Close small gaps when `auto_silhouette` builds the template | (suggest 0.5) | ≥ 0 | ours |

- **Outputs:** As PHOTO-LAYER.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The template and the feature image must be the same size (step 5). The template must be pure 0/255 (step 6).
  - Masking sets the feature image to 0 outside the template (step 7, Fig. 122).
  - The distance map is positive on the object and negative on the background, at 100 units per pixel. So "0 1000" keeps a 10-pixel band just inside the template edge, and "0 200" keeps a 2-pixel band (steps 8–9).
  - The Box light workflow uses "-1000 0" to get a band outside the letters (§3.2.8, PDF p.54–55). Here the band sits inside, so the outer edge matches the template exactly (our inference from steps 8–9).
  - Max(outline, masked feature) combines the two (step 10). Layering the result gives the shaped stack (Fig. 124).
  - The workflow has no export step between the 2D window and Layering. Other workflows export an image first (§2.13.1 step 5, PDF p.24; §3.2.8 step 6, PDF p.55).
  - §3.6.8 recipe:
    1. Make a solid template from the original photo with any image software (Fig. 125).
    2. Run the §3.6.7 process to get a shaped frame (Fig. 126 left).
    3. Layer both images, with the original on top as one layer. "The end result is the original photo supported by a beautiful layered structure" (Fig. 126 right).
  - Features that the mask cuts loose from the band fall under PHOTO-LAYER's island rule (our inference from §3.6).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **One option instead of ten steps:** Frame shape = Template plus a template file. Masking, banding and combining happen inside the generator, and the preview updates live as the band width or pattern position changes. LuBan needs ten manual steps across its 2D and 3D windows (§3.6.7).
  - **Band width in mm:** computed as a vector inset of the template outline (Clipper2) rather than a pixel distance-map threshold, so it does not depend on image resolution.
  - **No resizing:** the pattern is fitted (stretch/fit/fill), and it can be moved, scaled and rotated inside the template with live preview. LuBan requires same-size images (step 5).
  - **`auto_silhouette`:** replaces §3.6.8's "any image processing software" step. It takes the photo's outer contour, fills its holes, and optionally closes small gaps.
  - **Vector templates:** SVG/DXF templates are accepted directly. LuBan's blog documents DXF/SHP vector templates only for stencil and box lithophanes (blog: vector-image-template). The §3.6.7 workflow works on bitmaps only.
  - **Linked template:** the template stays linked in the project, so replacing the file regenerates the stack (PLAN §4 projects).
  - **Island warnings:** features cut loose by the mask are highlighted before export (PHOTO-LAYER `island_policy`).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Get template polygons from a trace (vtracer, research 03 §5) or a vector import.
  - masked = features ∩ template; band = template − inset(template, w); combined = band ∪ masked. Then run PHOTO-LAYER. These are Clipper2 operations (research 03 §13) that mirror the 2D steps in research 04 §B.10.
  - auto_silhouette = union of the outer contours with holes dropped, then offset +r and −r to close gaps.
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-LAYER; PLAN §3), together with PHOTO-LAYER.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - The default distance-transform threshold (step 8).
  - Whether newer LuBan builds accept a template directly in the Layering panel. The manual documents only the manual workflow.
  - Whether the 2D-window image must be exported to a file before Layering.
  - How pixels map to mm. A "10-pixel" band depends on image resolution and Layer size.
  - Related videos (titles only), which may show template preparation (relation UNCONFIRMED):
    - ue0o2PnOfZU "Photo to Template" (13:08)
    - wDikiVpunws "Add background shape to an image" (3:15)
    - Br-ojEQmZUM "How to prepare template and picture for Balloon lithophane" (4:35)
  - blog: overlay-photos describes overlaying images in the 2D window (Draw → Create → Image) with a Mask RGB value for transparency. It might be another way to composite the two images (UNCONFIRMED). Its tutorial is video xV3QRm2Io1Y "LuBan Overlaying photos" (5:22; title only, no transcript in the repo).

#### PHOTO-MORPH — Silhouette Morph (LuBan: Morphing, Photo)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Morphing, Photo, then Positive or Negative (§3.7–3.7.5, PDF p.74–77).
- **What it makes:** One 3D model made from two or three photos. Viewed along the X, Y or Z direction, it shows one of the photos (§3.7, Fig. 127). Negative mode instead makes hollow regions in a cubic model, and the hollows show the photos (§3.7.1, Fig. 128).
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D printing (our reading of Fig. 127). The manual names no process for Morphing; the §3 intro lists 3D printing, laser cutting and CNC machining for Photo magic in general (PDF p.46).
  - Fig. 127 (PDF p.74) shows a user's white print standing on a rectangular plate. It shows a bass clef from one side and a treble clef from the other (our reading).
  - Print orientation and supports are not stated (UNCONFIRMED). §3.7.5 rotates the photos to get a smaller model, and reorients the model horizontally to make X the axis of rotation. It says nothing about printing.
- **Inputs:** Two or three photos (§3.7; three-way since blog: morphing-4th-release), converted to black and white first (§3 intro, PDF p.46). Formats are not stated (UNCONFIRMED). AD3D: PNG/JPG and SVG/DXF.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Positive / Negative (from the §3.7.1 heading; control type UNCONFIRMED) | `polarity` | Positive: the solid shows each photo along its axis. Negative: a cube with hollows in the shapes of the photos | UNCONFIRMED (suggest positive) | positive, negative | §3.7.1 (PDF p.74); Fig. 128 (PDF p.75); blog: morphing-3rd-release |
| Photo / Text (from the §3.7.2 heading; the Cutter panel has a Photo / Text radio pair, so Morphing probably does too) | `source` | Morph photos, or typed text (see PHOTO-MORPH-TEXT) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest photo) | photo, text | §3.7.2 (PDF p.74); Fig. 64 (PDF p.46); blog: morphing |
| Select photo ("Browse") | `photos[]` | The silhouettes; each viewing axis shows one | none | 2 or 3 images | §3.7; Fig. 64 (PDF p.46); blog: morphing-4th-release |
| Model size X | `size_x_mm` | Size along X. X, Y and Z keep the morph's aspect ratio | UNCONFIRMED (suggest 60) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest > 0, within the printer bed). Unit UNCONFIRMED (suggest mm) | §3.7.3 (PDF p.75) |
| Model size Y | `size_y_mm` | Size along Y; follows the locked ratio | derived (§3.7.3) | locked ratio; unit UNCONFIRMED | §3.7.3 |
| Model size Z | `size_z_mm` | Size along Z; follows the locked ratio | derived (§3.7.3) | locked ratio; unit UNCONFIRMED | §3.7.3 |
| Base thickness | `base_thickness_mm` | Plate under the model; 0 = none | UNCONFIRMED | 0 disables the base (§3.7.4); maximum and unit UNCONFIRMED. Documented for text mode only. Availability in photo mode is UNCONFIRMED: the print in Fig. 127 stands on a plate, which the user may have added | §3.7.4; Fig. 127 |
| (Axis of rotation; no control described) | `shared_axis` | The axis both silhouettes share, i.e. the axis you turn the model about to see each one. LuBan uses Z for two photos, and §3.7.5 offers only a workaround | Z for two photos (§3.7.5) | AD3D: x / y / z / auto (suggest auto) | §3.7.5 (PDF p.75–76); Figs. 132–135 (PDF p.77) |
| (no control; §3.7.5 rotates the photos 90° before loading them, with no tool named) | `photos[].rotation_deg` | Rotate a silhouette before morphing. In Fig. 134 both photos are turned 90° the same way, counter-clockwise (our reading) | 0 (ours) | 0 / 90 / 180 / 270 (ours) | §3.7.5; Fig. 134 (PDF p.77) |
| (no control; §3.7.5 says only "orient the model horizontally", method UNCONFIRMED) | `lay_flat` | AD3D: orient the finished model for printing. In LuBan, laying the model horizontally (Fig. 135 right) only makes X the axis of rotation | (suggest auto) | on / off / auto (ours) | ours; §3.7.5; Fig. 135 (PDF p.77) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `photos[].mirror` | Mirror a silhouette | off | on/off | ours |
| — (AD3D addition) | `align` | Shift or scale silhouettes along the shared axis so that less of each image is lost | auto | none / auto | ours; §3.7.2 height rule |
| — (AD3D addition) | `block_margin_mm` | Negative only: solid border kept around the hollows | (suggest 2) | ≥ 0 | ours |

| — (AD3D addition) | `min_wall_mm` | Thinnest wall allowed before a warning | from the profile (suggest 2× nozzle) | > 0 | ours; PLAN §4 machine profiles |

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: not stated (UNCONFIRMED; presumably STL via Save model, see PHOTO-COMMON).
  - AD3D: one watertight STL, or a 3MF in mm with the morph and base as separate objects or as one body.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Two or three photos are merged into one 3D model. Viewed along X, Y or Z, it shows one photo each (§3.7, PDF p.74). Fig. 127 shows a user's print from several angles.
  - Positive mode represents the photos directly in each viewing direction. Negative mode makes hollow regions in a cubic model (§3.7.1). In Fig. 128 the heart and the gothic S appear as openings in the faces of the block (our reading).
    - The heart input is an outline. On the cube it appears as a heart-shaped ring groove, and the heart's interior stays at face level (our reading).
    - The page background shows through the S opening in places, which suggests a through-opening (our reading).
  - Model size X, Y and Z keep the morph's aspect ratio. Change X, press Enter, and Y and Z follow, and the reverse (§3.7.3; §1.8).
  - Axis of rotation (§3.7.5):
    - With two photos, "the axis of rotation to view the photos is the Z axis". You turn the model about Z and see the photos along two horizontal directions (Figs. 132–133). Z is the rotation axis, not a viewing direction.
    - In Fig. 133, two wide photos (a "Ford" script logo and a car) give a wide, flat model. The manual warns that this orientation "may produce a big-sized model".
    - Rotating both photos 90° and loading the rotated photos (Fig. 134) gives "a smaller-sized model" (Fig. 135 left).
    - If that model is oriented horizontally, "the axis of rotation to view the photos becomes the X axis". Turning it about X shows the original, unrotated photos (Fig. 135 right and caption). In Fig. 135 right, one photo is seen from above and the other from the side (our reading of the arrows).
  - Photos should be converted to black and white before morphing (§3 intro, PDF p.46).
  - History:
    - Two photos or two text strings (blog: morphing, Dec 2019).
    - Improved text morphing: text and base as one body (blog: morphing-2nd-release, Jan 2020; see PHOTO-MORPH-TEXT).
    - Negative (blog: morphing-3rd-release, Feb 2020).
    - Three-way (blog: morphing-4th-release, Oct 2020).
    - A grid option (blog: morphing-grid, Sep 2025; see PHOTO-MORPH-GRID).
  - Construction (research 04 §A, §B.10; not stated in the manual): the positive morph is the intersection of the silhouettes extruded along orthogonal axes ("Shadow Art", Mitra & Pauly 2009).
  - Consequence (our derivation from that construction): with two photos sharing Z, the view along Y shows photo A only at heights where photo B has pixels. Any part of A at other heights is lost. This is why text mode needs letters of uniform height (§3.7.2).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview:** dragging the size, or moving and scaling a silhouette, updates the model live with no Enter key (§3.7.3; PLAN §4).
  - **Fidelity insets:**
    - Three orthographic views (along X, Y and Z) sit beside the 3D view. Each overlays the silhouette the model actually casts on its target photo, with a % match and the lost regions in red.
    - `align` = auto shifts and scales the silhouettes along the shared axis to maximise the match.
    - A Shadow-Art-style deformation of inconsistent silhouettes is a Later option (research 04 §A).
  - **Orientation in the app:**
    - Per-photo rotate and mirror, and a choice of shared axis.
    - An auto mode picks the arrangement with the smallest bounding box, or one that fits the printer bed in the machine profile, and lays it flat for printing.
    - This replaces §3.7.5's workaround of rotating the photo files before loading them, then reorienting the model (Figs. 134–135).
  - **Shadow-wall preview:** three lights, one along each axis, cast the silhouettes onto walls with real shadow maps. This extends PLAN §4's realistic preview, which names Squama and lithophanes.
  - **Negative-mode checks:** warn when the hollows split the block into pieces or leave walls thinner than `min_wall_mm`. `block_margin_mm` keeps a solid border; in Fig. 128 the hollows run close to the block edges (our reading).
    - Outline silhouettes are the typical trap. If the heart ring in Fig. 128 went right through the block, the heart's interior would be a loose plug (our analysis).
    - AD3D finds such pieces with manifold `decompose()` and offers blind hollows (`hollow_mode`) instead.
  - **Printability:** positive intersections can leave small disconnected fragments (our analysis of the construction). AD3D reports them and offers to keep the largest piece or to tie the fragments to a base, which is also offered in photo mode. LuBan connects text pieces only through the base (Fig. 130).
  - **Watertight by construction:** booleans run in manifold, and `validate()` is checked in a proptest over random silhouettes (CLAUDE.md rule).
  - **3MF output:** in mm, with the morph and base as separate objects for a two-colour print (PLAN §4).
  - **Vector silhouettes:** SVG/DXF input gives crisp walls. LuBan's blog reports "bumpy artifacts" from bitmap templates and offers DXF/SHP templates only for stencil and box lithophanes (blog: vector-image-template). Morphing takes photos (§3.7).
  - **Batch:** the CLI runs a list of photo pairs or triples (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Trace:** each silhouette is traced to polygons (vtracer, research 03 §5; or findContours-style border following plus Douglas–Peucker, research 04 §C) and scaled to the box faces.
  - **Positive:** extrude each polygon through the box along its axis (manifold CrossSection extrude), rotate, and Boolean-intersect (manifold, Apache-2.0; research 03 §13).
  - **Negative** (our reading of Fig. 128): block − ⋃ extrusions, then manifold `decompose()` to check that the block is still one piece. With `hollow_mode` = blind, each extrusion runs only `hollow_depth_mm` in from its face (ours).
  - **Box size** (our model of §3.7.3's locked ratio): with shared axis Z and silhouettes A (w_A × h_A) and B (w_B × h_B), Z = H, X = H·w_A/h_A and Y = H·w_B/h_B.
  - **Fidelity:** rasterise the projections in parallel (rayon). For two photos the projection along Y is A restricted to the rows where B is non-empty, which needs no mesh and fits the ≤ 50 ms drag budget. While dragging, use coarser polygons (a larger Douglas–Peucker tolerance), and switch to full resolution on release (CLAUDE.md).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-BOX-LITHO; PLAN §3).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - No defaults, ranges or units are stated for Model size or Base thickness. Whether Photo magic has a unit setting is UNCONFIRMED; the 2018 Mesh → LuBan panel had one (luban-docs Get started p.3–p.4).
  - What are the exact panel labels and control types? No Morphing panel screenshot exists in the manual.
  - Which photo goes to which axis? File-name order as in poly-face lithophanes (§2.15.1, PDF p.26), selection order, or something else?
  - With three photos, how are inconsistent aspect ratios reconciled: stretch, pad or crop?
  - How is the negative built: through-tunnels, or the cube minus the positive morph? Fig. 128 suggests through-openings. If they are through-tunnels, what happens to enclosed regions such as the inside of the heart outline?
  - Is the "cubic model" a true cube, or a box of Model size X × Y × Z? Does negative mode work with three photos?
  - Is there a base in photo mode? Is there a resolution or smoothing control?
  - What is the output: one STL? File naming (see PHOTO-COMMON Save model)?
  - Related videos (titles only): U4nDFenp8uc "LuBan Morphing" (3:40); 9JtN27Z1V6Y "LuBan Morphing v3" (4:01); E9n_941lgyk "LuBan Morphing v4: 3-way morphing" (3:55).

#### PHOTO-MORPH-TEXT — Word Morph (LuBan: Morphing, Text)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Morphing, Text (§3.7.2, §3.7.4; PDF p.74–76).
- **What it makes:** A row of letter pieces on a shared base (§3.7.4; Fig. 129, PDF p.75). One word reads from one side and another word from the perpendicular side, e.g. "HELLO" and "SEE YOU" (our reading of §3.7 and Fig. 129).
- **Fabrication:** 3D printing, base down (our suggestion; not stated). Since Jan 2020 the text and base are generated as one body (blog: morphing-2nd-release).
- **Inputs:** Text typed into three text boxes (§3.7.2). The first release morphed "two text strings" (blog: morphing).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Photo / Text = Text | `source` = text | Morph typed strings instead of photos | n/a | n/a | §3.7.2 (PDF p.74) |
| (three text boxes; label UNCONFIRMED) | `texts[0]`, `texts[1]`, `texts[2]` | The strings to morph. All letters are converted to capitals | UNCONFIRMED | 3 boxes; how a third string is used is UNCONFIRMED | §3.7.2 (PDF p.74–75) |
| Font (the Cutter panel shows a "Font" button and "Arial") | `font` | Typeface | UNCONFIRMED whether Morphing has one (suggest: system font picker, bold sans) | installed fonts | Fig. 64 (PDF p.46); §3.4.2 (PDF p.62) |
| Model size X / Y / Z | `size_x_mm`, `size_y_mm`, `size_z_mm` | As PHOTO-MORPH | UNCONFIRMED | locked ratio | §3.7.3 (PDF p.75) |
| Base thickness | `base_thickness_mm` | Base that connects all the letters; 0 disables it | UNCONFIRMED (suggest 3) | 0 disables the base (§3.7.4); maximum UNCONFIRMED. Fig. 130 shows 5 and 0. Unit UNCONFIRMED (suggest mm) | §3.7.4; Fig. 130 (PDF p.76) |
| Text baseline | `baseline_cut_mm` | How much is cut off the bottom of the letters to join them with the base | UNCONFIRMED (suggest 2) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest ≥ 0). Fig. 131 shows 1, 5, 10. Unit UNCONFIRMED (suggest mm) | §3.7.4; Fig. 131 (PDF p.76) |
| (base shape; no control described) | `base_shape` | LuBan: a rounded rectangle since the 2nd release | rounded rectangle | AD3D: rounded rectangle / follow letters | blog: morphing-2nd-release; Figs. 129–131 |
| Positive / Negative | `polarity` | Whether negative mode applies to text is UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | positive (negative UNCONFIRMED) | §3.7.1 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `case_mode` | Capitals (LuBan), or letters as typed with each pair normalised to a common height | capitals | capitals / as_typed | ours; §3.7.2 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `pairing` | Which letters pair up when the strings differ in length. Auto (ours): skip spaces, then pair letter i of the longer string (m letters) with letter round(i·(n−1)/(m−1)) of the shorter (n letters). For "SEE YOU" and "HELLO" this gives exactly Fig. 129's pairs | auto | auto / manual map | ours; Fig. 129 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `letter_gap_mm` | Gap between letter pieces along the base | (suggest 2) | ≥ 0 | ours |
| — (AD3D addition) | `base_margin_mm` | How far the base extends past the letters | (suggest 3) | ≥ 0 | ours |
| — (AD3D addition) | `min_contact_mm2` | Minimum joint area between each letter piece and the base | (suggest 10) | > 0 | ours |

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: text and base as one body (blog: morphing-2nd-release); file format and naming UNCONFIRMED. With Base thickness 0 the letter pieces are separate bodies (Fig. 130); whether they are saved as separate files is UNCONFIRMED.
  - AD3D: one watertight STL, or a 3MF in mm with the base and letters as separate objects.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Text is typed directly into three text boxes (§3.7.2).
  - Unequal lengths: if the strings have different numbers of letters, "a letter of one string will be morphed with multiple letters in the other string" (§3.7.2).
    - In Fig. 129 the first "L" of "HELLO" morphs with "E" and "Y" of "SEE YOU".
    - That pairing only works if the space is skipped: S-E-E-Y-O-U is six letters against five (our inference).
    - Fig. 129 shows six pieces (our reading): H×S (two S-shaped slabs joined by the H's crossbar), E×E, L×E, L×Y, L×O and O×U. This matches the caption with the space skipped.
  - All letters are converted to capitals "because the underline morphing algorithm requires a uniform height of the letters. Lower case letters may have different heights that would cause problems" (§3.7.2, verbatim, including "underline").
  - "When morph text strings, you can generate a base to connect all the letters". Base thickness 0 disables the base (§3.7.4). In Fig. 130 (right), without a base the letter pieces are separate bodies.
  - Text baseline "determines how much to cut off from the bottom of the letters and join them with the base" (§3.7.4). In Fig. 131 the joining pads under the letters grow with the value (our reading).
  - Since Jan 2020 (blog: morphing-2nd-release):
    - the text and base are one body instead of "two disconnected, intersecting parts";
    - the strings are "aligned properly";
    - the base is a rounded rectangle.
  - Fig. 129 shows the letter pieces in a row along a long rounded-rectangle base. The exact layout (e.g. along a 45° diagonal so both words read side by side) is UNCONFIRMED.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live text:** the preview updates on each keystroke and while dragging the base or baseline values. LuBan's text boxes need Enter (§1.8), and Model size needs Enter (§3.7.3).
  - **Lowercase and any font:** with `case_mode` = as_typed, each letter pair is normalised to a common height band before intersecting, and each pair gets a fidelity score. Capitals stay the default. LuBan forces capitals (§3.7.2).
  - **Pairing editor:** shows the automatic pairing (e.g. Fig. 129's L ↔ E + Y) and lets the user change it or insert blanks.
  - **Guaranteed attachment:** each letter piece is checked to be one connected solid. `baseline_cut_mm` is raised automatically until its joint with the base reaches `min_contact_mm2`. LuBan's Text baseline is a manual value (§3.7.4).
  - **Two-colour 3MF:** letters and base as separate objects, or one watertight body. LuBan makes one body (blog: morphing-2nd-release); AD3D offers the choice (PLAN §4).
  - **Batch:** the CLI reads a CSV of word pairs (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Convert glyph outlines to polygons with flattened curves. Research 00 and 08 cite opentype.js for labels. A Rust font parser (e.g. ttf-parser, not yet vetted) would keep this in ad3d-core.
  - For each letter pair: scale both letters to a common height, extrude them along the two horizontal axes, and intersect (manifold).
  - Lay the pieces along the base. Cut each piece at the baseline height and extrude its cross-section down into the base (our reading of Fig. 131).
  - Make the base as a rounded rectangle with a Clipper2 round offset, then union everything into one watertight body (manifold; research 03 §13).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-MORPH; PLAN §3).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Does Morphing have a font control?
  - How is the third text box used (three-way text)?
  - Are spaces skipped, and what exactly is the pairing rule when the lengths differ? Fig. 129 fits skipped spaces and a linear index mapping (see `pairing`), but the manual states no rule.
  - What is the layout geometry and spacing of the letter pieces, and what are the base size and margin?
  - What units do Base thickness and Text baseline use?
  - Do negative text morphs exist?
  - What is the maximum string length?
  - Output: with Base thickness 0, are the letter pieces saved as separate files?

- **LuBan path:**

  - Video uCJ4y-P1iik "LuBan Morphing Grid" (7:47; title only, no transcript in the repo).
  - Not in the manual, which is dated 19 Aug 2025.
- **What it makes:** UNCONFIRMED. The only text is "A grid option is added to the morphing method." Hypothesis (ours, unverified): the morph built as a lattice of bars or pillars instead of a solid.
  - Context: LuBan's separate Grid method, added earlier in 2025, can "Generate a grid model from a 3D model" (blog: _grid, Mar 2025). Later posts add patterns, including patterns loaded from images (blog: grid-version-2, grid-version-3).
  - The morphing grid option may apply that kind of structure to the morph (hypothesis, ours).
- **Fabrication:** UNCONFIRMED (presumably 3D printing, like other morphs).
- **Inputs:** UNCONFIRMED (presumably as PHOTO-MORPH).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| grid (option; exact label UNCONFIRMED) | `structure` = grid | Switch the morph to a grid build | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: solid / grid) | blog: morphing-grid |
| (unknown) | `grid_pitch_mm` | Bar spacing, if it is a lattice | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | hypothesis (ours) |
| (unknown) | `bar_width_mm` | Bar width, if it is a lattice | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | hypothesis (ours) |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED.
- **Behaviour and rules:** UNCONFIRMED. Nothing is known beyond the one-line blog post.
- **How we will do it better:** these apply only if the lattice hypothesis is confirmed.
  - Build the lattice directly from silhouette occupancy: keep a bar only if it stays inside every silhouette, then mesh it watertight.
  - Tie the bar width to the nozzle in the machine profile (PLAN §4 machine profiles).
  - Reuse PHOTO-MORPH's fidelity insets and live preview (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** if it is a lattice, sample ⋂ extrusions on a grid at the bar pitch to get an occupancy grid, turn occupied cells into bars, and union them with manifold. Research 04 §B.8 notes that robust unions of thousands of tubes need manifold or a voxel/SDF method.
- **Milestone:** Later / maybe never (part 9). PLAN §3 puts Morphing in M5, but this option is undocumented beyond one blog line.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:** Everything. Watch video uCJ4y-P1iik before doing any spec work.

### Photo magic: Painting, Pillar, Puzzle (3.8–3.10)

Pillar and Puzzle use the photo's grey levels directly. For both, the manual says not to convert the photo to black and white first, which reverses its advice for balloon, box, cutter, extrusion and morphing (§3.9, §3.10; compare §3 intro, PDF p.46). §3.9 adds that in those earlier methods a manual conversion may beat "leaving LuBan to do the auto conversion", so LuBan converts automatically when the user does not (PDF p.76). Pillar and Puzzle are probably not the only grey-level methods: Cell (§3.3) is missing from the §3 intro's black-and-white list, its figures turn grey levels into hole sizes (PHOTO-CELL's reading of Fig. 90), and its "Bright vs. Dark" control is worded exactly like Pillar's (§3.3.1, PDF p.59; §3.9.1, PDF p.76). Pillar (AD3D: Slat Portrait) turns the photo into a row of vertical slats whose changing width shows the picture from the front only. Puzzle (AD3D: Relief Jigsaw) turns it into a relief cut into X × Y interlocking pieces, and it can also take a depth map of a 3D model (§3.10.8). Painting (AD3D: Colour Layers) is "still under development" in this Aug 2025 manual (§3.8), although the blog announced it in Oct 2021 (blog: painting). Its entries therefore rest on one-line blog posts and video titles and are almost entirely UNCONFIRMED. PDF pages 76–83 contain no parameter-panel screenshots for these methods (the only Photo magic panel, Fig. 64 on PDF p.46, shows the Cutter), so every LuBan default and range below is UNCONFIRMED. LuBan labels come from the manual's headings and text, and their on-screen spelling is UNCONFIRMED. None of the four transcribed videos covers these methods, and the Chinese luban-docs decks cover no Photo magic method at all (luban-docs notes §0).

#### PHOTO-PAINTING — Colour Layers (LuBan: Painting)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Painting. The method is listed as §3.8 (PDF p.76), and the dialog is described in the §3 intro (Fig. 64, PDF p.46). The manual's entire text is "This method is still under development." (§3.8, PDF p.76). Yet the blog announced the method on Oct 1, 2021 (blog: painting), almost four years before this Aug 2025 edition, so the manual text is out of date (our reading). Videos CUkIzyHSy8k "LuBan Painting" (8:21), PhuNaqDnMVA "LuBan Painting v2" (13:31) and LZxVjfdWLnc "LuBan Painting v3" (13:01) exist as titles only (channel/videos_dated.txt; no transcripts).
- **What it makes:** in the blog's words: "Extract color layers from a photo so that it can be 3D printed or laser cut. The assembly of the color layers is a painting based on the photo." (blog: painting). Whether the layers sit on top of each other or fit side by side is UNCONFIRMED.
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D printing or laser cutting (blog: painting).
  - Materials, layer thickness, joining and orientation are UNCONFIRMED.
  - Ours: a multi-material print, a single-nozzle print with filament changes at set heights, or one coloured sheet per layer on a laser.
- **Inputs:** one colour photo (blog: painting). Formats as in PHOTO-COMMON.
- **Parameters:** LuBan's panel is not documented anywhere, so every row is our proposal.

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UNCONFIRMED (no panel documented) | `image` | Colour photo to separate into colour layers (key as PHOTO-COMMON) | — | Formats per PHOTO-COMMON | blog: painting |
| UNCONFIRMED | `size_x_mm`, `size_y_mm` | Finished size of the picture; aspect ratio locked to the photo (ours, as LuBan does for Cell and Puzzle, §3.3.2 and §3.10.1) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: X = 150) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: > 0, up to the bed or sheet size) | AD3D (ours) |
| UNCONFIRMED | `n_colours` | Number of colour layers | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 4) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 2–8) | blog: painting ("color layers") |
| UNCONFIRMED | `palette` | `auto`: colours picked from the photo. `materials`: nearest colours from my saved filament or sheet library | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `auto`) | ours: `auto`, `materials` | AD3D; PLAN §4 (presets per printer, laser and material) |
| UNCONFIRMED | `layer_mode` | `stacked`: layer k holds colour k plus every colour above it, so each layer rests on the one below (layered-art style). `inlay`: each colour region is a separate piece set into a base | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `stacked`) | ours: `stacked`, `inlay` | AD3D; blog: painting ("assembly of the color layers") |
| UNCONFIRMED | `layer_order` | Order of colours from bottom to top | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `by_area`, largest area at the bottom) | ours: `by_area`, `light_to_dark`, `dark_to_light`, `manual` | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `layer_thickness_mm` | Thickness of each colour layer | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0.6 for print, i.e. 3 × 0.2 mm layers; laser = measured sheet thickness) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: > 0) | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `base_thickness_mm` | Backing plate under the layers; 0 = none | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 1.2) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: ≥ 0) | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `min_region_mm2` | Smallest colour region kept; smaller ones merge into a neighbour | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 4) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: ≥ 0) | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `edge_smoothing` | Boundary smoothing before vectorising | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0.5) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0–1) | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `tolerance_mm` | Inlay mode only: per-side clearance between a region piece and its pocket | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: −0.2 for print) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: signed, with the sign convention of §3.9.6) | AD3D; sign convention as §3.9.6 (PDF p.79) |
| UNCONFIRMED | `registration` | How layers line up: `none`, `frame`, or `pins` (alignment holes through every layer) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `pins` for laser, `none` for a one-body print) | ours: `none`, `frame`, `pins` | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | `fabrication` | Output route | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `print_multi_material`) | ours: `print_multi_material`, `print_filament_swap`, `laser` | blog: painting ("3D printed or laser cut") |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED in the sources. Ours, by route:
  - `print_multi_material`: one 3MF with one object per colour layer, each named and coloured, plus one STL per layer.
  - `print_filament_swap`: one 3MF/STL plus a text list of the Z heights at which to change filament.
  - `laser`: one SVG and one DXF per colour sheet, with a cut layer and an engraved layer number, nested to the sheet size.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Layers are extracted by colour, and assembling them forms the picture (blog: painting).
  - The colour-layered puzzle reuses the idea per piece: "Each puzzle piece consists of several color layers, similar to the Painting method" (blog: puzzle-2nd-release; see PHOTO-PUZZLE-COLOR).
  - The painting box is "a painting with a box" (blog: painting-box; see PHOTO-PAINTING-BOX). That its painting is this colour-layer painting is our reading.
  - The video titles "v2" and "v3" show at least two later revisions. What changed in them is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Everything else (layer count, colour choice, size controls) is UNCONFIRMED.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Real colours from my materials.** Pick the palette from a saved filament or sheet library (PLAN §4 material presets). The preview shows the assembled picture in those colours and updates live while `n_colours` is dragged (PLAN §4 live preview).
  - **Makeable regions, no specks.** Quantise in a perceptual colour space (CIELAB) with no dithering, so every region is solid. `min_region_mm2` and smoothing then remove regions smaller than the machine profile's nozzle width or kerf before any geometry is built (PLAN §4 machine profiles), and the panel reports how many were merged (ours).
  - **One generator, three routes:**
    - a multi-material 3MF with named, coloured parts (PLAN §4: 3MF with multiple parts);
    - a filament-change height list for single-nozzle printers;
    - laser SVG/DXF per colour with registration pins and engraved layer numbers, nested to the sheet (PLAN §4 cut/engrave layers; M4 nesting).
  - **Watertight layers.** Every layer is a watertight, consistently wound solid by construction, backed by a randomised-parameter test (CLAUDE.md generator rule).
  - **Projects and batch.** Undo/redo, project files and CLI batch runs (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Colour quantisation: k-means in CIELAB, or nearest-colour mapping to the material palette (ours).
  - Region cleanup: morphological open/close, then merge small regions into the dominant neighbour (ours).
  - Vectorise each colour mask with vtracer (MIT, Rust; research 03 §5), or with marching squares plus simplification. Clipper2 (BSL-1.0; research 03 §13) handles unions and offsets.
  - Stacked mode: layer k = union of the regions of colour k and of every colour above it, extruded as a prism, which is watertight by construction. Inlay mode: base pockets offset by `tolerance_mm`.
  - Adjacent prior art: Kromacut, colour-layered image prints (AGPL-3.0; research 03 §3). AGPL is acceptable here because CLAUDE.md allows GPL/AGPL for personal use.
  - Tests: proptest with random `n_colours`, sizes and thicknesses, each output checked by `validate()`; criterion benchmark at preview and full resolution (PLAN §5).
- **Milestone:** M7 (part 9, after FORM-SPRING). It is not in PLAN §3 M1–M5, and the sources are blog and video only. It builds on M5 Layering (stacked frames) and on M4 laser export and nesting.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Everything about LuBan's panel: labels, defaults, ranges, number of colours, how colours are chosen, layer order and thickness.
  - Whether the layers are stacked or fitted side by side (inlay), and whether a base or frame is generated.
  - Output files and formats.
  - What changed in v2 and v3 (videos PhuNaqDnMVA and LZxVjfdWLnc; no transcripts). Transcribing the three Painting videos would settle most of these questions.

#### PHOTO-PAINTING-BOX — Colour-Layer Box (LuBan: Painting box / Double-sided painting box)

- **LuBan path:** UNCONFIRMED. The feature is known only from three sources:
  - blog: painting-box (Apr 13, 2024): "Generate a painting with a box."
  - blog: double-sided-painting-box (May 7, 2024): "Generate a double-sided painting box."
  - video kNaPEE9p0w4 "LuBan double sided painting box" (12:14, title only).

  Whether it is an option of Painting (§3.8) or of Box (§3.2) is UNCONFIRMED.

  The releases mirror the lithophane box, which came just before: blog: lithophane-15th-release (Dec 9, 2023): "Generate a lithophane box."; blog: lithophane-18th-release (Mar 3, 2024): "Generate a double-sided lithophane box." The manual's box lithophane is a Box whose inlay lid is replaced by a lid-shaped lithophane (§3.2.9, PDF p.56–58; PHOTO-BOX-LITHO). By analogy, a painting box is probably a Box whose lid carries a colour-layer painting (our inference; UNCONFIRMED).
- **What it makes:** "a painting with a box" (blog: painting-box). In our reading, a colour-layer painting (PHOTO-PAINTING) on a box, probably on its lid as with the box lithophane (§3.2.9). The double-sided version carries a painting on two sides (our reading of the title).
- **Fabrication:** UNCONFIRMED. Painting itself is "3D printed or laser cut" (blog: painting).
- **Inputs:** one photo per painted side (UNCONFIRMED; the single-sided version presumably takes one photo). If it follows the box lithophane, it also takes a black-and-white template image for the box outline (§3.2.9, Fig. 83, PDF p.56; UNCONFIRMED).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UNCONFIRMED | `sides` | One painted side or two | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 1) | 1, 2 (implied by the two blog titles) | blog: painting-box; blog: double-sided-painting-box |
| UNCONFIRMED | `image_front`, `image_back` | Photo for each painted side | — | Formats per PHOTO-COMMON | blog: double-sided-painting-box (inferred) |
| — (AD3D) | `painting_face` | Which box face carries the painting | ours: `lid` | `lid`, `front`, `front_and_back` | AD3D; lid by analogy with the box lithophane (§3.2.9, PDF p.56) |
| UNCONFIRMED | (PHOTO-PAINTING keys) | `n_colours`, `palette`, `layer_mode`, `layer_thickness_mm`, `min_region_mm2`, `fabrication` | As PHOTO-PAINTING | As PHOTO-PAINTING | AD3D |
| UNCONFIRMED | (Box keys) | Template image, box size, wall, lid type, edge chamfer, tolerance | As PHOTO-BOX and PHOTO-BOX-LID | As those entries | §3.2 |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED. Ours: one 3MF with the box parts and the colour-layer parts as separate named objects; on the laser route, SVG/DXF per colour.
- **Behaviour and rules:** only the two blog sentences are known.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **One step, composed.** LuBan's documented way to put a picture on a box lid is a manual recipe across its 2D and 3D windows (§3.2.9, PDF p.56–58, box lithophane). Ours combines two generators we will already have (the M5 Box and PHOTO-PAINTING) in one step, builds the painting on the exact lid polygon, and any fix to either generator carries over (ours).
  - **Both sides read correctly.** A double-sided panel is built as two layer stacks, each oriented to read correctly from its own side (ours).
  - **Platform features.** Live preview, 3MF with multiple parts, and the shared tolerance test coupon (PLAN §4; research 07 §(e)4).
  - **Laser route.** Measured sheet thickness and kerf offsets per layer, SVG/DXF with separate cut and engrave layers, and registration features so the layers line up. The blog names only 3D print or laser cut (blog: painting; PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** PHOTO-PAINTING layers (palette quantisation → nested region masks → vectorise with TOOL-VECTORIZE → offset and extrude) are placed on a face panel from the Box generator. manifold (Apache-2.0; research 03 §13) is used only where a one-body print needs the layers fused to the panel. Kromacut (AGPL) is a reference for colour layering (research 03 §3).
- **Milestone:** M7 (part 9, after PHOTO-PAINTING). It needs PHOTO-PAINTING and the M5 Box. Gated: not started until video kNaPEE9p0w4 is transcribed (part 9).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Where it sits in the UI.
  - Which faces carry the painting.
  - Whether "double-sided" means both faces of one panel or two faces of the box.
  - Whether it needs a separate template image for the box outline, as the box lithophane does (§3.2.9, Fig. 83).
  - All parameters and outputs, and how the layers stack and how the box holds them.

#### PHOTO-PILLAR — Slat Portrait (LuBan: Pillar)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Pillar (§3.9, PDF p.76; dialog in the §3 intro, Fig. 64, PDF p.46). Blog: pillar (Oct 28, 2019): "Represent a photo by laser cut or 3D printed pillars." Video v0q7Ny662FM "LuBan Pillar" (3:59) exists as a title only.
- **What it makes:** a row of thin vertical pillars (slats) along X, spread in depth by the chosen pattern, on an optional base and under an optional cap. Each pillar's outline follows the photo's intensity in its column (our reading of Fig. 137 and Fig. 140), so the photo appears from the front and becomes unclear from the side (§3.9; §3.9.2, PDF p.76 and p.78; Fig. 136–137, PDF p.78).
- **Fabrication:**
  - The structure "can be 3D printed or laser cut" (§3.9, PDF p.76; blog: pillar).
  - Bright pillars are meant to be seen against a black background, and dark pillars against a white one (§3.9.1, PDF p.76). So (our inference): light material for LuBan's Bright (`backdrop` = `dark`), dark material for LuBan's Dark (`backdrop` = `light`).
  - The sign of the tolerance follows the process: positive for laser cutting, to make up for burnt material (e.g. +0.1 mm); negative for 3D printing, to make up for printed parts coming out larger (e.g. −0.2 mm) (§3.9.6, PDF p.79).
  - Fine structures are harder to make and wear out faster, so set the detail from the machine's precision and the material's strength (§3.9.4, PDF p.78).
  - Fig. 136 (PDF p.78) shows a user build: a dark, flat panel of slats in a rectangular frame, held in front of a bright background. Material and process are not stated. It matches the dark-pillar case of §3.9.1: the slats are wide where the photo is dark (hat, coat) and thin where it is bright (face, shirt) (figure observation).
  - A negative "3D printing" tolerance between pillars and cap/base only matters if they are separate parts, so pillars, cap and base are separate parts in print too (our inference from §3.9.6). The per-pillar labels (§3.9.7) support this.
  - Print orientation is UNCONFIRMED. Ours: lay each pillar flat, because a tall thin plate printed upright wobbles (research 08 §2.4, same issue for Squama).
- **Inputs:** one photo. Its greyscale intensity is used directly, so do not convert it to black and white first: that conversion "will remove useful information and produce suboptimal results" (§3.9, PDF p.76).
- **Parameters:** there is no panel screenshot, so labels come from the §3.9.x headings and text.

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Select photo (Browse button) | `image` | Input photo (key as PHOTO-COMMON); its greyscale intensity drives the pillar outlines. Do not pre-convert to black and white | — | Formats per PHOTO-COMMON | §3 intro, Fig. 64 (PDF p.46); §3.9 (PDF p.76) |
| Bright / Dark (the manual says "the bright and dark control"; the exact widget label is UNCONFIRMED) | `backdrop` | Where the pillars will be seen. Same key and values as PHOTO-CELL, whose control is worded identically (§3.3.1). `dark` = LuBan Bright: bright pillars on a black background, so pillar coverage follows the photo's brightness. `light` = LuBan Dark: dark pillars on a white background, so coverage follows darkness. The direction of mapping is our reading of Fig. 137: the face is drawn by wide white slats in the bright version, and the dark hair and background by wide blue slats in the dark version | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: `light`, a dark print on a pale wall, as for PHOTO-CELL) | Bright, Dark → `dark`, `light` | §3.9.1 (PDF p.76); Fig. 137 (PDF p.78); §3.3.1 (PDF p.59) |

- **Outputs:** not stated in §3.9 (UNCONFIRMED). The figures show one model with pillars on a base plate (Fig. 138–139, PDF p.79), and with a cap and a base (Fig. 137, PDF p.78; Fig. 141, PDF p.80). Ours, by route:
  - print: `slat_portrait.3mf` with each pillar, the cap and the base as separate named objects, laid flat and packed onto the bed, plus `pillar_NNN.stl`, `cap.stl` and `base.stl`;
  - `print_one_body`: a single STL/3MF;
  - laser/CNC: `sheet_NN.svg` and `sheet_NN.dxf` with cut and engrave layers;
  - all routes: `assembly.pdf` showing which slot each numbered pillar goes into.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The photo's intensity is used directly. Manual conversion to black and white "will remove useful information and produce suboptimal results" (§3.9, PDF p.76).
  - Bright vs. Dark picks the viewing situation that suits the target environment (§3.9.1). Fig. 137 (PDF p.78) shows the same photo as bright pillars (white render on a black background) and as dark pillars (blue render on a white background); both versions have a cap and a base. In both, and in Fig. 139–140, every pillar is one strip with a thin spine running its full height that widens where the image needs coverage (figure observation).
  - The photo is seen from the front; from the side it is unclear, "which presents a surprising factor to the viewer" (§3.9.2, PDF p.78).
  - Fig. 138 (PDF p.79), figure observation: with Ellipse the pillar tops trace a curved arc; Sawtooth zigzags; Sine forms a smooth wave; Random is irregular. All four stand on a flat rectangular base plate that spans the pattern's depth, not on a bar of pillar thickness. Line and Semiellipse are not pictured; the flat panels in Fig. 137 and Fig. 141 look like Line.
  - Fig. 139 (PDF p.79), figure observation: Wx is a call-out at the foot of one pillar along X; Dy spans the front-most and back-most pillar tops; Hz runs from the pillar tops down to the base plate (whether to its top or bottom face cannot be read at this scale); T is a call-out at the top end of one pillar.
  - A higher level of detail represents the photo better but is harder to make and less durable (§3.9.4). Fig. 140 (PDF p.80), figure observation: lower values give blockier outlines with longer runs of constant width, while the pillar count and spacing stay the same at all three levels.
  - Cap and base are enabled by a positive height, and their thickness defaults to the pillar thickness (§3.9.5).
  - Fig. 141 (PDF p.80), figure observation: the cap and base are full-width bars at the top and bottom. Between each bar and the picture runs a comb-like band of teeth. The teeth are much finer than the roughly 16 long vertical lines in the picture area but match the pitch of the picture's fine dashes, so they are probably the narrowed ends of many thin pillars (our reading). Ch and Bh measure that band plus its bar, and T measures the bar's thickness. The joint geometry is UNCONFIRMED.
  - The tolerance is signed and is found by trial and error, because it depends on the machine and the process settings (§3.9.6). The old Chinese deck gives the same sign rule for the Hash tolerance but words it as compensating at "part edges" (luban-docs Get started p.12).
  - A text size of 0 disables the labels (§3.9.7).
  - LuBan's text boxes only update the display after Enter is pressed (§1.8, PDF p.15–16; luban-docs Get started p.6). This is general LuBan behaviour.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview, no Enter key.** Every slider regenerates while being dragged, on the latest-wins job queue. A low-resolution preview (every other row, pillars drawn as GPU instances) appears in ≤ 50 ms, and full resolution follows on release (PLAN §4; CLAUDE.md speed rule). LuBan updates text boxes only on Enter (§1.8).
  - **See it as a viewer will.** The preview offers three views (PLAN §4, realistic preview):
    - a front orthographic view against the chosen black or white background;
    - a perspective view at a set viewing distance, which shows how deep patterns distort the picture up close;
    - an orbit that shows the side-on scramble (§3.9.2).
  - **Durability in millimetres instead of a unitless level of detail.** `min_feature_mm` comes from the machine profile (PLAN §4) and clamps every neck. Anything that would still be thinner is highlighted before export. LuBan leaves this to trial and error with "level of detail", whose scale is not stated (§3.9.4; Fig. 140 shows 100, 90 and 80).
  - **Fit from measured material, not trial and error.** On the laser:
    - slot width = measured sheet thickness − kerf + fit allowance;
    - cut outlines are offset by kerf/2, and engrave paths are not offset (research 08 §2.6; PLAN §4 machine profiles).

    `tolerance_mm` remains as the fit allowance. A fit-test coupon (one base strip with slots from −0.3 to +0.3 mm) replaces the trial-and-error loop of §3.9.6 (research 07 §(e)4).
  - **CNC-ready slots.** Dogbone reliefs are added at the inside corners of the cap and base slots, sized from the tool diameter (research 08 §2.7).
  - **One-piece laser panel.** For the Line pattern, `laser_one_piece` cuts the slats and frame bars as a single outline from one sheet, with no assembly and no tolerance. Fig. 136's build looks like such a panel (figure observation; LuBan's joint design is UNCONFIRMED).
  - **Assembly that is hard to get wrong:**
    - Labels go on the hidden tab or the back face, so they never change the silhouette.
    - Laser output is nested onto sheet-size SVG/DXF pages with separate cut and engrave layers.
    - A PDF assembly map shows where each numbered pillar goes (PLAN §4 better exports).
    - Print output is a 3MF with each pillar, the cap and the base as separate named objects, in mm (PLAN §4: LuBan has no 3MF).
  - **Each pillar is one watertight solid.** A continuous spine of at least `min_feature_mm` prevents floating islands. Every part passes `validate()` (watertight, consistent winding), backed by a randomised-parameter test (CLAUDE.md).
  - **Reproducible, extensible patterns.** A `seed` for Random, `pattern_periods` for Sine and Sawtooth, and a custom spline pattern (ours).
  - **Tone control.** Gamma, contrast and crop (PLAN §4), plus a curve that makes perceived brightness track slat coverage (ours). LuBan has a separate 2D halftone-line tool with adjustable line width (blog: halftone-line; TOOL-HALFTONE-LINE); Pillar is in effect a 3D line halftone (our reading).
  - **Batch/CLI.** The same generator runs headless from `ad3d-cli` with a parameter file (PLAN §1, §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  1. Photo luminance without thresholding, then the tone curve. Area-average into N columns (N = `pillar_count`) × M rows, where the row pitch comes from `detail_level` (ours).
  2. Coverage c = I for `backdrop` = `dark` (LuBan Bright) or 1 − I for `light` (LuBan Dark). Outline width w = clamp(c × Wx, `min_feature_mm`, Wx − `min_gap_mm`). LuBan's own mapping is UNCONFIRMED.
  3. Simplify by detail level (merge vertical runs, then Douglas–Peucker), keeping the outline z-monotone.
  4. Pillar solid: because the outline is z-monotone, the front and back faces are triangle strips between the left and right boundary polylines, so no general triangulator is needed. Add side quads and end tabs, then extrude by T. The result is watertight by construction.
  5. Placement: x_i = (i + ½) × Wx and y_i = Dy × f(x_i ÷ W), using our pattern functions for line, semi-ellipse, ellipse (alternating front and back halves), sawtooth, sine and seeded random. These match the shapes in Fig. 138, but LuBan's exact formulas are UNCONFIRMED.
  6. Cap and base: a plate polygon with slots at each (x_i, y_i). Clipper2 (BSL-1.0; research 03 §13) applies the fit offsets, kerf and dogbones. Triangulate with holes, then extrude.
  7. Labels: single-stroke (Hershey) numbers placed inside the part (research 00 §3 labels row; research 04 §B.13). They go on an engrave layer for laser, or as a shallow deboss on the tab for print. For `print_one_body`, use a manifold union (Apache-2.0; research 03 §13).
  8. Nesting for laser sheets reuses the M4 nester (SVGnest MIT or packingsolver MIT; research 03 §12).
  9. Research 04 §B.10 describes Pillar as "grayscale-driven pillar profiles (line, ellipse, sawtooth, sine, random) that show the photo from the front only" (its list omits Semiellipse), and §D rates Cell/Pillar Low (1–2).
  10. Tests: proptest over random Wx, Dy, Hz, T, detail, pattern and seed, with every part checked by `validate()`; criterion benchmarks at preview and full resolution (PLAN §5).
- **Milestone:** M5 (part 9, after PHOTO-LAYER-SHAPED). Pillar is not in PLAN §3's M5 list (Box, Cutter, Extrusion, Layering, Cell, Morphing), but research 07 §(c) v2 puts it in its Photo Magic subset. The print routes can follow M5 directly; the laser and CNC routes need M4 (kerf, measured thickness, slots, nesting, SVG/DXF).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - All defaults and ranges, and the exact on-screen labels. No panel screenshot exists on PDF pp.76–83.
  - How the overall size and the pillar count are set (photo aspect × Hz? a fixed count?).
  - Whether Wx is the pitch or the maximum width; whether the outline width varies symmetrically; whether LuBan keeps a minimum width or gap; whether a pillar can break into islands. Fig. 137, 139 and 140 show continuous spines, which suggests a minimum width.
  - The exact geometry of Line, Ellipse, Semiellipse, Sawtooth, Sine and Random (periods, front/back alternation). Only Fig. 138 shows them.
  - The scale and mechanism of the level of detail (Fig. 140 shows 100, 90 and 80).
  - The cap/base joint: slots, tabs, the comb band in Fig. 141, what "height" measures, and whether the thickness can be set independently.
  - Whether the tolerance changes the slot, the tab, or both. Research 08 §2.6 says LuBan's tolerance only changes slot width; the old Chinese deck says it compensates at "part edges" (luban-docs Get started p.12).
  - What the roughly 16 long vertical lines in Fig. 141's picture area are (pillar edges or render artefacts), given that the comb teeth are much finer.
  - How labels are placed: font, emboss or engrave, and the unit of text size.
  - Pillar output files and formats (not stated in §3.9).
  - Whether Random re-randomises on every Enter, as Puzzle does (§3.10.7).
  - Video v0q7Ny662FM "LuBan Pillar" (3:59) is untranscribed and could confirm defaults.

#### PHOTO-PUZZLE — Relief Jigsaw (LuBan: Puzzle)

- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Photo magic, Method = Puzzle (§3.10, PDF p.80; the path is spelled out in §3.10.8 step 5, PDF p.83). Sources outside the manual:
  - blog: puzzle (Mar 18, 2020): "Generate 3D puzzle from a picture".
  - blog: true-color-puzzle (Mar 24, 2020).
  - videos l3kbfVe7dEQ "LuBan Puzzle" (6:23) and InBslHXyYBQ "A puzzle without base" (8:06), titles only.
- **What it makes:** a flat jigsaw puzzle whose top surface is a relief. Photo intensity becomes surface height between the min and max thickness, and the puzzle is cut into X × Y interlocking pieces (§3.10, §3.10.2–3.10.3; Fig. 142–145, PDF p.80–82). "A puzzle can also achieve the effect of a lithophane with back lighting" (§3.10.2, Fig. 144, PDF p.81).
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D printing: the pieces are exported as STL (§3.10.7, PDF p.82).
  - The tolerance is "often" negative for printing, e.g. −0.2 mm (§3.10.6).
  - An edge chamfer between the flat bottom and the vertical wall cleans up the squashed, sharp bottom edge. It should be a few layer heights and needs no support (§3.10.5 → §3.2.6, PDF p.52).
  - Lithophane-style use needs a backlight. Fig. 144 shows a light-coloured print, backlit and front-lit (figure observation). The lithophane print tips (low speed of 30–50 mm/s, layer height = half the nozzle diameter, support disabled so removing it cannot damage the rough surface; §2.23, PDF p.43–45; LITH-PRINT-TIPS) apply by analogy (our cross-application). §2.23 also prefers printing a flat lithophane vertically, because a printer's XY resolution beats its Z resolution. That conflicts with printing jigsaw pieces flat, and which LuBan intends for a lithophane-style puzzle is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Full colour: OBJ files that "enclose the color information" are also exported when the photo has colour (§3.10.7; blog: true-color-puzzle). What they are for (a colour printer, a print service, rendering) is not stated.
  - Fig. 142 (PDF p.80) shows a large user build (Starry Night) whose pieces carry about five flat colours, with the lighter colours standing as raised layers on a dark-blue base (figure observation). That matches the colour-layered puzzle (blog: puzzle-2nd-release; PHOTO-PUZZLE-COLOR) better than a single-colour relief; the manual does not say how it was made.
  - Orientation: flat, base on the bed, relief up (our inference). The edge chamfer only makes sense with the base on the bed, because it fixes the squashed first layers at the base–wall edge (§3.10.5 → §3.2.6, PDF p.52), and the pieces in Fig. 143 have flat bottoms.
  - The manual does not mention laser cutting. It says only that the 2D pattern "may be useful for customized data processing" (§3.10.7).
- **Inputs:**
  - A photo, greyscale or colour. Do not convert it to black and white (§3.10, PDF p.80).
  - An FLT float depth map (a LuBan format) is accepted. BMP, JPG and PNG are named as lower-accuracy alternatives (§3.10.8, PDF p.83).
- **Parameters:** there is no panel screenshot; labels come from the §3.10.x headings.

A colour photo also gives coloured OBJ output | — | Images per PHOTO-COMMON; FLT depth maps accepted (ours: 16-bit PNG and 32-bit float TIFF instead of FLT) | §3.10 (PDF p.80); §3.10.7 (PDF p.82); §3.10.8 (PDF p.83) |
| Model size X | `size_x_mm` | Width of the puzzle | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 200) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 20 mm up to the bed size); its ratio to Y is fixed to the photo's aspect ratio (§3.10.1) | §3.10.1 (PDF p.81) |
| Model size Y | `size_y_mm` | Depth of the puzzle in its plane (it lies flat; heights are in Z) | Follows X ÷ photo aspect | Locked to X; editing either one and pressing Enter updates the other | §3.10.1 |

| — (AD3D) | `fabrication` | `print`; `laser` (one shared cut line per seam, optional photo engrave); `cnc` | ours: `print` | As listed | AD3D |
| — (AD3D) | `colour_export` | Per-piece colour output: `none`, `obj` (OBJ + MTL + texture), or `3mf` | ours: `3mf` when the photo has colour | As listed | AD3D; §3.10.7 |

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan: "the puzzle pieces will be exported as STL files"; if the photo has colour, "OBJ files that enclose the color information will also be exported". The 2D pattern is exported as DXF, SVG and SHP; SHP is LuBan-defined and opens in a LuBan 2D window (§3.10.7, PDF p.82). The blog adds that "The OBJ format contains the color information, while the STL format is colorless" (blog: true-color-puzzle).
  - The manual says "STL files" (plural), but whether there is exactly one STL per piece, and how the files and the export folder are named, is UNCONFIRMED (see PHOTO-COMMON). The Chinese deck also calls SHP LuBan's own 2D format (luban-docs Get started p.8).
  - Ours:
    - `relief_jigsaw.3mf` with one object per piece (`piece_r01_c01` …), in mm, with optional colour;
    - `pieces/piece_rRR_cCC.stl`, streamed binary;
    - optionally `relief_jigsaw.obj` + `.mtl` + `texture.png`;
    - `pattern.svg` and `pattern.dxf` with the cut graph and piece numbers on an engrave layer;
    - `cut_map.pdf`.
  - We write no SHP, because we use our own and open formats (CLAUDE.md).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Intensity becomes a surface height distribution, so do not convert the photo to black and white (§3.10, PDF p.80).
  - Height direction: Fig. 147 (PDF p.83) shows the brighter, nearer parts of a depth map becoming the raised relief, so bright = high at least for that FLT depth map. The manual feeds a depth map to the method exactly like a photo (§3.10.8), so photos probably map the same way (our inference; UNCONFIRMED). §3.10.2's lithophane comparison does not settle the direction.
  - The X:Y ratio is fixed to the photo's aspect ratio. Changing X and pressing Enter updates Y, and vice versa (§3.10.1).
  - Min and max thickness set the range of height variation and work like a lithophane's (§3.10.2). For lithophanes, thicker parts are stronger but need a stronger light, and a bigger variation gives more contrast but may need supports (§2.4, PDF p.19). Fig. 143 (PDF p.81), figure observation: flat-bottomed pieces under a raised relief (a heart); with 5/20 the relief is taller and the base thicker. Each piece is drawn in its own colour, here and in Fig. 147 (right). LuBan draws generated grid, panel and module parts in a different colour per part on screen (luban-docs Get started p.12, p.18, p.24), so these are display colours, not material colours (our reading).
  - X and Y section set the number of parts in each direction (§3.10.3). Fig. 145 (PDF p.82) renders the photo's colours on the pieces at 3 × 2 and at 12 × 9 (figure observation).
  - Resolution is in mm per pixel and behaves as for lithophanes (§3.10.4 → §2.5). Very small values are pointless when the input image or the machine cannot resolve that detail (§2.5, PDF p.20).
  - Shared semantics: min/max thickness and resolution work like LITH-COMMON's `thickness_min`, `thickness_max` and `pixel_size` (§3.10.2, §3.10.4). The lithophane panel labels them "Min thickness", "Max thickness" and "Resolution" and also shows a read-only "File size" (Fig. 10, PDF p.17; §2.6); whether the Puzzle panel has the same read-out is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Edge chamfer: see §3.2.6. Without it, extra material forms at the edge between base and wall because upper layers press down on the base. That edge can look ugly and even cut a finger (§3.2.6, PDF p.52).
  - Tolerance adjusts the tightness of the parts and is often −0.2 mm for 3D printing (§3.10.6). §3.2.7 adds that one value found by trial "can probably" be reused in every LuBan function that has a tolerance (PDF p.53).
  - The pattern comes from a random process: pressing Enter in an unchanged text box gives a new pattern (§3.10.7). Fig. 146 (PDF p.82), figure observation: two 4 × 4 patterns from identical parameters, with random knob directions, slightly wavy seams and a straight outer border.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview.** While size, thickness or section count is dragged, a GPU-displaced heightfield with the cut lines overlaid updates in ≤ 50 ms; the per-piece solids are built on release (PLAN §4; CLAUDE.md). LuBan needs Enter after each text edit (§3.10.1).
  - **Reproducible randomness.** An explicit `seed`, a Shuffle button and undo replace pressing Enter on an unchanged box (§3.10.7, Fig. 146). LuBan documents no way to get a previous pattern back. The same seed and parameters always give identical output, which can be cached (PLAN §1).
  - **Backlight preview** for lithophane-style use (§3.10.2, Fig. 144): light shining through, filament colour and an ambient-light slider (PLAN §4; shared with LITH-BACKLIGHT-PREVIEW). It also shows the terracing caused by the printer profile's layer height, with an option to snap heights to layer multiples (ours).
  - **3MF instead of loose files.** One object per piece, in mm, with optional per-piece colour. STL per piece is streamed, and OBJ/MTL/texture remains available for full-colour print services (§3.10.7; PLAN §4: LuBan has no 3MF).
  - **Pieces packed onto the bed.** Pieces are arranged automatically onto one or more build plates from the printer profile, with spacing (PLAN §4 machine profiles).
  - **A tolerance you can read.** The panel shows the actual gap between neighbouring pieces in mm. A two-piece fit-test coupon is printed at several tolerances (research 07 §(e)4). §3.10.6 says only "often −0.2".
  - **Piece-size mode.** Enter a target piece size and get near-square pieces, instead of choosing X and Y section counts by hand (ours).
  - **Laser and CNC routes (new):**
    - Laser: one shared cut line per seam, so the kerf becomes the play and nothing is cut twice. An optional raster engrave of the photo is included, and the SVG/DXF has separate cut and engrave layers (PLAN §4).
    - CNC: knob necks narrower than the tool diameter are rejected, since round tools cannot cut tight inside corners (research 08 §2.7).
  - **Robust cut layout.** Knob size and jitter controls. The generator checks that no piece falls below a minimum area and that no knob neck is thinner than the machine profile's minimum feature (ours).
  - **Optional tray/frame** to hold the assembled puzzle (ours). The LuBan video title "A puzzle without base" (InBslHXyYBQ) hints at a base-related option (UNCONFIRMED).
  - **Watertight by construction.** Every piece is watertight, checked by property tests over random sections, tolerances and seeds. Pieces are built in parallel with rayon, and the job can be cancelled (CLAUDE.md; PLAN §4).
  - **ML depth (Later).** Depth-Anything-V2-Small (Apache-2.0) can turn a photo into true depth before the jigsaw is cut (research 03 §4; PLAN §1, "Later: ort"). LuBan's channel has a video on photo-to-depth with Depth Anything V2 (hZpYLAkktgg, title only).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  1. Luminance, plus optional gamma (PLAN §4 image controls). Resample to (size_x ÷ res) × (size_y ÷ res) with an area filter (`image` + `fast_image_resize`; PLAN §1).
  2. h = min + m(I) × (max − min), where m = 1 − I (`dark_high`) or m = I (`bright_high`). Same maths as the lithophane: research 04 §B.1; heightfield OSS in research 03 §3 (s1lentCommit/stl-ready-image MIT, yomboprime/lithofun MIT).
  3. Jigsaw graph: a (pieces_x + 1) × (pieces_y + 1) lattice whose interior nodes are jittered. Each interior edge gets a knob curve (a cubic Bézier chain: shoulder, neck, head) with a random side and a small shape jitter from a seeded, platform-independent PRNG. Border edges are straight (Fig. 146).
  4. Piece outline = its 4 edges, densified to at most `res` spacing, then offset per side by the tolerance with Clipper2 (BSL-1.0; research 03 §13).
  5. Direct, watertight solid per piece:
     - top: constrained triangulation of the outline plus interior grid samples, with z = bilinear h;
     - walls: vertical quads that reuse the top's boundary vertices, so there are no T-junctions;
     - chamfer: a 45° ring from the outline inset by `edge_chamfer_mm` at z = 0 up to the full outline;
     - bottom: the inset outline, triangulated.

     Fallback: a manifold intersection (Apache-2.0; research 03 §13) of the full relief slab with the extruded outline. The triangulator crate is still to be vetted; research 03 does not cover it.
  6. Preview path: no per-piece meshing. One displaced grid plus a piece-ID texture and the seam lines are drawn on the GPU.
  7. Export: binary STL per piece (streamed); 3MF via zip + XML (PLAN §1); OBJ with UV = (x ÷ size_x, y ÷ size_y); SVG/DXF of the cut graph.
  8. Research 04 §B.10 describes Puzzle as "a grayscale heightfield (min/max thickness) cut into X×Y jigsaw pieces with tolerance", and §D rates it Medium (3).
  9. Tests: proptest over random size, thickness, sections, tolerance, chamfer and seed, with `validate()` per piece and a check that neighbouring pieces do not overlap when the tolerance is ≤ 0. Criterion benchmarks for a 200 × 150 mm puzzle at 0.2 mm/px (about 1.5 M top triangles) at preview and full resolution (PLAN §5).
- **Milestone:** M6 (part 9, after PHOTO-HALFTONE-3D). Research 07 §(c) v2 includes Puzzle in its Photo Magic subset. It reuses M2's heightfield, min/max thickness, resolution and backlight preview, plus M5's Photo magic panel.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Every default, and the lower and upper limits of the section counts.
  - Which way intensity maps to height for photos. Fig. 147 shows bright = high for a depth map; whether photos use the same direction, and whether a Positive/Negative switch exists as on the lithophane panel (Fig. 10, PDF p.17), is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Tolerance semantics (per side or total) and whether positive values are allowed.
  - Whether the chamfer is on the bottom edge only, or also on top edges.
  - Which print orientation LuBan intends for a lithophane-style puzzle: flat (implied by the chamfer) or vertical (§2.23's lithophane advice).
  - Knob shape and the amount of randomness; whether any seed or "repeat last pattern" control exists.
  - Whether there is one STL per piece and how files are named; whether the OBJ colour is per vertex or a texture.
  - Whether a file-size read-out exists, as for lithophanes (§2.6; the lithophane panel in Fig. 10 shows "File size 13 KB").
  - What "A puzzle without base" (video InBslHXyYBQ) means: zero min thickness, a no-tray option, or something else.
  - Whether there is a frame or tray.
  - How LuBan handles pieces that are too small for their knobs.
