- **Outputs:**
  - One STL per part:
    - single-printer mode: "Part_1, Part_2, etc.";
    - multi-printer mode: "P1_Part_1, P2_Part_2, P2_Part_3, etc.", where P and its number name the assigned printer (§4.5.2, PDF p.89–90). A prefix replaces "Part_" (CUT-LABEL).
  - "Tiny_1, Tiny_2, etc.": "very small parts that can be ignored" (§4.5.2, PDF p.90).
  - "*_Sequence.txt" in the export folder (§4.5.3; CUT-SEQUENCE).
  - Separate dowels when dowel connectors are used (§4.6.1); file naming UNCONFIRMED.
  - The older module also showed a "度量" (measure) readout after export: "部件" (parts) 5, "加工用时" (machine time) 16 h, "组装用时" (assembly time) 3 min, "总用时" (total) 16 h (CN Get started p.24).
  - AD3D: parts in the project. Export gives one 3MF per printer (parts named, oriented and packed per plate, units mm) and/or one binary STL per part, plus `sequence.json`, `assembly.txt` and a PDF guide (CUT-SEQUENCE).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - **Size first.** Set the desired model size first. If the model does not exceed the build volume, "you will be asked to print the model in one body and no cutting will be done" (§4.5).
  - **Printers.** With one printer, choose the single-printer option and set bed shape and X, Y, Z. With several, choose multi-printer and click "Set up multi-printer" (§4.5; CUT-MULTIPRINTER).
  - **Preview boxes.** A single printer is drawn as several cubes or cylinders tiled over the model (Fig. 160 left and centre). These are "not cutting planes. They just indicate the build volume of the printer with respect to the size of the model" (§4.5). The older module drew them as green boxes: "绿色方框示意一个打印机的打印体积" ("the green box shows one printer's build volume", CN Get started p.22).
  - **Fit guarantee.** "The size of the part is guaranteed to be not bigger than that of the printer", allowing a 90° turn about Z. Example: a 100-80-60 part fits a 90-110-60 printer (§4.5.2).
  - **Made of planar cuts.** "The modular cut consists of several planar cuts" (§4.5.3). One cut can split a group into more than two groups: the knot's first cut gives four (Fig. 165).
  - **Published algorithm (2019, paper CAD19):**
    1. Find the axis on which the model exceeds the build size by the largest factor.
    2. Cut with one plane or a series of evenly spaced planes, and close each section with new triangles.
    3. Re-check every new piece and cut again until all fit on that axis.
    4. Repeat for the next axis.
    - The paper's convergence criterion is volume. It notes other criteria are possible: a "no overhang" mould criterion was applied by hand.
  - **Multi-threaded since 2023.** The speed-up was best on Windows, then macOS 11/12, then macOS 10, and least on Linux; it is most obvious on files over 20 MB (blog: multi-thread-modular-cut).
  - **Newer options.** Non-axial planes since Dec 2024 (blog: non-axial-cut). Since Apr 2025 it is "improved to produce fewer parts when cutting a big model" (blog: fewer-parts-of-the-modular-cut).
  - **Older module.** Parts existed only after "导出部件" (Export parts) was clicked, and the measure readout stayed blank until then (CN Get started p.22–24). The same panel held planar/natural cut, plug/dowel, terrace/pyramid, plug shape, depth ratio and tolerance (CN Get started p.22). It had no single/multi-printer choice, no part-number imprint and no assembly sequence (CN Get started p.22–24).
    - Its preview tiled boxes or cylinders to cover the model: 4 boxes (1 × 2 × 2 in X × Y × Z) for a 200 × 150 × 140 bed and the 138 × 163 × 259 dragon, and 2 stacked cylinders for a Ø340 × 140 bed (CN Get started p.22–23).
  - **Multi-printer preview.** "Each printer is shown once" (§4.5; Fig. 160 right shows three printers).
  - **Tiny parts** come from model defects or residual cutting errors (§4.5.2).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **See the plan before committing.** Cut planes, coloured part regions, part count and per-part fit status update live as size, bed or options change. The preview works on a proxy of at most about 50k triangles by classifying vertices and drawing section outlines, with no booleans, so it stays within the 50 ms budget. The full-resolution cut runs on demand as a cancellable job. LuBan's preview boxes "are not cutting planes" (§4.5), and the older module made parts only on export (CN Get started p.22–23).
  - **A better fit test.** Allow any rotation about Z (rotating calipers on the footprint's convex hull), optionally lay a part on its largest flat cut face, and keep a per-side bed margin for brim and clips. Circular beds use the smallest enclosing circle. LuBan's guarantee assumes only a 90° turn about Z (§4.5.2; research 08 §2.11).
  - **Fewer, stronger parts by search.** An anytime beam search over candidate planes, axis-aligned and oblique, scores estimated part count, cut area, sliver risk and connector room (the Chopper approach). It runs in the background and improves the preview as it finds better plans; the CAD19 axis recursion is the instant first answer. LuBan's published method uses evenly spaced axis planes (paper CAD19), and it needed later fixes for oblique planes and part count (blog: non-axial-cut, fewer-parts-of-the-modular-cut).
  - **No slivers.** Reject planes that leave a part or neck thinner than `min_feature_mm`, and avoid cutting through corners (research 08 §2.11; paper Sass 2025: "Splitting does not occur inside corners (vertices)").
  - **Debris is never shipped silently.** Pieces under `min_part_volume_mm3` are merged back or dropped and listed in a report. CUT-REPAIR removes the root cause before cutting. LuBan writes Tiny_N files (§4.5.2).
  - **Print-ready export.** One 3MF per printer with named parts in mm, already oriented and packed per plate, plus streamed binary STL per part (PLAN §4: 3MF with units and multiple parts). LuBan writes loose STL files (§4.5.2).
  - **Machine profiles.** Bed shape, size and margin are saved once per printer and shared with Squama tiling (PLAN §4), instead of being retyped per job. The first profile is the owner's CR-6 SE (235 × 235 × 250 mm, bed moves in Y; START_HERE), and the fit test uses its usable area minus `bed_margin_mm`, not the nominal size.
  - **Bed-slinger aware.** Tall, thin parts are oriented with their broad face parallel to the bed's motion axis (`bed_motion_axis`; START_HERE). LuBan's fit test considers only size (§4.5.2).
  - **Cut even when it fits.** `force_split` and `max_part_size_mm` let you split a model that already fits: to print in several colours like the Fig. 148 castle, to reduce supports, or to print in parallel. LuBan refuses (§4.5).
  - **All cores, cancellable, on macOS too.** Independent sub-trees are cut in parallel with rayon, with a progress bar and Cancel (PLAN §4). LuBan's multi-threading gained least on Mac and Linux (blog: multi-thread-modular-cut).
  - **Stable results.** The generator is pure and deterministic: the same input and settings give the same parts and numbers, so a failed print can be re-exported alone (PLAN §1). LuBan's planning cannot account for print failures (§4.5.1).
  - **Connectors and labels placed together.** They are collision-checked against each other and need a minimum section size (research 08 §2.11; CUT-CONNECTOR, CUT-LABEL).
  - **Editable and scriptable.** Undo/redo and the project file keep the plan editable. The CLI runs the same job headless, for example `ad3d-cli cut-to-bed model.stl --bed 235x235x250 --pin 1.75 --out parts/` (the CR-6 SE volume) (PLAN §4; the command shape is ours).
  - **A part browser.** Each part is listed with size, volume, fit status and printer, and clicking a part selects it. The generic explode and select view is TOOL-EXPLODE.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Pipeline:**
    1. Repair (CUT-REPAIR) and scale to the target size.
    2. Plan on a decimated proxy (meshoptimizer).
    3. Execute the cut tree at full resolution: manifold `SplitByPlane` per node, with caps by construction, and `Decompose()` per piece (research 08 §1.4, §2.11).
    4. Add connectors (CUT-CONNECTOR) and labels (CUT-LABEL).
    5. Run `validate()` on every part, then export (PLAN §1).
  - **Planner:** the baseline is the CAD19 recursion (research 04 §B.12). The upgrade is a Chopper beam search (Luo et al. 2012, research 04 §A and §B.12; gregstarr/pychop3d, MIT, implements it, research 03 §6).
  - **Fit tests:** convex hull plus rotating calipers for rectangular beds; Welzl's smallest enclosing circle for circular beds.
  - **Plate packing for 3MF:** simple shelf packing first, then fontanf/packingsolver (MIT) or sparrow/jagua-rs (research 03 §12).
  - **Parallelism:** rayon over cut-tree sub-trees (PLAN §1).
  - **Tests:** proptest over random target sizes, beds and corpus meshes (PLAN §5; CLAUDE.md). Every part must pass `validate()` and fit some allowed orientation, and part volumes must sum to the input volume within tolerance. A criterion benchmark runs on a 1M-triangle mesh.
  - **Reference only:** Goodsmileduck/pasak3d does the same job with Tauri and manifold, but has no licence, so its code must not be copied (research 03 §6).
- **Milestone:** M3 (part 9, after CUT-PLANAR). PLAN §3's M3 scope is "modular cut; connectors; labels; assembly sequence".
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - On-screen labels and control types for the single/multi-printer choice, and the run/export button in today's UI.
  - Default bed shape and size. Screenshots show 100 / 100 / 100 (Fig. 161) and 200 / 150 / 140 (CN Get started p.22).
  - How today's single-printer UI takes a circular bed. CN Get started p.23 shows "基面直径" (bed diameter) 340, while Fig. 161's Circle row has Size X 250 and Size Y 200.
  - Whether LuBan tries rotations other than 90° about Z, or lays parts down.
  - Whether natural cut and connectors are still in today's Modular cut panel, and how axial or non-axial is chosen.
  - What "fewer parts" changed; video EuSTuybHofg was not transcribed.
  - The export folder name. Mesh → LuBan uses model_method_time, for example "duck_Stack_13-42-02" (CN Get started p.9). What "*" stands for in *_Sequence.txt.
  - Whether today's Mesh → Cut shows a measure readout (parts, machine time, assembly time).
  - The CR-6 SE's real usable area and the margin to keep for brim and clips (START_HERE gives only the nominal 235 × 235 × 250 mm); the owner should confirm with a test print.
  - How Fig. 160's rectangular preview arranges its cubes (it shows a 2-wide, 3-high stack), and whether the tiling starts at a model corner or is centred.

### CUT-MULTIPRINTER — Printer-farm split and scheduling (LuBan: Modular cut, multi-printer option)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → Cut, Modular cut. Choose the multi-printer option and click "Set up multi-printer" (§4.5 and §4.5.1, PDF p.89–90; Fig. 161). Blog: multi-printer-modular-cut (2021-03-30). Video CX5Q9yAN0uU "LuBan Multi printer modular cut" (6:46, title only).
- **What it makes:**
  - Cuts so that each part fits one of several printers, and assigns the parts so the printers "finish printing roughly around the same time" (§4.5.1).
  - "Cut an object based on multiple printers' volume so that the parts can be printed in parallel in these printers" (blog: multi-printer-modular-cut).
- **Fabrication:** Parallel printing on a printer farm. A segmented assembly can be arbitrarily large while its print time stays equivalent to that of one module, given enough printers (paper CAD19).
- **Inputs:** A printer table and the mesh.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| "Bed shape" | `printers[].bed_shape` | Bed of this printer type | shown: "Rectangle" | Rectangle, Circle | Fig. 161 |
| "Size X", "Size Y", "Size Z" | `printers[].size_mm` [x, y, z] | Build volume | shown: 100 / 100 / 100 in the entry fields. Table rows: Rectangle 100 × 100 × 100; Rectangle 240 × 200 × 150; Circle 250 × 200 × 200 | > 0 mm | Fig. 161 |
| "Relative speed" ("Speed" column) | `printers[].relative_speed` | Speed of this printer compared to the others. Multi-printer mode only ("In the multi-printer mode, you can also input the relative speed"); Fig. 161 outlines it in red | shown: 1 | > 0 (suggest); the table shows 1 and 2; limits UNCONFIRMED | §4.5.1; Fig. 161 |
| "Quantity" (spin control) | `printers[].quantity` | "The quantity of a type of printer": number of identical printers of this type. Multi-printer mode only; outlined in red in Fig. 161 | shown: 1 | integer ≥ 1 (suggest); the table shows 1, 1, 3; limits UNCONFIRMED | §4.5.1; Fig. 161 |
| "Add", "Remove" (buttons) | (list editing) | Add the entered printer to the table; remove the selected row | — | — | Fig. 161 |
| — (AD3D only) | `printers[].profile` | Link to a saved machine profile | n/a | profile id | AD3D proposal; PLAN §4 |
| — (AD3D only) | `printers[].throughput_mm3_per_min` | Calibrated print rate; replaces relative speed | n/a (suggest: calibrated from one sliced test part) | > 0 | AD3D proposal; §4.5.1 (LuBan's estimate is rough) |
| — (AD3D only) | `printers[].setup_min` | Set-up time per plate (preheat, plate swap, filament change) | n/a (suggest: 10) | ≥ 0 | AD3D proposal; §4.5.1 |
| — (AD3D only) | `assignment` | How parts are given to printers | n/a (suggest: `balance_finish`) | `balance_finish` (LuBan's aim), `fewest_plates`, `manual` | AD3D proposal; §4.5.1 |

- **Outputs:**
  - P{n}_Part_{k} STL files; each part is "not bigger than that of the printer" it is assigned to (§4.5.2).
  - AD3D: one 3MF per printer, a per-printer timeline, and filament estimates.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - In the multi-printer preview, "each printer is shown once" (§4.5). Fig. 160 right shows three volumes, a cylinder and two boxes, which match the three rows of Fig. 161; quantity 3 is still drawn once (our observation).
  - The assignment "may not be optimal because LuBan can only roughly estimate the time spent in machine set up and filament changes". LuBan also cannot account for "print failure and inaccurate speed settings" (§4.5.1).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Profiles, not tables.** Printers come from saved machine profiles (PLAN §4) instead of a table re-entered for each job.
  - **A visible time model.** Each part's time is estimated from its volume, height and the printer's calibrated rate plus per-plate set-up, and shown as a per-printer timeline. LuBan's estimate is rough and hidden (§4.5.1).
  - **Recover from failures.** Lock or move parts by hand, and re-balance after a failed print. Stable part IDs mean only the failed part is re-exported. LuBan cannot account for failures (§4.5.1).
  - **Farm-aware cutting.** Prefer cuts whose parts fit the faster printers. Plates are packed per printer and exported as one 3MF each (PLAN §4).
  - **Material estimate.** Filament per printer, in grams and metres, for buying spools. Video R0YZ624Z6KU, "How to get accurate estimate of material and time of a big 3D printing project" (title only), shows users want this.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Scheduling on uniform parallel machines with fit constraints: longest-processing-time list scheduling (largest part first, to the fitting printer that would finish it earliest), followed by local swaps. Research 04 §B.12 calls LuBan's version "greedy load balancing".
  - Time model: t = set-up + volume × infill factor ÷ rate, refined later by a slicer estimate.
- **Milestone:** Later / maybe never (part 9). M3 keeps printers as a list in the data model so this slots in. The owner has one 3D printer, a CR-6 SE (START_HERE), so this has low value for now.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Whether "P1" names a printer type (table row) or an individual printer when quantity > 1.
  - How a Circle row uses Size X and Size Y (250 vs 200 in Fig. 161).
  - LuBan's time model, and whether parts are cut differently in multi-printer mode (for example to suit faster printers).

### CUT-LABEL — Part names and embossed IDs (LuBan: Part number)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → Cut, Modular cut. Set the "part number" option to Yes, then optionally a start number and a prefix (§4.5.2, PDF p.90; Fig. 162). To see the imprint better, use "Edit → Edge → Enable" (§4.5.2).
- **What it makes:** Names the part files and, optionally, imprints each part's name on its surface (§4.5.2). Fig. 162's caption calls the imprint "a part name on a surface".
- **Fabrication:** A printed ID on each part shows where it goes during assembly. LuBan's imprint is faint (Fig. 162).
- **Inputs:** Parts from CUT-MODULAR (AD3D: from any cut).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| "part number" option (text) | `label_enabled` | Imprint the part number on each part | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: on) | Yes, No | §4.5.2 |
| start number (text) | `label_start` | First number | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 1; files start at Part_1) | integer | §4.5.2 |
| prefix (text) | `label_prefix` | Replaces the "Part_" string in part file names: with "er", files are named er1, er2, … | empty (optional) | text | §4.5.2; Fig. 162 shows the imprint "er1" |
| "Edit → Edge → Enable" (menu) | `view_show_edges` | Draw triangle edges so the imprint is easier to see | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: off) | on, off | §4.5.2; Fig. 162 |
| — (AD3D only) | `label_style` | Sunk or raised text | n/a (suggest: `deboss`) | `deboss`, `emboss` | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `label_depth_mm` | Depth or height of the text | n/a (suggest: 0.6) | 0.2–2 | AD3D proposal; answers Fig. 162 |
| — (AD3D only) | `label_height_mm` | Text height, shrunk automatically to fit | n/a (suggest: 6) | 2–30 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `label_face` | Where the text goes | n/a (suggest: largest free cut face) | `cut_face`, `outer_auto`, `manual` | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `label_order` | Numbering order | n/a (suggest: `assembly_order`) | `assembly_order`, `cut_tree` (LuBan-like), `spatial` (bottom to top, front to back, left to right) | AD3D proposal; §4.5.3; paper Sass 2025 numbering; research 04 §B.13 |

- **Outputs:**
  - File names Part_1, Part_2, … or P1_Part_1, P2_Part_2, …; with prefix "er", er1, er2, … (§4.5.2). The older UI listed "Part_01" (CN Get started p.24).
  - The imprinted name on each part (Fig. 162).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - "A part number may not be clearly seen by default. It can be viewed better by turning on the edge display" (§4.5.2, Fig. 162).
  - Fig. 162 shows "er1" drawn as rows of tiny square dots on a flat face (our observation). Prefix "er" plus number 1 suggests the prefix is imprinted too.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Legible labels.** An outline font at a set height and depth replaces a faint dotted imprint (Fig. 162), and the preview renders it clearly without edge display.
  - **Hidden after assembly.** Labels go on a cut face by default, in the area left after connector keep-outs, and read correctly from outside (never mirrored) (research 04 §B.13 edge cases; research 08 §2.11 connector/label collisions).
  - **Numbers that mean something.** Numbers follow a valid assembly order (CUT-SEQUENCE), so you build 1, 2, 3, …; the guide lists sub-assemblies.
  - **One ID everywhere.** The same ID appears in 3MF object names, STL file names, the guide and the viewer (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Glyph outlines from a bundled OFL font, merged and offset with Clipper2, extruded, then subtracted (deboss) or added (emboss) with manifold (research 04 §B.13; research 08 §2.13 on font licences).
  - Placement: pole of inaccessibility, or the largest inscribed rectangle, in the cut face minus connector keep-outs.
- **Milestone:** M3 (part 9, after CUT-CONNECTOR; "labels", PLAN §3).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Whether LuBan's number is raised or sunk, its size and depth, and which face it goes on.
  - Whether the start number renames the files or only changes the imprint.
  - Whether planar, grid and radial cuts can also be numbered.

### CUT-SEQUENCE — Assembly plan and guide (LuBan: Assembly sequence)

- **LuBan path:** Written automatically by Modular cut as "*_Sequence.txt" in the export folder (§4.5.3, PDF p.90–92). Video Li-qz2BHik8 "LuBan Assembly Sequence" (13:52, title only).
- **What it makes:** A text file that records the cut tree. "The correct assembly sequence is the reversed cutting sequence" (§4.5.3).
- **Fabrication:** Avoids dead ends where "a wrong assembly sequence would prevent some parts from being assembled. You would have to disassemble some other parts". This matters above about 20 parts (§4.5.3).
- **Inputs:** The cut tree from CUT-MODULAR (AD3D: from any cut method).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — (none: the file is always written) | — | LuBan has no setting for the sequence file | — | — | §4.5.3 |
| — (AD3D only) | `guide_formats` | Which assembly outputs to write | n/a (suggest: all) | `json`, `txt`, `pdf` | AD3D proposal; PLAN §4 (PDF assembly guides) |
| — (AD3D only) | `guide_views` | Include a rendered picture per step | n/a (suggest: on) | on, off | AD3D proposal |

- **Outputs:** *_Sequence.txt, with one line per part of the form "Part_k: i1, i2, …" (Fig. 164–165).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Planar, grid and radial results are "straightforward to assemble" using Object → Select and the toolbar slider. That also works for modular cuts with fewer than about 20 parts (§4.5.3).
  - Each number in a line is the group the part fell into at successive cuts in its branch (Fig. 164 annotations).
  - Cow example (Fig. 163–164):
    - File lines: `Part_1: 1, 1`; `Part_2: 1, 0, 1`; `Part_3: 1, 0, 0`; `Part_4: 0, 1`; `Part_5: 0, 0`.
    - Cuts: parts 1, 2, 3 are separated from 4 and 5; then 1 from 2 and 3; then 2 from 3; and 4 from 5.
    - Assembly: "Assemble Parts 4 and 5. Assemble Parts 2 and 3. Assemble Parts 1, 2, and 3. Assemble Parts 1, 2, 3, and 4 and 5" (§4.5.3).
  - Knot example (Fig. 165): one cut can create more than two groups.
    - File lines: `Part_1: 3, 1`; `Part_2: 3, 0`; `Part_3: 2, 1`; `Part_4: 2, 0`; `Part_5: 1`; `Part_6: 0, 1`; `Part_7: 0, 0`.
    - The first cut gives four groups: 1 and 2, 3 and 4, 5 alone, and 6 and 7. Three groups are cut further (§4.5.3).
  - A third-party GPL tool, ponyboypopart/luban-sequence-assembler, turns this file into instructions (research 03), which suggests the raw file is hard to use.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Step-by-step viewer.** Sub-assemblies join in a valid order, animated; the next part is highlighted with its push direction (the cut normal). No more decoding index lists (Fig. 164–165).
  - **PDF guide.** One step per page with a picture, part IDs, connector and pin counts, and glue notes (PLAN §4 "PDF assembly guides").
  - **Our own formats.** A machine-readable `sequence.json` (an n-ary tree of cuts, each with its plane, children and part IDs) and a plain `assembly.txt` in words ("Join 4 and 5 …"). Clean room: our own format.
  - **Every method.** Works for every cut method, not only modular (shared cut tree; CUT-WORKSPACE).
  - **Separability check.** For curved seams (natural, conic), check that each join can be made by a straight push, and warn if not.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - The executor records the cut tree. Assembly order is a post-order traversal: children before parents.
  - With planar cuts, each join is a translation along the plane normal, because the two sides lie in opposite half-spaces. Pegs parallel to that normal therefore never block a valid order.
  - The PDF is rendered from viewport snapshots with a PDF writer.
- **Milestone:** M3 (part 9, after APP-LABELS; "assembly sequence", PLAN §3).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - What "*" stands for in the file name, and how multi-printer names appear in the file.
  - Whether the order of index values means anything (they count down: 3, 2, 1, 0 in Fig. 165).
  - Whether any other method writes a sequence file.

### CUT-CONNECTOR — Pegs and pins (LuBan: Connector — Plug / Dowel)

- **LuBan path:**
  - Mesh → Cut, connector settings: "LuBan can automatically generate connectors on model parts to facilitate the assembly of a model" (§4.6–§4.6.6, PDF p.92–95).
  - The older module panel had "插头 / 暗榫" (plug / dowel), "棱台 / 棱锥" (frustum / pyramid, i.e. terrace / pyramid), "插头形状" (plug shape), "插头深宽比" (plug depth-to-width ratio) and "公差" (tolerance) (CN Get started p.22–24).
  - Blog: d-shape-plug-and-dowel (2019-03-18) and new-connector-claw (2020-04-18).
  - Short 4GfKzuMM4cY "LuBan Connector" (title only).
- **What it makes:**
  - Connectors on each cut face.
  - A plug is "a pair of male-female connector": a peg on one part and a socket in the other.
  - A dowel is "a pair of female-female connector with a separate dowel in the middle": sockets in both parts plus a loose pin (§4.6.1, Fig. 166).
  - AD3D names: plug → **peg**, dowel → **pin**.
- **Fabrication:**
  - Pegs print as part of the parts. Protruding pegs "may require additional support material during printing" (§4.6.1).
  - Pins can be printed, or bought as wood or metal dowels. "A LuBan user set a circular dowel size to 1.7 mm and used the 3D printing filament as the solid dowels" (§4.6.1).
  - Pyramid suits glued joints (§4.6.2). Claw "requires a printer with higher quality" (§4.6.2).
  - Printed parts come out slightly expanded, so use a negative tolerance (§4.6.6). Sockets may fill with support, hence the end gap (§4.6.6).
- **Inputs:** The cut faces (section polygons) and parts produced by any cut.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| plug / dowel (text); "插头 / 暗榫" (older UI) | `joint_kind` | Peg: male on one part, socket in the other; the plug's "cross-sectional size is auto-determined". Pin: sockets in both parts and a separate pin; "the cross-sectional size of a dowel is user-specified" | shown: plug ("插头" selected, CN Get started p.22–24) | plug → `peg`; dowel → `pin` | §4.6.1; Fig. 166 (PDF p.92); CN Get started p.22 |
| design: terrace / pyramid / claw (text); "棱台 / 棱锥" (older UI) | `profile` | Form of the connector. Terrace: alignment and friction, but hard to press home if misaligned. Pyramid: alignment, little friction, for glue. Claw: alignment and friction, more flexible than terrace, fine features | shown: terrace ("棱台", frustum, CN Get started p.22) | terrace → `block`, pyramid → `spike`, claw → `crown`. Claw added 2020: "Claw offers appealing mechanical properties compared to existing ones: Terrace and Pyramid" (blog: new-connector-claw; its capitalised names suggest the option labels "Terrace", "Pyramid", "Claw", UNCONFIRMED); the older UI had only terrace and pyramid | §4.6.2; Fig. 167 (PDF p.93); blog: new-connector-claw |
| shape (text); "插头形状" ("plug shape", older UI) | `section_shape` | Cross-section of the connector | shown: "正方形" (square, CN Get started p.22); Fig. 166–167 and 169–171 all show square connectors (Fig. 168 shows every shape) | triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, octagon, circle, D-shape | §4.6.3; Fig. 168; blog: d-shape-plug-and-dowel |
| depth ratio (text); "插头深宽比" (older UI) | `depth_ratio` | Connector depth ÷ cross-section size. For plugs the sign swaps the male and female side; for dowels a negative value equals its absolute value; 0 = no connectors | shown: 1 (CN Get started p.22–23); 2 (p.24) | any real number; Fig. 169 shows 1, 1.5, 3 and −3; maximum UNCONFIRMED | §4.6.4; Fig. 169 (PDF p.94) |
| size (text) | `pin_size_mm` | Cross-section size of dowels. "The size of plugs are auto-determined". The older panel shows no size field while Plug is selected (CN Get started p.22–24); whether it appears for Dowel is UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | mm (the 1.7 mm filament example, §4.6.1); Fig. 170 shows 1, 1.7 and 2.4. Rule of thumb: smaller than 1/3 of the cut section's width or height | §4.6.5; Fig. 170 (PDF p.94) |
| tolerance (text); "公差" (older UI) | `clearance_mm` (AD3D semantics, see the next row) | Tightness. "Setting the tolerance to -0.2 mm … produces a gap of 0.4 mm between the walls"; a positive value "makes the hole smaller than the male plug" | shown: −0.2 (CN Get started p.22–24) | mm; Fig. 171 shows 0, −0.2 and 0.2. Positive is "rarely used for 3D printing" | §4.6.6; Fig. 171 (PDF p.95) |
| — (AD3D only) | `clearance_mm` | Gap per side between mating walls; positive = looser. LuBan's tolerance t gives a per-side gap of −2t if its "0.4 mm" is per side, or −t if it is diametral (UNCONFIRMED; see Behaviour) | n/a (suggest: 0.2, from the printer and material profile) | 0–1 | AD3D proposal; PLAN §4 profiles |
| — (AD3D only) | `peg_size_mm` | Override the automatic plug size | n/a (suggest: auto) | auto, or mm | AD3D proposal; §4.6.1 (LuBan: auto only) |
| — (AD3D only) | `end_gap_mm` | Extra socket depth beyond the peg or pin end | n/a (suggest: 0.5) | 0–3 | AD3D proposal; §4.6.6 (LuBan always leaves one) |
| — (AD3D only) | `taper_deg` | Wall slope per side: > 0 = tip wider (holds once pressed in), < 0 = draft (easy insertion) | n/a (suggest: 0 for pins, 1 for pegs) | −5…5 | AD3D proposal; §4.6.6; Fig. 171 |
| — (AD3D only) | `min_wall_mm` | Material kept between a connector and the outer surface | n/a (suggest: 1.2) | 0.4–5 | AD3D proposal; §4.6.4 (punch-through) |
| — (AD3D only) | `shorten_policy` | What to do when a connector would punch through | n/a (suggest: `fit_max`) | `halve_once` (LuBan's rule for plugs), `fit_max`, `drop` | AD3D proposal; §4.6.4 |
| — (AD3D only) | `max_per_face`, `placement` | Cap on connectors per cut face; automatic or hand-placed | n/a (suggest: 4; auto) | 1–20; auto, manual | AD3D proposal; §4.6.5 (LuBan: the count cannot be set) |
| — (AD3D only) | `male_side` | Which part of each pair gets the pegs | n/a (suggest: auto, by print orientation) | auto, side_a, side_b | AD3D proposal; §4.6.1 (supports under protruding plugs) |

- **Outputs:**
  - Parts with pegs merged in and sockets cut out (plug), or sockets in both parts plus separate pin parts (dowel; Fig. 166 right shows the loose pin). The number and naming of pin files are UNCONFIRMED.
  - AD3D: pins become separate 3MF objects or STL files, or a bill-of-materials line when stock pins are chosen.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - **Plug vs. dowel (§4.6.1).** "You may use plugs for the convenience of 3D printing since they are integrated in the parts". Use dowels "to avoid the protrusive male plugs, which may require additional support material during printing". Dowels can be printed or bought (wood, metal), and filament works as dowels.
  - **Designs (§4.6.2, Fig. 167).** Terrace gives alignment and friction but "may be hard to assemble since any mis-alignment … can prevent two sides of a terrace from pressing into each other". Pyramid gives alignment "but not so much friction", "preferred in an assembly where glue will be applied". Claw gives alignment and friction and "is more flexible than the terrace", but its fine-scale structures need a better printer.
    - In Fig. 167 the terrace is a flat-topped prism (the older UI calls it "棱台", frustum), the pyramid tapers almost to a point, and the claw is a crown of spikes on a base.
    - Each panel shows one tall and one short connector, consistent with the halving rule below (our observation).
  - **Shape (§4.6.3).** All shapes "work similarly except that the circular shape does not constrain the rotation of two parts if there is only one connector between them". D-shape "allows the orientation of two parts to be uniquely determined" (blog: d-shape-plug-and-dowel).
  - **Depth ratio (§4.6.4).** A small ratio gives a short connector and a large ratio a long one. For a plug, a negative value reverses the male and female side (Fig. 169: at −3 the peg hangs from the other part); for a dowel it equals its absolute value; zero means no connector.
    - A non-zero ratio does not guarantee a connector. A dowel that would "punch through the surface of the model" is not generated. For a plug, "LuBan will halve the depth ratio internally. If the shortened connector still intersects the model, it will not be generated". So some plugs end up shorter than others, "while all generated dowels are of the same length".
  - **Size (§4.6.5).** A smaller size tends to give more dowels, a bigger size fewer. "The actual number cannot be user-specified or predicted as it is determined based on the shape of the cut section". If the size is too big for the section, no dowels are generated. Rule of thumb: dowel size below 1/3 of the section's width or height. In Fig. 170, size 1 gives two dowels and sizes 1.7 and 2.4 give one each. The dowels in Fig. 170 also get longer as the size grows, as expected since depth = depth ratio × size (§4.6.4; our observation).
  - **Tolerance (§4.6.6).**
    - At 0 the side walls coincide, which "is likely to result in a very tight fit because a 3D printed object is often slightly expanded".
    - −0.2 mm gives a 0.4 mm gap. Positive makes the hole smaller than the plug.
    - Fig. 171 shows both the plug and the hole changing by similar amounts, so the tolerance appears to move each wall. Whether "0.4 mm" is per side or across the diameter is UNCONFIRMED.
  - **End gap (§4.6.6).** "The hole is always deeper than the male plug, leaving a gap at the end surface". This is intentional: a hole may fill with support material that is hard to remove completely.
  - **Slanted walls (§4.6.6).** "The wall of the connector is not straight but slightly slanted … You press hard to assemble a connector; once two parts attach, they will not detach easily". Fig. 169 and Fig. 171 show the plug slightly wider at its tip than at its root; we measured about 3° per side from Fig. 171's pixels (UNCONFIRMED).
  - **LuBan's sign convention elsewhere.** A positive tolerance compensates laser burn, a negative one the thickening of 3D-printed edges (CN Get started p.12, Hash method). In Projection, the author recommends a negative tolerance for 3D-printed film and socket, giving "0.2 mm gap between the two", and a positive one for a laser-cut film (video VA67Jm3ijHg @00:05). That is a different feature and the value giving 0.2 mm is not stated, so it does not settle per side vs diametral here.
  - **Where connectors are documented:** §4.6 figures show connectors on a single flat section (Fig. 166, Fig. 169–171) without naming the cut method; the older panel had them in the module (modular) cut (CN Get started p.22–24). Blog: d-shape-plug-and-dowel lists "Mesh -> LuBan, Method Module and Mesh -> Split".
  - **Real use at scale.** The 1.0 m, 129-part dragon shows square sockets on its cut faces (CN Introduction p.22).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Visible and editable before export.** Each cut face shows its connectors and their count; drag to move, click to add or remove, and lock a layout. LuBan: the count "cannot be user-specified or predicted" (§4.6.5).
  - **Nothing dropped silently.** A per-face report lists connectors shortened or skipped and why (punch-through, section too small), with one-click fallbacks: smaller size, pin instead of peg, or lap seam (CUT-LAPJOINT). LuBan halves or drops quietly (§4.6.4).
  - **Clear fit settings.** `clearance_mm` is the gap per side, positive = looser, stored in a printer + material profile (PLAN §4). A printable fit coupon (pegs and sockets at stepped clearances) calibrates it (research 07 §(e) risk 4, "a generator for test coupons"). LuBan's single signed tolerance, where "−0.2" means "0.4 mm gap" (§4.6.6), is easy to misread.
  - **Size from geometry, not a rule of thumb.** For each face, compute the largest connector that fits with `min_wall_mm` (eroded section), and warn when the chosen size won't fit. LuBan offers the "< 1/3 of the width or height" rule (§4.6.5).
  - **Pegs where they print well.** Put pegs on the side that faces up in its print orientation and sockets on the side that faces down, or suggest pins. LuBan notes that protruding plugs may need supports (§4.6.1).
  - **Real-world pins.** The peg size can be overridden (LuBan: auto only, §4.6.1). Pin presets match stock: 1.75 mm filament, 3/4/5/6/8 mm wood dowels, steel pins. The guide carries a bill of materials with pin length and count (§4.6.1 filament trick).
  - **Rotation-safe by default.** If a face gets only one connector, switch to D-shape or another non-circular shape automatically (§4.6.3; blog: d-shape-plug-and-dowel).
  - **LuBan's good details, made explicit.** The socket end gap (§4.6.6), retention taper (§4.6.6) and pyramid for glued joints (§4.6.2) become documented settings.
  - **No collisions.** Connectors keep clear of labels, other connectors and the section edge (research 08 §2.11).
  - **Watertight and tested.** manifold booleans keep parts watertight by construction, and `validate()` runs in property tests over random sizes, ratios and shapes (CLAUDE.md; PLAN §5).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Placement per cut face:**
    1. Take the section polygons in the cut plane and erode them by half the connector size plus `min_wall_mm` (Clipper2).
    2. Choose centres: the pole of inaccessibility (polylabel) for one connector; farthest-point sampling at spacing ≥ 3 × size for more. The count comes from the eroded area, capped by `max_per_face` (research 00 table: "Dowel or plug at the eroded cap's polylabel with a wall check").
  - **Depth check:** slice the part at 3–5 depths along the connector axis; the wall-offset connector polygon must lie inside every slice (the Clipper2 difference is empty). This stands in for LuBan's punch-through test. Then apply `shorten_policy`.
  - **Solids:** a 2D cross-section extruded with manifold `Extrude`. Block uses `scaleTop` for taper, spike uses a near-zero top, and crown is a union of thin prongs.
    - Peg: part A ∪ peg; part B − (peg grown by `clearance_mm` and lengthened by `end_gap_mm`).
    - Pin: both parts − socket; the pin is a separate solid.
  - **Research:** research 04 §B.7 summarises LuBan's connector behaviour; research 07 plans terrace and pyramid "with draft and tolerance" (3 weeks); research 08 §2.11 asks for a minimum cross-section and connector/label collision checks.
  - **Tests:** property tests over random face shapes, sizes and ratios, including negative and zero. Every part must stay watertight, and the measured peg-to-socket gap must equal `clearance_mm` within 1e-3 mm. Golden tests cover each shape (PLAN §5).
- **Milestone:** M3 (part 9, after CUT-MODULAR), for peg and pin with block and spike profiles in all seven shapes. Crown (claw) is an M3 stretch goal because of its fine features (§4.6.2).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - On-screen labels and control types in today's UI, and the true defaults. Screenshots show plug, terrace, square, ratio 1 and tolerance −0.2.
  - How LuBan sizes plugs and places connectors.
  - For dowels, whether "depth" is per side or total; which side gets the male for positive ratios.
  - Whether the tolerance is per side or diametral; the socket end-gap depth; the wall slope (about 3° from Fig. 171).
  - Whether connectors work with grid and radial cuts; how pin files are named.
  - Research 02 lists a "cut chamfer" connector option and groups native and lips connectors with the designs. That research partly relies on LuBan's binary, so both points are UNCONFIRMED.

### CUT-CONN-NATIVE — Section-shaped tenon (LuBan: Native connector)

- **LuBan path:** UNCONFIRMED; not in the manual. Blog: native-connector (2022-09-12): "Generate a native-shaped connector that follows the shape of a cut section." Video 2MSuURqw5Yo "LuBan Native Connector" (5:16, title only).
- **What it makes:** A connector whose outline follows the cut section (blog).
- **Fabrication:** A self-aligning, rotation-locked joint for irregular sections such as limbs. Our reading.
- **Inputs:** A cut face and its two parts.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — (none stated) | — | The post names no setting | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | blog: native-connector |
| — (AD3D only) | `tenon_inset_mm` | How far the tenon outline sits inside the section edge | n/a (suggest: 2) | 0.8–20 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `tenon_depth_mm` | Tenon length | n/a (suggest: 5) | 1–50 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `clearance_mm`, `end_gap_mm`, `taper_deg` | As CUT-CONNECTOR | from the profile | as CUT-CONNECTOR | AD3D proposal |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED. Ours: one part with a tenon and its mate with a matching pocket.
- **Behaviour and rules:** None stated beyond the post.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - Chosen automatically when a section is too narrow or irregular for pegs. A non-circular outline fixes the orientation, which solves LuBan's single-circle rotation problem (§4.6.3).
  - Previewed and reported like the other connectors (CUT-CONNECTOR), instead of LuBan's silent drops and unpredictable counts (§4.6.4–§4.6.5).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** Offset the cut-face polygons inwards by `tenon_inset_mm` (Clipper2), extrude by `tenon_depth_mm`, add the result to one part, and subtract its clearance-grown version plus end gap from the other (manifold).
- **Milestone:** M10 (part 9, after CUT-RADIAL). Gated: not started until video 2MSuURqw5Yo is transcribed (part 9).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:** Everything beyond the post, including whether it is an option in the connector "design" list. Watch the video first.

### CUT-LAPJOINT — Stepped lap seam (LuBan: Lap joint)

- **LuBan path:** UNCONFIRMED; not in the manual (Aug 2025). It is generated at cut sections, so it probably sits beside the connector settings of Mesh → Cut (§4.6; our reading).

- **Fabrication:** Thin-walled parts, such as shells, vases and hollowed models, where plugs and dowels don't fit (blog). Typically glued (our reading).
- **Inputs:** A cut face and its two parts.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |

| — (AD3D only) | `lap_split_fraction` | Where the wall is split across its thickness | n/a (suggest: 0.5) | 0.2–0.8 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `clearance_mm` | As CUT-CONNECTOR | from the profile | 0–1 | AD3D proposal |
| Tolerance (connector setting) | (`clearance_mm` above) | Fit of the joint; for connectors, −0.2 mm gives a 0.4 mm gap between walls | UNCONFIRMED for lap joints | signed value | §4.6.6 (PDF p.94–95) |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED. Ours: the two parts with interlocking steps.
- **Behaviour and rules:** Only what the posts say: v2 handles solid polygon sections, and lap joints suit thin walls where plugs and dowels fail (blog: lap-joint-v2). In the manual, a connector that would "punch through the surface of the model" is not generated if it is a dowel; for a plug, LuBan halves the depth ratio and drops the plug only if the shortened one still intersects the model, "That is why you might see some generated plugs shorter than others" (§4.6.4, PDF p.93–94). Thin sections that cannot hold any connector are the gap lap joints fill (blog: lap-joint-v2). Our reading of "now applicable to a solid polygon cut section": version 1 handled only hollow, thin-wall sections.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - Offered automatically when CUT-CONNECTOR finds a section too thin. LuBan's post says plugs and dowels "cannot be generated due to thin cut sections" (blog: lap-joint-v2).
  - The joint type is chosen per cut section, with the reason shown. LuBan silently skips connectors that do not fit, and the user cannot predict how many are made (§4.6.4–4.6.5, PDF p.93–94).
  - Previewed live, with the fit shown in a cross-section before export, and uses the same clearance profile as other joints. LuBan applies changes on Enter (§1.8; PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - Split the section into an outer band and an inner band with an inward offset (Clipper2).
  - Cut the outer band at the plane and the inner band at the plane shifted by `lap_overlap_mm`, so the parts interleave as a stepped seam.
  - Build with manifold booleans so the result is watertight by construction.
  - Prior art: the MIT DDF "segment lapping" with a cross overlapping depth (research 04 §A, project pages).
- **Milestone:** M10 (part 9, after CUT-HOLLOW). Pairs with CUT-HOLLOW. Gated: not started until videos XPUc0p3AGJY and l1scuEsFTIM are transcribed (part 9).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Everything beyond the two posts: what limited version 1 (our reading above is unconfirmed), and whether the lap direction and length can be chosen.
  - Videos XPUc0p3AGJY "LuBan Lap joint" (7:17) and l1scuEsFTIM "LuBan Lap joint v2" (10:40), titles only.

### CUT-HOLLOW — Shell before cutting (LuBan: "Hollow and Cut", video title only)

- **LuBan path:** UNCONFIRMED. The only source is video nzyQWbjfCCI "LuBan Hollow and Cut" (17:02, title only). The manual and blog give no hollow-and-cut workflow.
- **What it makes:** Our reading of the title: a model made hollow with a set wall thickness, then cut into parts.
- **Fabrication:** Saves material and time on big prints, mainly for resin. FDM slicers already use sparse infill (our note). Thin walls need lap or native joints rather than pegs (blog: lap-joint-v2).
- **Inputs:** A repaired mesh.
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — (none stated) | — | No source names a setting | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | video nzyQWbjfCCI (title) |
| — (AD3D only) | `hollow` | Make the model a shell before cutting | n/a (suggest: off) | on, off | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `wall_mm` | Shell thickness | n/a (suggest: 3) | 0.8–20 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `drain_hole_mm` | Diameter of drain or vent holes (resin) | n/a (suggest: 0 = none) | 0–10 | AD3D proposal |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED.
- **Behaviour and rules:** None stated.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - The shell is computed in-app, on all cores and cancellable, so a large model does not freeze the UI (PLAN §4, Native and fast).
  - Connectors switch automatically to lap or native joints on thin ring sections. LuBan's plugs and dowels "cannot be generated due to thin cut sections" (blog: lap-joint-v2; CUT-LAPJOINT, CUT-CONN-NATIVE).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** An inward offset through an SDF (winding-number SDF plus manifold `levelSet`), then a manifold difference (research 08 §2.10; PLAN §6).
- **Milestone:** M10 (part 9, after CUT-CONN-LIPS). Gated: not started until video nzyQWbjfCCI is transcribed (part 9).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:** Whether LuBan has a Hollow tool and what it exposes. Watch the video first.

### CUT-FLEXI — Articulated split (LuBan: Flexi cut)

- **LuBan path:** UNCONFIRMED; not in the manual.
  - Blog: flexi-cut (2025-11-13): "Cut a model to convert it to a flexi model."
  - Video 8orZ5yMM2CA "LuBan Flexi cut" (12:30, title only).
  - Related photo-based method "Flexi" (blog: flexi, 2023-09-24: "Generate a flexi 3D model from a photo."; video bCRl7UC0YNQ, title only; PHOTO-FLEXI). It is probably a Photo magic method (our reading). Flexi cut probably sits under Mesh → Cut (our reading).
- **What it makes:** Converts a model into a "flexi" model by cutting it (blog). Our reading: a chain of segments joined by print-in-place hinges, so the printed model bends. UNCONFIRMED.
- **Fabrication:** UNCONFIRMED; our reading: 3D print, print-in-place. Print-in-place joints usually need a tuned clearance (our note).
- **Inputs:** A 3D model (blog: flexi-cut).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| — (none stated) | — | The post names no setting | UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | blog: flexi-cut |
| — (AD3D only) | `segment_count` | Number of segments along the chosen axis | n/a (suggest: 8) | 2–100 | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `segment_axis` | Axis along which the model is segmented | n/a (suggest: longest bounding-box axis) | x, y, z, or a curve | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `joint_type` | Print-in-place joint between segments | n/a (suggest: hinge) | hinge, ball | AD3D proposal |
| — (AD3D only) | `clearance_mm` | Gap inside each joint | n/a (suggest: 0.3) | 0.1–1 | AD3D proposal |

- **Outputs:** UNCONFIRMED.
- **Behaviour and rules:** None stated.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - It reuses the cut engine (planes along an axis) with a live preview that shows the motion range. LuBan's panels update on Enter (§1.8; PLAN §4).
  - Joint clearance comes from the printer profile, with a printable test coupon. LuBan's connector Tolerance is a number typed into the cut panel (§4.6.6, PDF p.94–95; PLAN §4).
  - A test checks that the joints really move (no fused contacts below the clearance) and print without supports. No source says LuBan checks either (PLAN §5).
  - The result stays one print job in a 3MF. LuBan exports no 3MF (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** Successive planar splits (CUT-PLANAR), then ball or hinge joint solids added and subtracted at each seam with manifold and the chosen clearance.
- **Milestone:** Later / maybe never (part 9).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - The whole feature: menu path, geometry and settings. Watch video 8orZ5yMM2CA "LuBan Flexi cut" (12:30, title only; 1.9k views) first.

## 5. Mesh → forms

### Mesh → LuBan forms: intro, Cocoon, Contour, Stack, Hash, Plate (5 intro, 5.1–5.5)

Mesh → LuBan turns one imported 3D model into a fabrication "form": an encasing shell (Cocoon), engraved display sheets (Contour), glued layer stacks (Stack), slotted waffles (Hash) or finger-jointed panels (Plate). This section specifies those five forms plus the shared workspace and the shared sheet / kerf / label / nesting / export pipeline; Contour, Stack and Hash are milestone M4 and are specified to implementation depth, while Cocoon and Plate are Later. Facts come from the manual (§5 intro–§5.5, PDF pp.96–108, with panel values from Fig. 172), LuBan's official Chinese decks in `docs/reference/luban-docs/` (cited "CN-GS p.N" for 《LuBan Get started 快速入门》, PDF dated Mar 2019, and "CN-IN p.N" for 《LuBan Introduction 简介》, PDF dated Jan 2019; other spec sections cite them as "luban-docs Get started / Introduction p.N"). Their screenshots show panel values the manual omits, but the Get started walkthrough was captured on a 2018 build (its export folder is dated 15/8/2018, CN-GS p.9–10), so its labels and values may differ from current LuBan. LuBan also keeps a settings file and "remember[s] the last used settings" (video DzvYxTm8pbo @00:08), so a value seen in any screenshot is not necessarily a default. The "2019" tags below mean these decks. Further sources: the blog; video titles (none of the videos for these five methods has a transcript in the repo, but the Thermal F20FZvL0r9g and Projection VA67Jm3ijHg transcripts show shared Mesh → LuBan and viewer behaviour); the Chen & Sass papers in `docs/research/papers/`, research notes 00/02/03/04/07/08 and PLAN. LuBan labels come from the Fig. 172 screenshot or from the manual's section titles and quoted text; where no screenshot shows a control its exact on-screen spelling is UNCONFIRMED, and every "(suggest: …)" value and every "ours" rule is an AD3D proposal, not a LuBan fact.

**Owner's machines (docs/START_HERE.md).** Every machine-dependent default below is a "(suggest: …)" tied to one of three real profiles: the printer, a Creality CR-6 SE (235 × 235 × 250 mm, bed-slinger, bed moves in Y); the laser, a "3015" machine (3000 × 1500 mm class; fiber or CO2 is UNCONFIRMED, START_HERE open question 1); and the CNC, a "1325" router (1300 × 2500 mm class; spindle and tooling not given). LuBan's manual names no machine, bed size or kerf for these forms, and its screenshots use 600 × 450 or 800 × 400 sheets (CN-GS p.6; Fig. 172), far smaller than either of the owner's sheet machines. Which forms the 3015 can make depends on the laser type: on a CO2 machine it covers plywood, cardboard and clear sheet; if it is a fiber laser, wood, cardboard and clear acrylic would go to the 1325 router or elsewhere, and the laser would cut sheet metal (UNCONFIRMED: the laser type is not known and no repo source describes fiber versus CO2 behaviour; resolve with the owner before setting M4 material presets).

#### FORM-WORKSPACE — Mesh Forms workspace (LuBan: Mesh → LuBan mode)

- **LuBan path:** open a 3D model, then Mesh → LuBan, and pick a method from the drop-down "Method" list (manual §5 intro, PDF p.96; Fig. 172). 2019 deck: 网格 → 鲁班 (Mesh → LuBan), then 选择成型方法 "choose a forming method" (CN-GS p.3, p.5).
- **What it makes:** A mode, not a generator. A left control panel with Input, Output and Measure sections plus an export button drives one method; the right pane shows a live 3D display of the result (§5 intro; Fig. 172). It hosts every Mesh → LuBan method; this section covers Cocoon, Contour, Stack, Hash and Plate.
- **Fabrication:** 3D printing, laser cutting or CNC machining, depending on the method (§5 intro).
- **Inputs:** one 3D model in OBJ, PLY or STL (CN-GS p.2). AD3D: STL, OBJ, PLY and 3MF through the M3 import-and-repair pipeline (PLAN §3; PLAN §4 "Mesh doctor").
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Method | `form` | Which generator runs. | UNCONFIRMED (the 2019 list starts at 无 "none", CN-GS p.5) | This section: Cocoon → FORM-ENCASE; Contour → FORM-ETCHED; Stack → FORM-STACK; Hash → FORM-WAFFLE / FORM-WAFFLE-RADIAL; Plate → FORM-PANELS. 2019 list: 无 (none), 一维切片 ("1D slicing" = Stack), 正交网格 ("orthogonal grid" = Hash), 环状网格 ("ring grid" = radial Hash), 互锁面板 ("interlocking panels" = Plate), 三维模块 ("3D modules" = modular cut); a later build in the same deck adds 线框压印 ("wireframe imprint" = 2D Wireframe) (CN-GS p.26). The Aug 2025 manual documents ten methods: Cocoon, Contour, Stack, Hash, Plate, Relief, Spin, Spring, Wave and Wireframe (§5.1–§5.10); the drop-down's full current contents are UNCONFIRMED (the blog announces later methods) | §5 intro; §5.1–§5.10; Fig. 172 (PDF p.96); CN-GS p.5, p.26 |
| Unit | `input_unit` | Unit in which the imported file's numbers are read. A 2026 video still picks it on entering Mesh → LuBan ("select the unit millimeter"). | UNCONFIRMED (Fig. 172 shows mm; CN-GS p.6 shows 毫米 mm) | 2019 dialog 选择单位 lists 米 m, 分米 dm, 厘米 cm, 毫米 mm, 英寸 inch (list may scroll); Cancel reuses the last-used unit ("按撤销键即为使用上一次的单位") | Fig. 172; CN-GS p.4, p.6; video F20FZvL0r9g @00:03 |

It appears to start at the file's bounding box in the chosen unit: the duck enters at 98.5 × 76.7 × 70.2 (CN-GS p.5–6), and a model with tiny coordinates comes in tiny and must be resized by hand (video F20FZvL0r9g @00:11). Fig. 172 shows 168.4 | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: > 0); aspect-locked (§5 intro) | §5 intro; Fig. 172; CN-GS p.6; video F20FZvL0r9g @00:11 |

The 2019 panel also shows total time; times read in minutes (分钟) or hours (小时). | — | — | §5 intro; CN-GS p.6, p.12, p.18, p.24 |

The 2019 folder dialog is titled 导出部件到 …… and has a 选择文件夹 "Select folder" button. | — | laser: DXF, SVG, SHP; 3D print: STL or OBJ; 3D scene: FGD + FGS | §5 intro; CN-GS p.7 |

- **Outputs:**
  - LuBan writes a new folder named `<model>_<Method>_<HH-MM-SS>`, e.g. "duck_Stack_13-42-02", inside the chosen export folder (CN-GS p.9). The method token is English ("Stack") although the 2019 UI showed 一维切片 (CN-GS p.6, p.9).
  - For Stack that folder holds `duck_Cut_DXF` and `duck_Cut_SHP` (cutting files), `duck_Asm_DXF` and `duck_Asm_SHP` (one assembly drawing per layer, for reference during assembly), `duck_STL` (3D-printing files), plus `duck_Asm3D.dxf`, `duck_Asm3D.fgd`, `duck_Asm3D.fgs` and `duck_Readme.txt` (CN-GS p.10).
  - Laser sheets are named like `Sheet_1.shp` and open in LuBan's 2D window (CN-GS p.8).
  - AD3D: an `.ad3d` project file plus an export folder in our own layout (FORM-SHEETS). No SHP, FGD or FGS (clean room: our own formats).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The control panel can hold drop-down lists, radio buttons, check boxes, spin buttons and text boxes. Every change updates the display at once except a text-box change, which needs the Enter (Return) key; Enter stands in for an Apply button (§1.8). The 2019 deck says the same: "改变文字输入框的数字后要按回车键以更新模型" (after changing a number in a text box, press Enter to update the model) (CN-GS p.6). By that rule the 2019 sliders (ring width, layer counts, tilt, font size, finger width) update live, while sheet sizes, thickness and tolerance, which are text boxes, need Enter (inferred from §1.8 and the panels in CN-GS p.6, p.12, p.18).
  - The model size ratio is fixed to the original's aspect ratio: changing X and pressing Enter rescales Y and Z, and vice versa (§5 intro).
  - The unit is chosen on entry: a 选择单位 dialog in the 2018 build (CN-GS p.4), and still "select the unit millimeter" in a 2026 video (video F20FZvL0r9g @00:03). A model whose file coordinates are tiny comes in tiny, and its model size has to be typed (video F20FZvL0r9g @00:11).
  - With Method = 无 (none) the Output and Measure sections are empty and the export button is disabled (CN-GS p.5). In the 2019 Stack panel the 布局 (Layout = Nesting) drop-down sits below the Measure section, just above the buttons (CN-GS p.6).
  - LuBan keeps a settings file and "remember[s] the last used settings" between runs (video DzvYxTm8pbo @00:08); whether that covers method parameters is UNCONFIRMED.
  - "Some settings are shared among several methods" (§5 intro): sheet size, ring width, text size and nesting are shared by Stack and Hash (§5.4); direction and nesting by Contour and Stack (§5.3).
  - The Measure section shows the model size for Cocoon, and part count, machine time and assembly time for Contour, Stack, Hash and Plate (§5 intro). 2019 samples:
    - Stack, duck 98.5 × 76.7 × 70.2 mm, 5 mm sheet: 16 parts, 6 min machine, 16 min assembly, 22 min total (CN-GS p.6).
    - Orthogonal Hash, duck 168 × 131 × 120 mm: 21 parts, 20 min machine, 24 min assembly (CN-GS p.12).
    - Radial Hash, duck 210 × 164 × 150 mm: 24 parts, 34 min machine (CN-GS p.14).
    - Plate, 70 mm cube frame, 3.2 mm sheet: 30 parts, 16 min machine, 41 min assembly, 57 min total (CN-GS p.18).
    - So assembly time is not a fixed number of minutes per part across methods (inferred: about 1.0, 1.1 and 1.4 min per part in the Stack, Hash and Plate samples).
  - SHP is LuBan's own 2D format and opens in a 2D window; FGD stores data blocks and FGS the 3D scene settings; opening the FGS loads its FGD (§5 intro).
  - Previews use flat colours: Cocoon shells are translucent over the model (Figs. 174–176), Contour frames are orange wireframes (Figs. 178–181), Stack layers are cyan, and Hash ribs and Plate plates get one colour per part (Figs. 172, 185–186, 190–197; CN-GS p.6, p.12, p.18). Slider labels show their current value, e.g. "环片宽度: 29", "转角: 8 度" (CN-GS p.6, p.12).
  - Parts are inspected with Object → Select and Object → Explode / Object → Restore (§5.4.4; blog: exploded-view). The manual describes Select as highlighting one part while a slider on the toolbar steps through the parts (§3.2.5); the 2019 deck shows instead a small floating dialog titled 选择J with the part name ("Part_01"), a slider and a 删除 "Delete" button (CN-GS p.24). Current builds use the keyboard shortcuts J for Object → Select and E to explode the components (video VA67Jm3ijHg @00:01; video F20FZvL0r9g @00:05). The status bar shows the viewing angle (Fig. 172). The 2019 panel also has a Close (关闭) button (CN-GS p.5).
  - Related videos (titles only, no transcripts): UiDXdb4nAHM "What can I do with LuBan", s_43eCcNUM8 "Magic of LuBan".
- **How we will do it better:**
  - Every numeric field regenerates while dragging or scrubbing, not just sliders: a low-res preview during the drag, full resolution on release, on a latest-wins cancellable job queue (PLAN §1, §4). LuBan needs Enter for every text field (§1.8).
  - STL carries no unit, so LuBan asks for one each time (CN-GS p.4; video F20FZvL0r9g @00:03), and a file in the wrong unit has to be resized by typing (video F20FZvL0r9g @00:11). We guess the unit from the bounding box, remember the choice per file, and read units from 3MF (PLAN §4).
  - Every import passes the mesh doctor (holes, non-manifold edges, self-intersections) before a form runs, because every slicer and boolean here needs a closed manifold (research 08 §2.10–2.11; PLAN §4).
  - An orientation gizmo and arbitrary slicing directions inside the workspace; LuBan needs a separate Object → Transform pre-rotation (§5.2.2).
  - A part browser in the same panel: search by label (e.g. "10.3.4"), isolate, highlight, explode slider. LuBan uses separate Object → Select / Explode modes (§5.4.4).
  - A Measure panel driven by the machine profile: parts, sheets, sheet utilisation, cut and engrave length, machine time, assembly time, material area and mass. LuBan documents parts, machine time and assembly time only (§5 intro).
  - Undo/redo, `.ad3d` project files holding parameters and the source mesh, presets per machine and material, recent files (PLAN §4).
  - Every form callable from the CLI for batch jobs (PLAN §1, §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:** parameter panels generated from each generator's schema; a job queue with preview and final quality; binary mesh transfer (PLAN §1). Import repair: weld, orient, fill holes, a generalized winding-number inside test (libigl, MPL-2.0), voxel remesh as the last resort (research 08 §2.10; research 07 §e.1).
- **Milestone:** M4 (part 9, first in its row). Import and repair come first in M3 (PLAN §3); the workspace shell lands in M4 with the first form (Stack).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - The default method, and whether the unit step is still a dialog. The 2018 build had both a 选择单位 dialog on entry and a 单位 drop-down in the panel (CN-GS p.4, p.6); Fig. 172 shows the drop-down, and video F20FZvL0r9g @00:03 only says the unit is selected.
  - How LuBan estimates machine time and assembly time. Research 02 §3E also lists area and weight in the panel; its source is unclear, and research 02 drew partly on strings in LuBan binaries (research 02 §2–3), which the clean-room rule excludes, so it is not used here.
  - The full current method list and menu order.
  - Whether the 2019 export folder layout is unchanged; the 2019 listing has no SVG folder although the slide mentions SVG (CN-GS p.8, p.10).

#### FORM-SHEETS — Sheet layout, kerf, labels and cut-file export (LuBan: shared Sheet, Tolerance, Text size and Nesting settings + Save model)

- **LuBan path:** settings shared by Contour, Stack, Hash and (per CN-GS p.18) Plate: Sheet width, Sheet height, Sheet thickness (§5.2.1, PDF p.99; Fig. 172); Nesting (§5.2.5, PDF p.101, reused by Stack §5.3 and Hash §5.4); 2D labels (§5.3.3, PDF pp.102–103); Save model (§5 intro). Video Lx5tmdVsGdk "LuBan 2D Nesting" (title only). The 2019 deck counts 2-D nesting (平面套料) as a core technology feeding laser cutting, beside 3-D nesting (立体套料) for printing (CN-IN p.3).
- **What it makes:** Turns the flat parts of a laser or CNC form into machine-ready sheets: parts nested on fixed-size sheets, labels engraved, kerf and fit applied, written as layered SVG and DXF plus an assembly guide.
- **Fabrication:** laser cutter (cut and engrave) or CNC router (cut, optional engrave); sheet stock such as plywood, cardboard or transparent sheet (Figs. 178, 183, 184, 188; CN-GS p.11, p.13). The owner's targets are the 3015 laser and the 1325 router (START_HERE); which materials go to which machine waits on the laser type (UNCONFIRMED, see the header note).
- **Inputs:** 2D part polygons with holes, engrave paths and labels from FORM-ETCHED, FORM-STACK, FORM-WAFFLE, FORM-WAFFLE-RADIAL and FORM-PANELS.
- **Parameters:**
