On a single-sided positive relief, 0 means no base at all (text typo: "singled-sided") | UNCONFIRMED | ≥ 0; figure values 0, 5, 30; Thermal's copy shown going 5 → 1 | §5.6.6; Figs. 205–206 (PDF p.111); video F20FZvL0r9g @08:00 |
| Border size | `frame_width_mm` | Determines "the appearance of the frame". In Fig. 207 a larger value gives a wider frame, so we read it as the frame's width. If it or Border thickness is 0, there is no frame | UNCONFIRMED | ≥ 0; figure values 0, 5, 20. Thermal describes its copy as "the extended region around the contour", shown going 5 → 10 → 1 | §5.6.7; Fig. 207 (PDF p.111); video F20FZvL0r9g @08:00 |
| Border thickness | `frame_height_mm` | Depth (height) of the frame. 0 means no frame | UNCONFIRMED | ≥ 0; figure values 0, 5, 20 | §5.6.7; Fig. 207 (PDF p.111) |
| Clearance (text and caption: "boundary clearance") | `frame_clearance_mm` | Shortest distance from the relief surface to the frame. More clearance makes the generated relief larger | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 5 and 20; range UNCONFIRMED | §5.6.8; Fig. 208 (PDF p.112) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `view_dir` | Any view direction (current camera or a direction gizmo) instead of pre-rotating the model | = `view_axis` | any unit vector | AD3D (suggest); removes the §5.6.1 limit |
| — (AD3D addition) | `resolution_mm` | Spacing between depth-map samples | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0.2 at full resolution, coarser while dragging) | (suggest: 0.05–2) | AD3D (suggest) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `depth_mapping` | Linear depth scaling (as LuBan appears to do) or gradient-domain bas-relief compression | (suggest: linear) | linear, compressed | AD3D; research 04 §B.6 (which mapping LuBan uses is UNCONFIRMED) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `wall_draft_deg` | Minimum draft of walls at depth jumps. 0 keeps vertical cliffs like LuBan | (suggest: 0) | (suggest: 0–45) | AD3D (suggest); Fig. 200; video F20FZvL0r9g @06:00 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `frame_chamfer_mm` | Size of the sloped inner edge of the frame | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 1) | ≥ 0 | AD3D (suggest); Figs. 200, 207 show a sloped inner edge |

- **Outputs:** one STL (§5.6). Print files are saved as STL or OBJ, and the scene as an FGD+FGS pair (§5 intro). The measure section shows the generated model's size (§5 intro). Whether relief, base and frame form one body is UNCONFIRMED. AD3D writes `<name>_relief.3mf` (one object, mm units) or a binary STL, plus an optional 16-bit depth image (`<name>_depth.png`).
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - Only six directions are available; any other direction needs Object → Transform first (§5.6.1).
  - A double-sided relief allows only +X, +Y and +Z, because -X/-Y/-Z is just the opposite side of the same relief (§5.6.2).
  - Model size and relief thickness together set the relief's X, Y and Z size (§5.6.4).
  - Bury hides parts of the relief so that the top-most part of the surface distribution stands out, and the base area is adjusted to the remaining area (§5.6.5). At 80 % only the cow's head is left, on a smaller framed base (Fig. 204, PDF p.110).
  - On a positive relief the base sits under the relief surface. On a negative relief it merges with the walls, so a negative relief looks thicker than a positive one with the same base thickness (§5.6.6; Fig. 205, PDF p.111).
  - Base thickness 0 on a single-sided positive relief gives a relief with no base (§5.6.6); Fig. 206 shows a bare swan relief.
  - If either border size or border thickness is 0, there is no frame (§5.6.7).
  - More clearance makes the generated relief larger (§5.6.8).
  - Jumps in depth become vertical walls: the +Z and -Z reliefs in Fig. 200 have tall cliffs. The Thermal video calls the resulting 90° edge slope a problem and uses bury to reduce it (video F20FZvL0r9g @06:00–07:00).
  - Figs. 200 and 207 show the frame's inner edge sloped (chamfered). Whether that slope is fixed or adjustable is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Thermal (Oct 2026) says its settings are "borrowed from a relief method", then walks through Direction, Relief thickness, Bury, Base thickness and Border size (video F20FZvL0r9g @04:00–08:00). So the height-field builder should be a shared core module, used by this entry and by THERMAL-FORM (part 6).
  - Text-box values take effect only after Enter (§1.8, PDF pp.15–16).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live preview, no Enter key.** Cache the depth map per (mesh, direction, resolution). Relief thickness, bury, polarity, base and frame then only remap the cached samples or redo cheap 2D work, so a preview mesh rebuilds on every slider tick within the ≤ 50 ms budget, and the full-resolution mesh follows on release. LuBan applies text-box values only on Enter (§1.8).
  - **Any direction.** Keep the six axis presets and add "use current view" plus a draggable direction gizmo. This removes the Object → Transform round trip (§5.6.1).
  - **Bury you can see.** Show a depth histogram with a draggable cut line, report the cut in mm as well as %, and let the user choose a percentile cut or a depth-range cut, since LuBan's definition is UNCONFIRMED (§5.6.5).
  - **Printable cliffs.** Offer optional gradient-domain compression (Weyrich et al. 2007; research 04 §A) and `wall_draft_deg`. Together they turn the 90° silhouette cliffs (Fig. 200; video F20FZvL0r9g @06:00) into slopes that print, and give a negative relief a release draft when it is used as a mold (§5.6.3).
  - **CNC-aware.** Add a ball-end preview: a morphological closing of the height field by the tool shape from the CNC machine profile (equivalently, an opening of the air above it) shows which valleys that cutter cannot reach. Export the height field as a 16-bit PNG/TIFF for CAM. The manual sends users to MasterCAM (§5.6), and full toolpaths stay in external CAM (research 08 §2.7 and §3).
  - **Laser.** Export a greyscale depth image for 3D/greyscale engraving, the laser route the blog mentions (blog: relief).
  - **Double-sided without supports.** Offer an optional split at the base's mid-plane into two flat-backed halves with registration pins, reusing the M3 connectors, so each half prints flat.
  - **Watertight by construction.** Build one closed shell directly from the height field (relief, base, frame and side walls, with no booleans). `validate()` plus a property test over randomised parameters covers every combination of sides × polarity × base × frame (CLAUDE.md).
  - **Scale-aware start.** Derive the starting depth, base and frame values from the model's size, and warn on tiny or unit-less imports. The Thermal video, which borrows these settings, had to rescue a tiny horse by retyping the model size (video F20FZvL0r9g @11:00).
  - **Exports and bed fit.** 3MF with mm units, streamed binary STL and a fit check against the printer bed in the machine profile (PLAN §4), plus automatic flat-on-bed orientation (ours).
  - **More inputs.** Accept a depth image (16-bit PNG/TIFF), or a photo converted to depth with Depth-Anything-V2-Small via `ort` (PLAN §1; PLAN §3 "Relief (AI depth)"). LuBan has a related video, "Photo to depth image by Depth Anything V2" (hZpYLAkktgg, title only).
  - **CLI/batch.** For example `ad3d bas-relief --axis +y --depth 20 in.stl -o out.3mf`, run over a folder (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Depth map:** orthographic depth rasterisation along the view direction gives a float height field plus a coverage mask. It runs in a Rust software z-buffer, with rayon over tiles. LuBan's own Mesh → Depth map utility does the same job: it takes a direction and a resolution and saves a float FLT image (§3.10.8, PDF p.83; blog: depth-map-of-a-3d-mesh, 2019-06-13). Whether Relief uses it internally is UNCONFIRMED.
  - **Height mapping:** normalise the depths, then clip at the bury threshold (whether LuBan then rescales is UNCONFIRMED), scale to the relief thickness, and invert for a negative relief (research 04 §B.6). Gradient-domain compression is optional (Weyrich et al. 2007; research 04 §A). References: wingated/digital-bas-relief (MIT), GistNoesis/StlToRelief (mesh to relief; licence NOASSERTION, so read it for reference only) and, for the photo input, opensourcecnc/CarveAnything (image to bas-relief; NOASSERTION, reference only) (research 03 §4).
  - **Mesh:** a direct height-field mesher shared with Squama and lithophane (research 08 §2.2; research 07 (a)), with vertical or drafted walls at the mask boundary. Base and frame outlines and the clearance come from Clipper2 offsets of the mask outline or of the chosen shape (research 03 §13).
  - **Double-sided:** build the front from the +axis view and the back from the -axis view, and stitch them through the base plate.
- **Milestone:** M6 (part 9, after TOOL-DEPTHMAP). PLAN §3 lists "Relief (AI depth)" under Later; part 9 moves it up because it reuses the M1/M2 height-field mesher. The photo/AI-depth input (TOOL-PHOTO-DEPTH) follows it.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Every default and every numeric range, plus the units (assumed to be the panel unit, mm).
  - The exact on-screen labels and control types (drop-down, radio button, check box, slider or text box) of every setting: the manual shows no Relief panel, so only the section headings and quoted text give the labels.
  - How bury is defined (a linear fraction of the depth range or a percentile), and whether the remaining relief is stretched back to the full relief thickness.
  - The full list of base shapes, and whether round bases are circles or ellipses fitted to the relief (Fig. 201 looks elliptical).
  - Whether the frame's inner slope can be changed.
  - LuBan's depth-map resolution, and whether it compresses depth (research 04 §B.6, §D).
  - In a double-sided relief: whether the relief thickness applies per side.
  - Whether the output is a single body.
  - The mirror convention: in Fig. 200 the +X and -X profiles face the same way.
  - How LuBan laser-engraves a relief (blog: relief).

#### FORM-SPIN — Wrap Array (LuBan: Spin)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → LuBan, Method = Spin (manual §5.7, PDF p.112; blog: _spin, 2020-04-09). Related videos (titles only): "LuBan Spin" (2WzKbtNaoyo, 6:00) and the user video "LuBan Spin, by Mike Settles at Eitri 3D" (7tuhpyU2VNs, 8:33).
- **What it makes:** Copies of the model, deformed and duplicated around a revolving axis (vertical in every figure) "to produce a spinning effect" (§5.7). The copies are bent onto a cylinder, cone, vase, sphere or spiral, and can be trimmed and joined by a cap ring and a base ring (§5.7.1, §5.7.10). The result "carries different forms and functions from the original model", e.g. a vase (§5.7; Fig. 209, PDF p.112).
- **Fabrication:**
  - **3D print:** Fig. 209 (PDF p.112) is a user's fluted vase made from a twisted bar.
  - **Defects:** low vertex density may give defects such as self-intersections, so apply Mesh → Densify first (§5.7; Fig. 210, PDF p.113). An unsuitable combination of arc angle and repeat may make copies intersect each other, and self-intersections are "hard to fix" (§5.7.7).
  - **Orientation:** the figures show the base ring at the bottom (Figs. 211–220; only the right model in Fig. 220 has a cap and no base), so print base-down (our reading). Sphere and cone overhangs may need supports (UNCONFIRMED).
- **Inputs:** one 3D mesh with "reasonable vertex density" (§5.7), in OBJ, PLY or STL format (Get started (zh) p.2).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit; Model size X / Y / Z | `input_size_mm` (AD3D: mm only) | Original model size, with the aspect ratio locked. Model size Z and Model thickness together set each copy's aspect ratio | the loaded model's size (UNCONFIRMED) | > 0 | §5 intro (PDF p.96); §5.7.9 |
| Spin shape | `shape` | The surface the copies are bent onto. Each shape has its own controls, and some controls are shared | UNCONFIRMED | cylinder, cone, vase, sphere, spiral (the five in Fig. 211; the text says "several", so whether more exist is UNCONFIRMED) | §5.7.1; Fig. 211 (PDF p.113) |
| Repeat | `repeat` | Number of copies. They are "equally spaced by default" and all deformed the same way | UNCONFIRMED | integer ≥ 1; figure values 1, 5, 11 (spiral) | §5.7.2; Fig. 212 (PDF p.113) |
| Direction | `facing` | Which direction of the original model points at the revolving axis | UNCONFIRMED | +X, -X, +Y, -Y | §5.7.3; Fig. 213 (PDF p.114) |
| Inner diameter | `inner_diameter_mm` | Size of the inner hole (cylinder, vase). Outer diameter = inner diameter + 2 × model thickness | UNCONFIRMED | > 0; figure values 50, 80 | §5.7.4; Fig. 214 (PDF p.114) |
| Top diameter (from "Top and Bottom diameter") | `top_diameter_mm` | Cone: inner diameter at the top | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 40 and 100 | §5.7.5; Fig. 215 (PDF p.114) |
| Bottom diameter | `bottom_diameter_mm` | Cone: inner diameter at the bottom. In Fig. 215 the base ring's hole follows it | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 100 and 40 | §5.7.5; Fig. 215 (PDF p.114) |
| Sphere angle | `sphere_angle_deg` | Sphere: vertical angular span of one copy | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 180°, 300°; limits UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 10–350°) | §5.7.6; Fig. 216 (PDF p.115) |
| Arc angle | `arc_angle_deg` | Horizontal angular span of one copy (cylinder, cone, vase, sphere) | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 30°, 90°, 150°. Copies collide when arc angle > 360°/repeat (our reading of §5.7.7) | §5.7.7; Fig. 217 (PDF p.115) |
| Separation | `spiral_gap_mm` | Spiral: gap between neighbouring copies along the spiral | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 10, 30, 50 | §5.7.8; Fig. 218 (PDF p.115) |
| Model thickness | `radial_thickness_mm` | Outer radius minus inner radius of each copy | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 10, 20, 30 | §5.7.9; Fig. 219 (PDF p.116) |
| Cap line | `cap_cut_pct` | Percent of the model cut off at the top, where a cap is attached. 0 means no cut and no cap | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0) | percent; figure values 0, 5, 10 | §5.7.10; Fig. 220 (PDF p.116) |
| Cap thickness | `cap_thickness_mm` | Thickness of the cap | UNCONFIRMED | figure value 5 | §5.7.10; Fig. 220 (PDF p.116) |
| Base line | `base_cut_pct` | Percent of the model cut off at the bottom, where a base is attached. 0 means no cut and no base | UNCONFIRMED | percent; figure values 0, 5, 10 | §5.7.10; Fig. 220 (PDF p.116) |
| Base thickness | `base_thickness_mm` | Thickness of the base | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 5, 10 | §5.7.10; Fig. 220 (PDF p.116) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `vase_profile` | Editable curve of inner radius against height, for the vase shape | (suggest: an S-curve like Fig. 211) | control points | AD3D (suggest); LuBan's vase lithophane uses control points (blog: lithophane-6th-release) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `spiral_pitch_mm`, `spiral_start_diameter_mm` | Spiral geometry, which the manual does not describe | UNCONFIRMED | > 0 | AD3D (suggest) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `start_angle_deg`, `spacing` | Rotation of the first copy; equal or custom spacing | (suggest: 0; equal) | equal, custom | AD3D (suggest); §5.7.2 "equally spaced by default" |
| — (AD3D addition) | `base_fill` | Base as a ring (as in LuBan's figures) or a solid disc for a vase with a closed bottom | (suggest: ring) | ring, disc | AD3D (suggest); Figs. 211–220 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `overlap_policy` | What to do when copies would collide | (suggest: warn) | warn, clamp, fuse | AD3D (suggest); §5.7.7 |

  Shape applicability, as stated in the manual:

| Control | Cylinder | Cone | Vase | Sphere | Spiral | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inner diameter | yes | – | yes | – | – | §5.7.4 |
| Top / Bottom diameter | – | yes | – | – | – | §5.7.5 |
| Sphere angle | – | – | – | yes | – | §5.7.6 |
| Arc angle | yes | yes | yes | yes | – | §5.7.7 |
| Separation | – | – | – | – | yes | §5.7.8 |
| Repeat, Direction, Model thickness, Cap / Base | not restricted by the text; which shapes use them is UNCONFIRMED. The figures show Repeat on the spiral (Fig. 212) and Model thickness on the vase (Fig. 219); the shapes in Figs. 213 and 220 are not named | | | | | §5.7.2–5.7.3, §5.7.9–5.7.10 |

- **Outputs:** STL or OBJ (§5 intro). The measure section shows the model's size (§5 intro). The figures draw the cap and base rings in a different colour from the copies (Figs. 211–220); whether LuBan exports one body or several is UNCONFIRMED. AD3D exports one fused, watertight body in 3MF (mm) or STL, with an option to write the rings as a separate 3MF object for two-colour prints.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The input needs reasonable vertex density, or the deformation may produce defects such as self-intersections; LuBan's answer is Mesh → Densify (§5.7). Fig. 210 shows a cylinder's long side triangles subdivided.
  - Copies are equally spaced by default (§5.7.2). With Repeat = 1, Fig. 212 shows a single copy on a sector of the spiral base.
  - Direction picks which side of the model faces the axis (§5.7.3). Fig. 213 shows statues facing in, out and sideways.
  - Outer diameter = inner diameter + 2 × model thickness (§5.7.4).
  - The cone's top and bottom diameters are inner diameters (§5.7.5).
  - An unsuitable arc angle and repeat may make copies intersect, and LuBan leaves this to the user to avoid ("set the arc angle and the repeat settings wisely", §5.7.7).
  - Model thickness and model size Z together set each copy's aspect ratio (§5.7.9).
  - Cap and base lines are percentages cut from the top and bottom; a line of 0 gives no cut and no cap or base (§5.7.10). Fig. 220 shows cap and base as rings matching the copies' annulus. The spiral shape uses a spiral-strip base (Figs. 212, 218).
  - In Fig. 218 the copies look narrower along the spiral as separation grows, at the same repeat (our observation; the rule is UNCONFIRMED).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **No manual Densify step.** Subdivide adaptively inside the generator: split edges until each bent edge stays within a chord tolerance of the true arc (suggest 0.05 mm), and only where the bend needs it (§5.7; Fig. 210).
  - **A collision guard instead of silent defects.** For cylinder, cone, vase and sphere, copies cannot touch while arc angle ≤ 360°/repeat, and the slider shows that limit. Past it, the user picks warn, clamp or fuse; fuse unions the overlapping copies into one valid solid with manifold (§5.7.7). For the spiral, check the pitch against the model thickness.
  - **Live while dragging.** For cylinder, cone, vase and sphere the copies are rotations of one another, so compute one bent copy (O(V), rayon) and draw it `repeat` times with GPU instancing. Spiral copies sit at different radii, so bend each copy in parallel instead. Either way, dragging shape, angles, diameters or thickness stays inside the 50 ms budget. The cut lines, rings and the union run on release.
  - **One watertight body.** Fuse the copies, cap and base with manifold. `validate()` plus a property test over randomised parameters runs in CI. Export 3MF with mm units (PLAN §4).
  - **A vase you can shape and fill.** Add a control-point profile editor and a solid-disc base option, so the Fig. 209 use case (a vase) can actually hold flowers.
  - **Physical readouts.** Show outer diameter, height and per-copy arc length in mm next to the controls. Save presets ("ring", "vase") in the project file, and expose the generator through the CLI (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Prepare the model:** rotate it about Z so the chosen ±X/±Y side faces the axis (§5.7.3). Apply the cap and base line cuts to the original height with manifold `splitByPlane`; whether LuBan cuts before or after bending is UNCONFIRMED. Then normalise the bounding box to u (tangential), v (radial) and w (height).
  - **Map each vertex onto the chosen shape:**
    - cylinder: θ = θₖ + u·arc, r = r_in + v·t, z = w·H;
    - cone: r_in(w) linear between the bottom and top inner radii;
    - vase: r_in(w) = profile(w);
    - sphere: spherical coordinates with elevation span = sphere angle. The radius is UNCONFIRMED; we suggest R = H / sphere angle in radians, which preserves length;
    - spiral: along an arc-length-parameterised spiral, with copies spaced by copy length + separation (UNCONFIRMED);
    - for cylinder, cone, vase and sphere, θₖ = k·360°/repeat (equal spacing, §5.7.2); spiral copies are spaced along the spiral instead (§5.7.8).
  - **Rings:** union an annulus (or a spiral strip) of the given thickness at the cut planes. Research 04 §B.15 summarises the method as "Spin (revolve, duplicate, deform)".
  - **Libraries:** manifold (Apache-2.0) for cuts and unions. Subdivision is our own midpoint split or pmp-library (MIT) (research 03 §13).
- **Milestone:** M11 (part 9, after THERMAL-FORM). It needs M3's manifold FFI and import repair: the bent copies are only watertight if the input is (PLAN §3 puts import and repair, "on the critical path for every mesh feature", in M3; research 08 §2.11).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Every default and range, and the units (assumed mm and degrees).
  - The vase profile: is it fixed or editable, and what are its controls? What does "inner diameter" mean on a vase?
  - What sets the sphere's radius?
  - The spiral: its type, pitch and start radius, and how separation trades off against copy width (Fig. 218).
  - Which of Repeat, Direction, Model thickness and Cap/Base apply to the sphere and spiral shapes.
  - Whether spacing can be non-equal (§5.7.2 says "by default").
  - Whether the cap and base are fused with the copies, and what outline they take for each shape.
  - Whether the cap and base lines cut the original model or the bent copies.
  - The exact on-screen labels and control types: the manual shows no Spin panel.
  - Related videos and methods not covered here:
    - LuBan's later "Spinner" (blog: spinner, 2025-07-28; video P6vR5tXJmvI, title only) is a separately announced method, specified as FORM-SPINNER (part 7).
    - "RingTutorial, made by LuBan user Amanda Napthine" (video dZKLQN9SFfA, title only; the same user made Fig. 209) may show Spin.

#### FORM-SPRING — Coil Shell (LuBan: Spring)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → LuBan, Method = Spring (manual §5.8, PDF p.116; blog: spring, 2020-04-29). Related video (title only): "LuBan Spring" (AJn9VmhlgkE, 4:03). The blog also links two third-party "Make Anything" videos on printing spring models (DQ1PZZgt28w, HgY7ovYWplg); they are not in the repo.
- **What it makes:** A layered, hollow version of the model that "can be compressed and stretched like a spring" (§5.8). Fig. 221 (PDF p.117) shows a printed moai pulled up into what looks like one continuous coil (our observation).
- **Fabrication:**
  - **FDM, no supports.** Set the separation to a multiple of the slicer's layer height so the gaps come out even, and keep the gap small. The layers bond only weakly, so you separate them by hand with a scraper after printing (§5.8.3; Fig. 225, PDF p.118).
  - **Filament:** with brittle filament use a larger thickness. Otherwise a small thickness makes the spring more flexible (§5.8.2).
  - **Overlap:** the layer width must be large enough for neighbouring layers to overlap, so no supports are needed (§5.8.1).
  - **Layer height:** the manual says it is often set to the nozzle radius (§5.8.3).
- **Inputs:** one 3D mesh (OBJ, PLY or STL; Get started (zh) p.2). If the model is hollow, its inner surface is ignored and the model is treated as solid (§5.8).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit; Model size X / Y / Z | `input_size_mm` (AD3D: mm only) | Original model size, with the aspect ratio locked | the loaded model's size (UNCONFIRMED) | > 0 | §5 intro (PDF p.96) |
| Layer width | `band_width_mm` | "Determines the width of the spring". Our reading of Fig. 222: the band's width, measured horizontally inward from the outer surface. Wider means stronger but less flexible | UNCONFIRMED | should not be smaller than Thickness; figure values 10, 20 | §5.8.1; Fig. 222 (PDF p.117) |
| Thickness | `band_thickness_mm` | Thickness of each layer (vertical, since the layers are horizontal in Figs. 222–224). Thicker means stronger but less flexible; choose it for the filament | UNCONFIRMED | figure values 2.5, 5, 10 | §5.8.2; Fig. 223 (PDF p.118) |
| Separation | `layer_gap_mm` | Gap between two layers. It should be a multiple of the slicer's layer height, which is a different thing from the spring's layer thickness | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 2 × layer height, e.g. 0.4) | figure values 0.4, 2, 4 | §5.8.3; Fig. 224 (PDF p.118) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `layer_height_mm` | The slicer's layer height, taken from the printer profile. Separation and Thickness snap to whole multiples of it | (suggest: 0.2) | > 0 | AD3D (suggest); §5.8.3 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `coil_form` | True helix, or flat rings joined by one ramp per turn | UNCONFIRMED which one LuBan builds | helix, ramped_rings | AD3D (suggest); Figs. 221–222 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `solid_end_layers` | Number of solid, unseparated layers at the bottom and top, for bed adhesion and a closed top | (suggest: 0) | ≥ 0 | AD3D (suggest); Fig. 221 shows the bottom staying behind as a base (UNCONFIRMED) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `axis` | Coil axis | (suggest: +Z) | +Z (the figures show horizontal layers) | AD3D (suggest); Figs. 222–224 |

- **Outputs:** STL or OBJ (§5 intro). The measure section shows the model's size (§5 intro). AD3D exports one watertight coil in 3MF (mm) or STL, together with the print checklist.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - A hollow input is treated as solid (§5.8).
  - Width should be at least the thickness, so neighbouring layers overlap and need no support (§5.8.1).
  - Separation should be a multiple of the layer height; otherwise the gaps between layers come out uneven (§5.8.3).
  - In practice no support is needed, and the layers come apart with a scraper (§5.8.3; Fig. 225).
  - At layer width 20 the top of the moai closes over; at 10 it shows a small opening (Fig. 222; our observation).
  - The bottom views in Fig. 222 show a seam where consecutive layers join, and Fig. 221 looks like one continuous coil (our observation). Whether the layers form a true helix or rings with joints is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Manual quirk: §5.8 cites "Figure 209" for the spring, but the spring figure is Fig. 221.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Slicer-aware numbers.** Take the layer height and nozzle from the printer profile, snap Separation and Thickness to whole layers, and show the result as e.g. "= 2 layers". The manual leaves this arithmetic to the user (§5.8.3).
  - **A support check you can see.** For each layer, compute the part of the band that does not sit over the band below (a plan-view difference with Clipper2). Show it in red with its overhang distance, and suggest the width that would fix it. This enforces the §5.8.1 overlap rule instead of only stating it. Width < thickness gets a warning.
  - **Live preview.** Slice the model once and cache the cross-sections. Changing width, thickness or separation then only redoes 2D offsets (Clipper2, rayon per layer), and the preview draws ring slabs. The joined, watertight coil is built on release.
  - **One watertight coil.** A defined, tested structure (one manifold band per island), checked by `validate()` and a property test over randomised parameters. Layers with several islands (arms, legs) are reported to the user, not silently exported as loose pieces.
  - **Hand-over checklist exported with the model.** It lists the layer height to use, "no supports", "separate the layers with a scraper" and a filament note (§5.8.2–5.8.3; CLAUDE.md hand-over rule). Export as 3MF with units, and expose the generator through the CLI.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Solid input:** slice the outer surface only. A winding-number inside test drops inner shells (libigl winding number; research 08 §2.10).
  - **Slicing:** slice at z_k = z₀ + k·(T + S), using manifold's slice or our own plane–mesh intersection shared with Stack (research 04 §B.2).
  - **Band per layer:** the cross-section minus its inward offset by W (Clipper2).
  - **Coil:** two options, to be decided in a spike:
    - (a) extrude each ring by T, cut a short radial slit, add a ramp joining ring k to ring k + 1, and union with manifold. This follows slicer layers exactly;
    - (b) intersect the shell with a helical slab of pitch T + S, defined as an SDF and meshed with manifold `levelSet`. This gives a true helix.
  - Research 04 §B.15 calls the method a "layered compressible shell".
- **Milestone:** M7 (part 9, after FORM-WIREFRAME-3D). It reuses M4's slicing and Clipper2 offset code.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - Helix or joined rings, and how and where the layers connect.
  - Every default and range, and whether the axis is always Z.
  - Whether layer width is measured horizontally or along the surface normal.
  - How the ends are treated (solid base or top).
  - What happens where the width exceeds the local half-width (Fig. 222 suggests the layer closes up), and with several islands in one layer.

#### FORM-WAVE — Ripple (LuBan: Wave)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → LuBan, Method = Wave (manual §5.9, PDF p.119; blog: _wave, 2019-09-21). The oscillation direction was added in 2020 (blog: wave-update, 2020-03-22). Related videos (titles only): "LuBan Wave 1/2/3" (zeegDNlWSSY 4:56, 1jaM4XxtiKo 2:25, 13wfjQ8_lIQ 2:16) and "LuBan Wave v2" (-QWOe2WU6VA 2:29).
- **What it makes:** Deforms a model with a wave form from one or more point sources, for effects such as ripples on a lithophane (§5.9; Fig. 226, PDF p.119). It can also save a sequence of states to make a wave-propagation video (§5.9.8).
- **Fabrication:** 3D print of the deformed model (STL/OBJ; §5 intro). Fig. 226 shows a printed wave-edited lithophane, both backlit and from the front. The model needs high vertex density, so densify it first (§5.9). High amplitude or a small wavelength may cause self-intersections (§5.9.4, §5.9.6).
- **Inputs:** one 3D mesh, often a lithophane made earlier (Fig. 226), in OBJ, PLY or STL format (Get started (zh) p.2).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit; Model size X / Y / Z | `input_size_mm` (AD3D: mm only) | Original model size. Amplitude and wavelength scale with its largest dimension | the loaded model's size (UNCONFIRMED) | > 0 | §5 intro (PDF p.96); §5.9.4, §5.9.6 |
| Oscillate in (heading: "Oscillate") | `oscillation` | X, Y, Z: a "2D spherical wave". Source: a "3D spherical wave". The text calls this the direction of wave propagation. The double-headed arrows in Fig. 227 and "oscillation direction" in blog: wave-update suggest it is the direction vertices move | UNCONFIRMED | X, Y, Z, source (exact option labels UNCONFIRMED) | §5.9.1; Fig. 227 (PDF p.119); blog: wave-update |
| Number of sources | `sources` (list) | How many point sources. Each has its own position, amplitude, attenuation, wavelength and phase | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 1) | ≥ 1; figures show 1, 2 and 4; maximum UNCONFIRMED | §5.9.2; Fig. 228 (PDF p.120) |
| Adjust source | `active_source` (UI state, not a generator input) | Picks which source the controls edit. The selected source is drawn as a red sphere, the others cyan | UNCONFIRMED | 1…N (whether indices start at 0 or 1 is UNCONFIRMED) | §5.9.2; Fig. 228 (PDF p.120) |
| X, Y, Z (sliders) | `sources[i].position` | Position of the source. Each slider is normalised to [-1, 1] (relative to the model's bounding box: UNCONFIRMED) | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0, 0, 0) | [-1, 1] per axis | §5.9.3 (PDF p.120) |
| Amplitude | `sources[i].amplitude` | Wave amplitude, proportional to the model's largest dimension and set as a normalised factor. High values deform the model a lot and can self-intersect | UNCONFIRMED | 1–10; figure values 1, 5, 10 | §5.9.4; Fig. 229 (PDF p.120) |
| Attenuation | `sources[i].attenuation` | How fast the amplitude drops along the direction of propagation. 0 means no drop | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0) | ≥ 0; figure values 0, 5, 10; upper limit UNCONFIRMED | §5.9.5; Fig. 230 (PDF p.121) |
| Wavelength | `sources[i].wavelength` | Wavelength, proportional to the model's largest dimension and set as a normalised factor. Small values can self-intersect | UNCONFIRMED | The text says 1–10, but Fig. 231 shows 2, 10 and 20 (they conflict) | §5.9.6; Fig. 231 (PDF p.121) |
| Phase | `sources[i].phase_deg` (LuBan's control takes a step index) | Phase of the wave form: an integer 0–35, meaning 0–350° in 10° steps | UNCONFIRMED (suggest: 0) | LuBan 0–35; figure values 0, 9, 18 (0°, 90°, 180°); AD3D 0–360° continuous | §5.9.7; Fig. 232 (PDF p.121) |
| Save model (with sequence option) | `sequence` {`property`, `frames`, `from`, `to`} | Saves the current model and, optionally, a series of models while one property of the selected source changes, for making a video | (suggest: off) | property: position, amplitude, attenuation, wavelength, phase. Frame count and value range UNCONFIRMED | §5.9.8 (PDF p.121) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `units_mode`, `amplitude_mm`, `wavelength_mm` | Enter amplitude and wavelength in mm, or as LuBan-style normalised factors | (suggest: mm) | normalised, mm | AD3D (suggest); §5.9.4, §5.9.6 |
| — (AD3D addition) | `max_edge_mm` | Target edge length for automatic subdivision | (suggest: shortest wavelength / 8) | > 0 | AD3D (suggest); §5.9 (Densify note) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `decay_law` | Law for attenuation | (suggest: exponential) | exponential, inverse_distance | AD3D (suggest); §5.9.5 gives no law |

- **Outputs:** the deformed model as STL/OBJ (§5 intro), plus an optional sequence of models (§5.9.8; file naming UNCONFIRMED). The measure section shows the model's size (§5 intro). AD3D exports 3MF/STL, plus optional PNG frames or an STL/3MF sequence.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The source is drawn as a red sphere. With several sources, the selected one is red and the others cyan (§5.9.1–5.9.2).
  - Each source has its own parameters (§5.9.2), and several sources interfere: Fig. 228 shows overlapping ring patterns. How they combine is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Amplitude and wavelength are proportional to the model's largest dimension (§5.9.4, §5.9.6), so the look does not depend on scale (our inference).
  - High amplitude or a short wavelength may make the surface self-intersect (§5.9.4, §5.9.6); Fig. 229 at 10 and Fig. 231 at 2 show torn, jagged surfaces.
  - Phase moves in 10° steps (§5.9.7).
  - X, Y and Z are sliders (§5.9.3). §1.8 makes text boxes the only controls that need Enter; every other change updates the display at once.
  - In Fig. 227: Y puts rings on the face perpendicular to Y, X makes the side face wavy, Z makes the top wavy, and Source puts rings around the source (our observation).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Real-time GPU preview.** The displacement is analytic, so a vertex shader can show it at display rate while any control is dragged, including phase animation. The CPU builds the final subdivided mesh on release.
  - **Direct manipulation.** Drag source spheres across the model's surface in the viewport instead of setting three normalised sliders per source (§5.9.3). Add or remove a source with a click.
  - **Physical units.** Amplitude and wavelength in mm, with the normalised 1–10 factors kept as an option. This also sidesteps the range conflict between §5.9.6 and Fig. 231.
  - **Continuous phase** from 0 to 360°, instead of 10° steps (§5.9.7).
  - **No manual Densify step.** Subdivide adaptively to an edge length ≤ λ/8, and only where the displacement is non-negligible (§5.9).
  - **Fold guard.** Warn when the local slope 2π·A/λ (after attenuation) reaches about 1, run a BVH self-intersection test before export, and offer "clamp to fold-free amplitude" (§5.9.4, §5.9.6).
  - **Animation export.** Keyframe any parameter of any source; LuBan varies one property of the selected source (§5.9.8). Export rendered PNG frames, including the lithophane backlight preview, and/or an STL/3MF sequence. Frames are generated in parallel and the job can be cancelled.
  - **As a height-field modifier.** In lithophane and relief jobs, apply the ripple to the height field before meshing. A ripple lithophane (Fig. 226) then needs no dense remesh and stays watertight by construction.
  - **Watertight by construction.** Displacement keeps the mesh topology, and `validate()`, the self-intersection test and a property test over randomised parameters back this up.
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Displacement (our reconstruction, UNCONFIRMED):**
    - Axis modes (e ∈ {X, Y, Z}): p′ = p + e·Σᵢ Aᵢ·g(αᵢ, rᵢ)·sin(2π·rᵢ/λᵢ − φᵢ). Here rᵢ is the distance from source i measured in the plane perpendicular to e, which gives a circular ("2D spherical") wave.
    - Source mode: rᵢ = |p − sᵢ|, and vertices move along (p − sᵢ)/rᵢ, which gives a 3D spherical wave.
    - Scaling: Aᵢ = aᵢ·D·k_A and λᵢ = wᵢ·D·k_λ, where D is the model's largest dimension (§5.9.4, §5.9.6). Fit k_A and k_λ to Figs. 229–231 (suggest λ ≈ w·D/30).
    - Decay: suggest g = exp(−α·r/D).
  - Research 04 §B.15 summarises Wave as "point-source sinusoidal displacement".
  - **Building blocks:** rayon per vertex; adaptive midpoint subdivision (our own, or pmp-library, MIT); a BVH triangle–triangle self-intersection test (our own, or manifold's status check).
- **Milestone:** M6 (part 9, after FORM-RELIEF). It is small, and the height-field form can ship as a lithophane modifier once M2 exists.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - The exact displacement formula, the attenuation law, how sources combine, and the sign of the phase.
  - The scaling constants for amplitude and wavelength, and the wavelength range (§5.9.6 says 1–10, but Fig. 231 shows 20).
  - Whether "oscillate in" is the direction of propagation (the text) or of displacement (the Fig. 227 arrows; blog: wave-update).
  - The maximum number of sources, the attenuation range, and what [-1, 1] is normalised to.
  - Sequence export: frame count, value range and file naming.
  - Whether the wave moves every vertex or only some (for example only a lithophane's front face).

#### FORM-WIREFRAME-2D — Wire Drawing for laser (LuBan: Wireframe, 2D)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → LuBan, Method = Wireframe, 2D (manual §5.10, §5.10.1, PDF pp.122–123; blog: 2d-wireframe, 2019-03-17). The Chinese Get-started guide shows its panel as method "线框压印" ("wireframe imprint"; Get started (zh) pp.26–29). That panel has no 2D/3D choice; the deck (2019-03-19) predates the 3D wireframe post (blog: 3d-wireframe, 2019-05-15). Related videos (titles only): "LuBan Wireframe" (by8r-dpDmU4, 4:22; _43C9sgVzN8, 1:03).
- **What it makes:** A 2D vector drawing of section lines on the model's surface for laser engraving, with a red boundary to cut. The engraved sheet gives "a projected 3D effect" (§5.10; Fig. 233, PDF p.122). The saved file adds the boundary line and a base socket (§5.10.1; Fig. 235 centre, PDF p.123).
- **Fabrication:**
  - **Laser:** in the laser program, cut the red line (the boundary) and engrave the black lines (§5.10.1).
  - **Example:** Fig. 233 and Get started (zh) p.29 (the same two photos; Fig. 233 credits LuBan user Thomas Pascoe) show a clear acrylic sheet, engraved, standing in a lit base and glowing from its bottom edge.
  - **Socket:** the manual calls it "the base socket" (§5.10.1), and Fig. 235 (centre) draws it as a rectangular tab at the bottom of the boundary. In Fig. 233 the lying-flat photo shows a tab on the sheet's bottom edge, and the standing photo shows the sheet in a lit base (our observation). Contour's "Base light socket" is the same idea: "an extended region at the bottom of a frame … used to insert a frame to the socket of a base light", with user-set width and height (§5.2.4, PDF p.100; research 04 §B.3). Whether Wireframe's tab size can be set is UNCONFIRMED; the 2019 panel has no tab setting (Get started (zh) pp.26–27).
- **Inputs:** one 3D mesh (OBJ, PLY or STL; Get started (zh) p.2).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

In the 2D wireframe screenshot the boxes look greyed out (98.5 / 76.7 / 70.2), so whether they can be edited for this method is UNCONFIRMED | the loaded model's size (UNCONFIRMED) | > 0 | §5 intro (PDF p.96); Get started (zh) p.26 |
| 2D vs. 3D | `mode` (AD3D splits this into two generators: `wire_drawing` / `wire_lattice`) | Laser drawing or printed lattice; the two versions "work quite differently". The 2019 panel has no such control and makes only the 2D drawing | UNCONFIRMED | 2D, 3D | §5.10, §5.10.1 (PDF p.122); Get started (zh) pp.26–27 |

Radial: vertical planes around a rotation axis parallel to Z, plus horizontal Z layers | UNCONFIRMED (Orthogonal is selected in Get started (zh) p.26) | orthogonal, radial (radio buttons in the 2019 panel) | §5.10; §5.4.2 (PDF p.104); Fig. 190; Get started (zh) pp.14, 26–27 |

In radial mode, the number of vertical planes around the axis: for the radial grid, X and Z count the "vertical and horizontal slices" | UNCONFIRMED (24 shown) | integer slider whose label shows its value ("X 层数: 24"); range UNCONFIRMED (the handle positions suggest a maximum near 75–80 if the minimum is 0: inferred, not stated) | §5.10; §5.4.3 (PDF p.104); Get started (zh) pp.15, 26 |

Whether Wireframe has this control is UNCONFIRMED: it is absent from Get started (zh) p.27 |

Compare Contour's "boundary clearance", "the shortest distance from a frame to a set of contours" (§5.2.3) | UNCONFIRMED (5 shown) | text box, so it needs Enter; ≥ 0 (UNCONFIRMED) | Get started (zh) pp.26–27; §5.2.3 (PDF p.100); not in the manual's §5.10 |

- **Outputs:** DXF, SVG and SHP. Red lines are the boundary (cut) and black lines are engraved (§5.10.1; §5 intro). In the 2019 build the save button is labelled "压印" ("Imprint"), in place of 导出部件 ("Export parts"), and the export folder holds DXF and SVG vector drawings "for laser cutting and engraving" (Get started (zh) pp.26–28). AD3D writes SVG and DXF with named CUT and ENGRAVE layers. It writes no SHP, which is LuBan's own format.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The live preview shows the wire lines on the model but not the boundary or socket, because those take too long to compute in real time. Only the saved file has everything (§5.10.1; Fig. 235 left vs centre).
  - The 2D preview draws only the lines on the visible side of the model, while the 3D preview draws all of them (Fig. 235 left vs right; Get started (zh) pp.26–28; our observation).
  - The sources show different boundaries (our observation):
    - the 2019 guide's saved drawing: an offset that follows the outline, with no tab (Get started (zh) p.28);
    - the 2025 manual's saved drawing: a hull-like polygon with a rectangular tab at the bottom (Fig. 235 centre);
    - the user's sheet shown in both (Fig. 233 = Get started (zh) p.29): a boundary that follows the letter outline, with a tab at the bottom.

    So whether the boundary type depends on the version, a setting or the model is UNCONFIRMED.
  - Y layers exist only in orthogonal mode (§5.10; Get started (zh) p.27).
  - The layer counts and the tilt are sliders ("drag the scroll bars to change the number of wireframe lines in each direction", Get started (zh) p.26), so by §1.8 they update without Enter. Boundary spacing is a text box and needs Enter (§1.8; Get started (zh) p.6: "after changing a number in a text box, press Enter to update the model").
  - The 2019 panel's measure section lists parts, machining time, assembly time and total time, but all four stay blank for this method (Get started (zh) pp.26–27). The 2025 manual's measure list does not mention Wireframe (§5 intro).
  - The settings are "similar to" Hash (§5.10): the radial axis is parallel to Z and positioned by center X/Y (§5.4.2), layers are evenly spaced (§5.4.3), and tilt gives an artistic result (§5.4.4). See FORM-WAFFLE and FORM-WAFFLE-RADIAL (Hash, §5.4) elsewhere in this spec; their keys for the same settings are `x_layers`, `z_layers`, `fin_count`, `radial_center_x` / `radial_center_y` and `tilt_deg`.
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Live cut line and tab.** An outline or hull offset with Clipper2 takes milliseconds, so the boundary and socket appear in the live preview. LuBan leaves them out as too slow (§5.10.1).
  - **Laser-ready files.** SVG/DXF with named CUT/ENGRAVE layers and colours. The kerf/2 offset from the machine profile is applied to the cut boundary (socket tab included) only, never to engraved lines, so the tab comes out at its nominal width and height for the base's socket (research 08 §2.6; PLAN §4).
  - **A matching stand.** An optional printable or laser-cut light base, with a slot sized from the measured sheet thickness plus a fit allowance.
  - **Any view.** The drawing follows the current camera or typed view angles, in orthographic or perspective projection. LuBan's view rule is UNCONFIRMED; Fig. 233 is an oblique view.
  - **Clean hidden lines.** A depth-buffer visibility test runs along each polyline and splits segments where visibility changes, so lines end cleanly at silhouettes. Engrave paths are ordered to cut down travel, with a time estimate from the laser profile.
  - **Boundary choice.** Outline offset or hull offset, with the margin in mm. These are the two LuBan variants (Get started (zh) p.28 vs Fig. 235).
  - **Fast lines at high layer counts.** Plane–mesh intersections use a BVH, with rayon across planes, so line updates stay ≤ 50 ms at typical sizes.
  - **CLI/batch** (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Layer planes:** orthogonal (X/Y/Z), or radial (vertical planes through an axis parallel to Z, plus horizontal planes), rotated by the tilt (§5.4.2–5.4.4).
  - **Section lines:** plane–mesh intersections chained into polylines, using the same code as Stack and Hash (research 04 §B.2, §B.4, §B.8).
  - **Projection:** project the lines to the view plane and remove hidden lines with a z-buffer.
  - **Boundary:** an outline or hull offset (Clipper2) plus the socket tab. SVG/DXF writers come from PLAN §1 (io). Research 00 §3 sums up the method as "Hash-style section curves → engrave drawing".
- **Milestone:** M7 (part 9, first in its row). PLAN §3 lists wireframe under Later; part 9 places it right after M4, since it reuses the Hash layer system, SVG/DXF export and kerf handling.
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - How the drawing is projected: the current view or an axis view, orthographic or perspective.
  - How the boundary is built, how big the socket tab is, and whether either depends on the sheet thickness.
  - Which boundary current LuBan draws (outline offset or hull-like polygon), and whether the socket tab is always added or can be switched off.
  - The English label and the range of 边界间距 (boundary spacing).
  - Whether Wire thickness changes the 2D output.
  - Whether Wireframe has radial center X/Y.
  - Defaults and ranges for every layer count and for tilt (the screenshot shows 24/27/21 and 0°).
  - Whether silhouette or outline lines are engraved as well as the section lines.

#### FORM-WIREFRAME-3D — Wire Lattice for printing (LuBan: Wireframe, 3D)

- **LuBan path:** Mesh → LuBan, Method = Wireframe, 3D (manual §5.10–5.10.2, PDF pp.122–123; blog: 3d-wireframe, 2019-05-15). The related videos are the same as for FORM-WIREFRAME-2D.
- **What it makes:** A hollow wire structure for 3D printing whose wires follow section lines of the model's surface (§5.10; Fig. 234, PDF p.122; Fig. 236, PDF p.123).
- **Fabrication:**
  - Print with no supports. With enough layers, the printer can bridge every gap (§5.10.1).
  - Thicker wire prints more easily. Thinner wire suits a dense wireframe with many layers (§5.10.2).
  - Fig. 234 is a user's print of a torso in yellow filament (material UNCONFIRMED).
- **Inputs:** one 3D mesh (OBJ, PLY or STL; Get started (zh) p.2).
- **Parameters:**

| LuBan label | AD3D key | Meaning | Default | Range / options | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit; Model size X / Y / Z | `input_size_mm` (AD3D: mm only) | Original model size, with the aspect ratio locked | the loaded model's size (UNCONFIRMED) | > 0 | §5 intro (PDF p.96) |
| 2D vs. 3D | `mode` = 3d (AD3D generator `wire_lattice`) | Selects the printed lattice | UNCONFIRMED | 2D, 3D | §5.10.1 (PDF p.122) |
| Orthogonal vs. Radial | `layout` | Same as FORM-WIREFRAME-2D: planes perpendicular to X/Y/Z, or vertical planes around a Z-parallel axis plus Z layers | UNCONFIRMED | orthogonal, radial | §5.10; §5.4.2 (PDF p.104); Get started (zh) pp.14, 26–27 |
| X layer / Y layer / Z layer | `x_layers`, `y_layers`, `z_layers` | Number of evenly spaced planes per direction. Y exists in orthogonal mode only. In radial mode, X counts the vertical planes around the axis | UNCONFIRMED | integers; ranges UNCONFIRMED | §5.10; §5.4.3 (PDF p.104); Get started (zh) pp.15, 26–27 |
| Tilt | `tilt_deg` | Rotates the planes | UNCONFIRMED | the Hash figures use 20°, 45°; range UNCONFIRMED | §5.10; §5.4.4; Fig. 192 (PDF p.105) |
| Center X / Center Y (Hash, radial mode) | `radial_center` [x, y] | Position of the radial axis. Whether Wireframe has it is UNCONFIRMED | UNCONFIRMED | looks normalised (our reading of Fig. 190) | §5.4.2; Fig. 190 (PDF p.104); blog: radial-center-adjustment |
| Wire thickness (caption: "Thickness") | `wire_thickness` | Normalised wire thickness. Choose small for dense wireframes with many layers, large for easier printing | UNCONFIRMED | 1–5 (whether only whole numbers is UNCONFIRMED); figure values 1, 3, 5 | §5.10.2; Fig. 236 (PDF p.123) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `wire_diameter_mm` | Wire diameter in mm, with a minimum taken from the nozzle (suggest ≥ 2 × nozzle width) | (suggest: 2.0) | > 0 | AD3D (suggest); PLAN §4 machine profiles |
| — (AD3D addition) | `wire_profile` | Wire cross-section | (suggest: round) | round, square | AD3D (suggest); the wires in Fig. 236 look round (our observation) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `wire_placement` | Wires centred on the surface, or inset by their radius so the outer silhouette keeps the model's size | (suggest: inset) | centered, inset | AD3D (suggest) |
| — (AD3D addition) | `max_bridge_mm` | Longest unsupported span the printer can bridge, from the printer profile | from the profile | > 0 | AD3D (suggest); §5.10.1 |

- **Outputs:** STL or OBJ (§5 intro). The preview draws lines without thickness, so you have to save to see the real wireframe (§5.10.1; Fig. 235 right). AD3D exports one watertight lattice in 3MF (mm) or STL.
- **Behaviour and rules:**
  - The preview shows lines only (Fig. 235 right). The real wires appear only after saving (§5.10.1).
  - No supports are needed; with enough layers the printer bridges the gaps (§5.10.1).
  - The layer settings are the same as in 2D (§5.10).
  - Figs. 235 (right) and 236 show the radial layout: meridians meeting at the top and bottom poles, plus horizontal rings (our observation).
  - In radial mode the wires crowd together near the poles: the dense "star" in Fig. 235 right and the converging wires in Fig. 234, where the thick printed wires merge into a dense knot (our observation).
- **How we will do it better:**
  - **Real wires while dragging.** Draw instanced cylinders and node spheres at the chosen diameter on the GPU, which stays cheap at any layer count. The exact union runs in the background on release, with progress and cancel. LuBan only shows the real wires after saving (§5.10.1).
  - **Diameter in mm.** Wire diameter in mm, with a nozzle-aware minimum from the printer profile. The normalised 1–5 scale stays as an option (§5.10.2).
  - **Bridge check.** Measure each unsupported span between crossings, flag any span longer than the profile's maximum bridge, and suggest more layers. This turns "count on a 3D printer to bridge" (§5.10.1) into a check.
  - **Pole thinning.** In radial mode, merge or trim meridians near the poles where neighbouring wires would overlap by more than one diameter.
  - **Watertight by construction.** Either mesh one implicit surface (the union of capsule SDFs, meshed by dual contouring or manifold `levelSet`) or run a native, multi-threaded manifold batch union. Both give one closed shell with consistent winding, checked by `validate()` and a property test over randomised parameters. Research 08 §1.4 measured single-threaded WASM unions as slow, so this runs natively on all cores.
  - **Loose-wire report.** Flag wire pieces that do not connect to the main structure. Hash has the same problem with contours that do not interlock (§5.4.3).
  - **Exports.** Fit-to-bed check, 3MF with units, and the CLI (PLAN §4).
- **Algorithm / building blocks:**
  - **Polylines:** the same section polylines as FORM-WIREFRAME-2D, simplified with Douglas–Peucker, or with the mesh pre-decimated by meshoptimizer (research 03 §8, §13).
  - **Tubes:** sweep each polyline into a tube with sphere joints, then union them with manifold (Apache-2.0) or take the SDF route. Research 04 §B.8: "sweep each section polyline as a tube or square wire of normalized thickness 1–5 and union them". Research 00 §3: "sweep tubes → union".
  - **Not a fit:** the OSS in research 03 §8 (osresearch `wireframe.c`, TrussFab) builds strut-and-node lattices, which is a different structure; so does the dowel-and-printed-node lattice of Dritsas, Chen & Sass 2017, which research 04 §A says "works differently" from LuBan's Wireframe. Use them as references only. That structure is closer to LuBan's later Pipe method ("a structure made of pipes and connectors", blog: _pipe, 2021-09-08), specified as FORM-PIPE (part 7).
- **Milestone:** M7 (part 9, after FORM-WIREFRAME-2D). FORM-WIREFRAME-2D provides the section curves. It needs the manifold FFI (M3) and the Hash layer system (M4).
- **UNCONFIRMED / open questions:**
  - How the normalised thickness 1–5 maps to mm.
  - The wire cross-section, and how joints at crossings are shaped.
  - Whether the wires sit centred on the surface or inset.
  - Whether the result is a single body.
  - Every default and range.

### Part 5 notes

#### Related blog-only method: Voronoi wireframe (specified elsewhere)

The blog's "Voronoi wireframe" ("Generate a Voronoi wireframe model from a 3D model", blog: voronoi-wireframe, 2025-01-15; video Pt9ssfggSMM "LuBan Voronoi wireframe", 10:16, title only, no transcript in the repo) is not in the manual, whose §5.10 covers only the 2D and 3D wireframe. It is specified once, as FORM-VORONOI (part 7), so it has no entry here. Two notes for that entry from this section (ours): reuse FORM-WIREFRAME-3D's tube pipeline (instanced live preview, watertight union, bridge check), and consider a `domain` option (cells on the surface only, or through the volume).

## 6. Projection family, Thermal, Mold and Create objects

This section covers LuBan features that the Aug-2025 manual does not document: the File → Create → Projection family (Squama, Fence, the slide projector, Pandora, plus Moire and Lenticule), the other items of the 3D window's File → Create submenu (3D shape, Bamboo-copter, Bottle, Dice, Eyeglasses, Glider), and two 2026 mesh methods for forming and casting (Thermal, Mold). Shadow Plate (PROJ-SQUAMA, milestone M1) is specified to implementation depth from the Squama video's narration and frames, our two Python prototypes and a re-run of their shading study; Fence, Projection and Thermal come from video transcripts; everything else rests on one-line blog posts and channel titles, so most of those parameters are UNCONFIRMED. Lithophane and Photo magic, the remaining Create items, are specified in parts 2 and 3, the app shell (launcher, viewport light, size snapping, export) in part 1, the manual's Cocoon, Plate and Relief methods that Thermal and Mold cross-reference in part 5, and other blog-only features in part 7.

**Conventions used in this section**
- Video sources: Wd26qsSIRY8 = "LuBan Squama" (captions `docs/research/squama-video/captions.txt`, research 01); `f_NNN` = frame `docs/research/squama-video/frames/f_NNN.jpg`, taken at (NNN−1)×4 s (f_060 = 3:56). VA67Jm3ijHg = "LuBan Projection", t2-1zMjWUAw = "LuBan Fence", F20FZvL0r9g = "LuBan Thermal" (transcripts in `docs/research/channel/subs/`, one-minute blocks, cited by the minute the block starts: "@2:00" = block [00:02]). Inside an entry whose LuBan path names one video, a bare "@m:ss" refers to that video. `channel: <id>` = title, length and approximate date only (`docs/research/channel/videos_dated.txt`).
- Other sources: `blog: <slug>` = `docs/research/luban-blog/posts-all.txt`; `§x.y (PDF p.N)` = the manual (PDF page = printed page + 1, where the printed page is the number in the page footer; the TOC's page numbers run 5 lower, e.g. §5.1.4 is TOC p.92, footer 97, PDF p.98); `luban-docs Get started p.N` / `luban-docs Introduction p.N` = the 2018–19 Chinese decks in `docs/reference/luban-docs/`, read through `docs/wip/spec-sections/00-luban-docs-notes.md` (cited as "luban-docs notes §N"; the decks cover only old mesh methods, so for this section they give UI conventions, units and export-folder facts, never Projection or Squama behaviour); `papers/CAD16`, `papers/CAD19` = `docs/research/papers/CAD16-chen-sass.txt`, `CAD19-chen-sass.txt`.
- "Initial value" = what a panel showed when the video first opened it. LuBan stores "parameters in many functions" in its settings file and reloads them at start (§1.6, PDF p.14; the install video says LuBan will "remember the last used settings", video DzvYxTm8pbo @8:00), so an initial value may be a remembered value rather than a factory default.
- "Ours", "our reading", "— (ours)" and "(suggest: …)" mark AD3D proposals and interpretations, never LuBan facts. "Ours (sim)" marks numbers from our pure-Python re-run of the prototype shading study (`prototypes/squama-centre-pivot/shadow.py`, `shadow2.py`): the same synthetic target image as `squama.py`, 300 mm wide, cell 6 (50 × 63 cells), 32 samples per cell, horizon-sweep cast shadows, "match" = Pearson correlation between target grey and simulated cell brightness. The re-run scripts are not in the repo; a second run during the fact-check reproduced every number quoted here.
- Clean room: the binary-derived listings in research 02 §2–4 and the matching feature list in research 00 §2 (menu groups, Projection sub-modes, Create items, Squama setting names, file formats read from LuBan's executables) are not used as sources, and sub-modes or items known only from them get no entry; where research and video disagree, the video wins (research 08 §2.1).

### PROJ-SQUAMA — Shadow Plate (LuBan: Projection → Squama)
- **LuBan path:** File → Create → Projection, then Mode = Squama (video Wd26qsSIRY8 @3:36–3:56; f_055, f_060). Narration: "the squama is under the projection menu. It is a projection method" (@3:44–3:50). Released 2026-10-01 (blog: squama, "Generate a projection image based on a structure of squama pattern."). The name means fish scale; the author avoided "scale" because it means size in 3D printing (@3:21–3:41).
- **What it makes:** One photo becomes one solid plate covered with a grid of small flat facets, each tilted by a different amount. Under one low, grazing light from the designed side each facet reads lighter or darker according to its tilt, and the photo appears; under room or ambient light alone the plate looks almost blank (@0:44–1:06, @13:02–13:25; research 01 §2). It automates an artist's hand-glued wooden "shadow" panels (@1:17–3:20), whose pieces "are all the same color", so the image comes from light and shadow only (Instagram caption in f_046).
- **Fabrication:**
  - 3D printing (FDM). Print the plate standing up "to get the maximum resolution", "just as with a lithophane" (the captions mishear the word as "a little thing"; research 01 §2); printed flat on the bed the tilted facets come out poorly (@10:09–10:40). The manual explains why for lithophanes: filament is laid continuously in X and Y but in discrete layers in Z, so an upright plate keeps richer depth variation; it also suggests 30–50 mm/s instead of 80–100 mm/s, layer height = half the nozzle diameter, tight belts and a clean extruder (§2.23, PDF p.43–45; applies here by the author's analogy).
  - With Top/Bottom light and a large surface angle, the steps between rows need support when printed upright (@9:30–10:07).
  - Facet relief is only about 0.35–0.7 mm; cells under about 3 mm may not read (PLAN §6, UNCONFIRMED; research 08 §2.5). That range is the cell 4 / S = 10° case: (cell/2) × tan S for a centre pivot up to cell × tan S for a low-corner pivot. At LuBan's initial cell 6 / 10° it is 0.53–1.06 mm, and at the video's final cell 4 / 20° it is 0.73–1.46 mm (ours).
  - Owner's printer: Creality CR-6 SE, 235 × 235 × 250 mm, bed moves in Y, so a tall thin plate should stand with its face parallel to Y (START_HERE, owner's machines). LuBan's plate at its default width (300 mm; 300 × 378 for the 4:5 Mona Lisa, f_060 → f_066) does not fit upright (research 08 §2.4), nor flat (300 > 235 mm); even the video's final 200 × 252 plate (f_225) is 2 mm taller than the 250 mm Z when stood up (ours, from START_HERE). See PROJ-SQUAMA-TILE.
  - Display: no room light (under room light "you see nothing on the panel") and one light "installed close to the panel at a small incision [incidence] angle" from one specific direction, the side the plate was designed for (@13:02–13:28, describing the artist's set-up, which the plate copies). The result "depends on the quality of your print and also how you install the light" (@14:44–14:50).
  - Material and colour: UNCONFIRMED for LuBan (suggest: matte white or light-grey PLA; ours). The source artwork needs no surface pattern: the artist's wood grain "doesn't matter. You can use any pattern or you can use a panel without pattern" (@2:15–2:31), and his pieces "are all the same color" (f_046).
- **Inputs:** One photo, any subject ("You can select any photo", @3:58; the demo loads `MonaLisa.jpg`, f_062), loaded with "Shadow: Browse" into a "Select image" dialog whose filter reads "All supported format (*.bmp;*." followed by a clipped character (f_065 @4:16; research 01 read it as "*.j…"; the rest of the list is cut off). The input is a 2D photo, not a mesh (research 01 §2). LuBan's colour-to-grey conversion: UNCONFIRMED. Ours: PNG, JPEG, BMP, TIFF and WebP, with the EXIF orientation applied on import; HEIC UNCONFIRMED (suggest: through the macOS image decoder, Later).
